#3205. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3203. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3198. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3196. Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined – update both ASAP

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The latest version of Firefox fixes 167 security vulnerabilities, most of which are of high severity, while the newest version of Chrome patches 52 flaws, four of which are critical.

With security vulnerabilities continually plaguing the software we use, it’s time once again to update both Firefox and Chrome browsers to protect yourself from the latest exploits.

Also: Half of all cyberattacks start in your browser: 10 tips for staying safe

This week, Mozilla updated Firefox to version 159, not just for Windows but also for Android, MacOS, and Linux. The latest version includes fixes for 167 security bugs. Among these, 108 are rated of high severity, while the rest are considered moderate or low.

Almost 100 of them are defined as use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, which are memory management flaws that an attacker could exploit to crash the browser or trigger malicious code. Several of the bugs also refer to Firefox’s Sandbox, which means that hackers could break through the browser’s protected Sandbox area to execute malicious code.

Given the nastiness of the security bugs, you’ll want to update Firefox ASAP. For that, open the browser, click the three-line icon at the upper right, move to Help and Report, and select About Firefox. The latest update will then be installed. Restart Firefox to finish the process.

Also: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back

Beyond the security patches, Firefox 159 adds a few handy new features.

With Firefox for the Mac, sharing a page in the browser now displays the built-in MacOS share picker. Here, you can see a preview of the page you want to share along with recent contacts and specific apps such as AirDrop and Messages.

Next up, you’re now able to access Firefox’s passwords tool in the sidebar. This lets you more easily view any website passwords that you’ve saved to the browser. To see this in action, first make sure the sidebar is visible. For that, click the Sidebar button on the Address bar and then click the key icon to display your saved passwords.

And as perhaps the most helpful new feature, Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window can now watch specific web pages for changes and send you a notification when the page is updated. For this, turn on the option for Smart Window if it’s not already enabled. Click the Firefox icon in the upper right and select Smart Window. Navigate to the website for which you’d like to be notified of any changes. At the chat window, type /watch, fill out the form, and then click the Create Task button.

That takes us to Chrome with version 56.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux. Here, the latest update patches 52 security bugs. Out of these, four are rated critical, while 46 are rated high.

The four severe ones point to a memory corruption problem. But like some of the Firefox bugs, they also reference the browser’s Sandbox. In this case, an attacker who exploits any of these vulnerabilities could bypass Chrome’s protected Sandbox area to run malicious code. Also as in Firefox, several of the bugs point to use-after-free (UAF) issues that would allow an attacker to exploit memory management flaws to crash the browser or install malicious code.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

To update Chrome, click the three-dot icon at the top, move to Help, and select About Google Chrome. If prompted, allow the latest update to download and then restart the browser to finish.

Beyond many of the bugs themselves, Firefox and Chrome also share an increasing reliance on AI to find and resolve security flaws. In its advisory, Mozilla cited Amy Burnett, a security research and analyst at OpenAI, for uncovering many of the bugs. In its blog post, Google attributed the discovery of several flaws to Anthropic’s Claude and a few to OpenAI.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3193. Google’s Legend of Zelda Easter Egg Will Take You Back in Time. Here’s How to Find It

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Crank up Céline Dion: You can catch a glimpse into what Google was like back in 1998.

Nintendo is gearing up to release its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Thursday, and Google is marking the occasion with an Easter egg that transports the search engine back to 1998 – the year the original game was released.

If you go to Google.com now and search for “Zelda,” the game’s legendary Master Sword appears in the bottom right corner of the screen. In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the sword is a means to travel back and forth in time. (Searching for “Master Sword” also manifests the legendary weapon.)

When you click the sword, it thrusts into a pedestal and an animation plays before revealing a pre-2000s search page. In this view, you see the classic blue links, the I’m Feeling Lucky button and instead of seeing “Google” in the top-left corner of the page, you see the retro-looking “Google!” with an exclamation point. (Google removed the exclamation point from its logo in 1999.) If you stay real quiet and listen closely, you might also be able to hear Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On in the background.

What you won’t see on this page are any ads, AI overviews or random social media posts. It’s such a retro experience, and a fun reminder of what using Google was like back in the day. The neater, less cluttered layout made me feel instantly calmer than Google’s normal view.

However, this change isn’t permanent. As soon as you search for something else in this view, you’re transported back to the current version of Google Search. I wish there were an option to permanently enable this view, but for now, I’ll enjoy this slice of internet nostalgia.

#3192. Your headphones have hidden LE Audio features you’ll want to know about

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Your JBL, Sony, or Bose Bluetooth headphones got a top-to-bottom wireless makeover -- not just Auracast.

The shift from Classic Bluetooth to LE Audio is in full swing, as JBL and Sony release flagship headphones and earbuds with built-in LE Audio. Bose is the latest to upgrade its flagship headphones via an OTA firmware update.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Auracast, the Bluetooth protocol that enables one-to-many audio streams and is the most popular LE Audio feature, but several other LE Audio upgrades don’t get as much attention. These features improve wireless voice call quality, reduce battery drain in true wireless earbuds, and remove ecosystem barriers to low-latency mobile gaming. Here’s why they matter just as much as Auracast.

LE Audio includes the Low Complexity Communication Codec (LC3), which includes the unified Telephony and Media Audio Profile (TMAP) to handle audio streams and voice calls simultaneously. Bluetooth Classic relies on the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile (A2DP) and Hands-Free Profile (HFP), which handle the same functions but require both profiles.

Also: Bluetooth’s latest could solve a common connectivity problem

The profiles in Bluetooth Classic, given that they must alternate, result in extremely poor voice quality during hands-free calls over cellular or video calls on Zoom or Teams. These profiles also account for degraded voice quality when chatting while playing a mobile game.

LE Audio consolidates these two profiles, creating higher-quality, bidirectional audio and preserving voice call quality when using wireless headphones.

Earlier this year, JBL gave its flagship Tour Pro 3 earbuds an OTA firmware update to support LE Audio, and Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds, released in February, have LE Audio support out of the box. There’s one major true wireless earbud improvement wrapped in LE Audio: native multi-stream audio.

Also: Frustrated with multipoint? How it works – and why it sometimes won’t

In Bluetooth Classic, your source device, such as your phone, sends audio to one earbud, which then retransmits it to the other earbud. This complex audio transmission method is why one of your earbuds always has a lower battery than the other. Though premium earbuds usually have an independent stream workaround, many midrange and budget earbuds don’t, and that’s where LE Audio comes in handy.

LE Audio enables independent audio streams built into the Bluetooth stack, so manufacturers don’t need to implement their own methods to avoid asymmetrical battery drain.

Software ecosystems, like Apple’s iOS and Samsung’s Galaxy, dictate which audio features are reserved for devices inside of them and withhold features from devices outside of them. Hardware ecosystems are equally responsible for the fragmentation of audio features across manufacturers, typically through codecs.

Sony’s LDAC codec for high-quality audio is only available on Sony headphones, earbuds, and smartphones with the proper hardware, which is limited in the US market. Snapdragon’s AptX codecs aren’t as widely available on phones either, leaving most people to rely on Bluetooth Classic SBC and AAC codes, even though their headphones support more advanced ones.

Also: Your iPhone may support Bluetooth Channel Sounding – and it’s a big deal

LE Audio eliminates the tedious codec issue, especially in wireless gaming contexts, delivering lower latency, improved voice audio streams, and eliminating asymmetrical audio transmission.

For now, as long as you have a compatible Android phone, you have access to several models of headphones, earbuds, and Bluetooth speakers that support LE Audio. As more manufacturers update their devices to support the Bluetooth audio streaming protocol, this suggests the technology is becoming more reliable.

So, what about your AirPods? I wouldn’t bet on it anytime soon.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

#3187. The Swift Observatory Is Dropping Back to Earth This Week. Here’s What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of the space telescope is slated to burn up in the atmosphere, but some fragments may make their way down to Earth.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory — formerly known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — is in its final days. The space telescope was launched into orbit on Nov. 20, 2004. Almost 22 years to the day, it’s expected to come crashing back down on Wednesday.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA, said in a statement last month.

NASA says the telescope should hit the atmosphere on Nov. 4 at around 3:30 a.m. ET, but the agency acknowledges an 11-hour window during which reentry is possible. That means it could come down in the middle of the night or the middle of the day. Most of the telescope is likely to burn up in orbit, with only a few components expected to reach Earth.

The location where those components splash down depends entirely on when Swift reenters the atmosphere. However, NASA says that the surviving fragments are “limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude.” On a map, that would create a band around the middle of the Earth terminating just above and just below the equator.

“The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely — approximately 1 in 2,100,” NASA said in a statement. “NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.”

In preparation for Swift’s reentry, NASA shut down operations in late October after conducting its final observation on Oct. 20. It was orbiting at just 171 miles above Earth’s surface at that point, and the increased atmospheric drag prevented Swift from doing any further work. It was a bittersweet moment for those who worked on the project.

“It is a sad time at the Penn State Mission Operations Center, as we have carefully tended Swift to control its science operations, its health and safety, and responded to anomalies day or night, every day for 22 years,” John Nousek, director of mission operations for Swift and professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET.

Swift’s initial mission was a runaway success and helped advance science’s understanding of gamma-ray bursts and their role in phenomena such as the birth of black holes and the history of the early universe.

That initial mission ended on Nov. 4, 2004, but the observatory was doing so well that NASA left it up there to continue collecting data. Its name changed to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory on Jan. 10, 2018, in honor of pioneering NASA astrophysicist Neil Gehrels, who served as the agency’s chief of the Astroparticle Physics Laboratory from 1995 until his death in 2017.

The space telescope was designed to help solve the mystery of gamma-ray bursts by rapidly detecting them, determining their sources and then further analyzing them for study back on Earth. It also enabled unique sampling to observe newly discovered objects only minutes after their light reached Earth, said Nousek.

The amount of science conducted using Swift’s data cannot be overstated. According to NASA, it scanned over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, took 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope and sent home 12 TB of data. That data is showcased in an estimated 7,000 research papers, which averages out to just under one study per day over its 22-year run.

“We hope Swift has set the standard for time domain astrophysics,” Nousek said. The space telescope also helped pioneer many policies that ultimately shaped those discoveries, such as making data immediately accessible and providing over 1,000 guest investigators with the opportunity to use Swift throughout its long life, according to Nousek.

It’s only a stroke of bad luck that kept the observatory from floating for even longer. NASA attempted a rescue of Swift over the summer of 2026. However, after a series of engineering difficulties and control issues, the attempt was abandoned, sealing Swift’s fate. NASA turned the instruments back on and kept recording data as long as possible.

No more reverse engineering or cloning of games with Claude

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the past few weeks, there have been so many instances of AI being used to tinker around with popular video games.

That practice has led to the trend of video game decompilations, which is the process of a developer working backward from a compiled, machine-code game to reconstruct readable, human-understandable source code. Reverse engineering games has also popped up as of late, which is all about a developer analyzing compiled machine code or raw binary files to understand their internal logic, rebuild that source code or port games to new platforms.

Because of those AI uses in connection with video games, Halo: Combat Evolved has been made completely playable within a web browser, Super Mario 64 has been decompiled to also work as a playable title on PC and even game mashups have popped up in the form of Minecraft becoming playable in Elden Ring.

But when it comes to using AI tools to completely recreate those popular types of games, Anthropic is making sure that practice won’t be doable with its Claude Code and Opus 5.5 AI models. Here’s how the AI company is blocking any future attempts at prompting the recreation, reverse-engineering and cloning of identifiable video games.

News of Anthropic’s Claude update blocking the cloning of recognizable video games surfaced after a user on X named @chasmmmmmmmmmmm noticed a new rule added to Claude Code that’s meant to block prompts that request the recreation of existing titles. That rule, which is entitled “tengu_heron_brook,” puts forth the following edict:

“Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”

In response to that X user’s Tweet, Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic, gave this statement on the matter:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

“We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.October 30, 2026

It’s interesting to see Anthropic fight back against people using its AI tools to alter certain video game titles in a major way or remake them altogether.

Looking at the list of games that have had Claude involved in their reverse engineering practices points to just how many retro classics have been altered in a surprising way. Witnessing Skate 3 skateboarding physics crossing over with Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 multiplayer maps and seeing Escape from Tarkov's gunplay, loot systems and extraction mechanics make their way into the fantasy realm of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim has come courtesy of AI coding assistants like Claude Opus 5.5.

It’s been interesting to see the flood of reverse engineering video game projects that have begun popping up all over the net. There’s even a GitHub project page dedicated to games that have already been reverse-engineered, decompiled and rebuilt thanks to the implementation of numerous AI models and agentic tools.

The manner in which AI tools have been used to tinker with popular video games has been crazy to see. I never imagined that I’d get to see Marvel’s Spider-Man from the PlayStation series of games be able to swing around Batman’s rain-soaked Gotham City from Arkham Knight. But that has become possible due to the use of AI tools.

Claude’s new AI model update is blocking attempts to completely copy someone else’s video game IP, which also falls in line with Anthropic making sure Claude isn’t used to reverse-engineer smart TVs as well. It seems like Anthropic is moving against any more attempts to have its AI models be used to get caught up in the copyright infringement of existing video game titles.

I’ve never claimed to be the most organized person, and I’m fully aware I need to take steps to be more on top of appointments, schedules, to-do lists, and everything that comes with family life. I’ve been tempted by smart display calendars like the Skylight, but they seemed a little gimmicky and expensive for what’s essentially a large tablet. (ZDNET’s Maria Diaz argues against that gimmick notion, by the way.)

The Echo Show 16, though, might just be the device that gets me to take the leap.

Also: Echo Show 16 makes Apple’s 7-inch HomeView look puny

When I first saw this device, I admit, it wasn’t the first thing to catch my eye. But then I started learning more about what it can do — and now I’m ready to boot my Echo Show 5 for an upgrade. It won’t be a cheap upgrade (I’ll address that later), but if it does what Amazon is promising, it’ll be more than worth it to me.

The first thing I noticed was how sleek the device looks. Amazon says it has 10% more viewing area than the Echo Show 15, but a frame that’s almost 40% thinner. According to Amazon, this doubles the range of Visual ID from 8 feet to 17 feet (from the previous generation). The Show 16 also adds night vision, making it much easier to keep an eye on your home when it’s dark.

I check in on my dogs several times a day, and my current Show does an OK job, but it’s pretty much useless at night. The improved camera on the Show 16 offers a whole new level of functionality.

My biggest concern? The price. The Echo Show 16 starts at $500. If you add any accessories or upgrade to the anti-glare Nanomatte display, you’re closer to $600. That’s double the price of the similarly sized 15-inch Skylight calendar. At the time I’m writing this, a $100 coupon is available, bringing the price down to $400.

I’m already heavily invested in the Amazon ecosystem, so it makes sense that I’d bring a display into the fold as my new smart home centerpiece. A purchase like this is hardly a necessity, but if it can wrangle just a little of my life’s chaos, it’ll be a worthy investment.

#3183. Forget the AI Notetaker, Someone From Iceland Will Knit a Summary of Your Meeting

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Research shows that people are drained by meetings – and AI tools exacerbate it. A new initiative by Visit Iceland aims to remind you of what matters most.

Is there anything worse than a meeting that really should have been an email? Visit Iceland has a new, albeit quirky, way to combat increasing meeting fatigue.

Rather than turning to AI tools and notetakers to take your place or keep track of what’s important in meetings, a real, crafty person will show up to listen. The AI Knittakers initiative from Visit Iceland will let you book an authentic Icelandic knitter to join your virtual meeting who will knit a sign with a single word that sums up the meeting, like “align,” “pivot,” “reset,” “huh?” or, my personal favorite, “WTF?”

Meeting fatigue is real. A December 2023 survey of 5,000 workers found that 78% of respondents said work meetings make it hard for them to get their work done, and 76% said they feel drained on heavy meeting days, highlighting that the growing number of virtual meetings since the COVID-19 pandemic is both ineffective and exhausting. Many stressed-out workers (65%) are now turning to AI notetakers to sometimes attend meetings for them.

“An AI notetaker hears every word,” said Salka Sól Eyfeld, the program’s chief AI Knittaker. “A knitter hears the sigh. We listen for the one thing that actually matters, and then we knit it.”

The initiative is available now and will run through Nov. 20.

The booking couldn’t be simpler: Pick an available Knittaker from the website, book them during a meeting when your schedules align and give your coworkers the surprise of a lifetime while you do something more fun. The AI Knittaker will also email you a photo of your knitted one-word meeting summary, with the option to have it shipped to you if you live in Europe or the US.

According to the press release, some Knittakers will also be available to attend meetings in languages other than English. Just explore the list of Knittakers to see their language capabilities.

The idea of giving your coworkers a shock while also making a statement about your precious work time sounds appealing, but it also signals a broader global attitude.

People are drained by meetings, and AI tools exacerbate it. A recent study in Harvard Business Review found that certain uses of AI tools, such as switching between different chatbots, can lead to cognitive fatigue they call “brain fry.”

After conducting a survey that found that workers spend about 8 hours per month in meetings that they deem unnecessary, Visit Iceland wanted to remind you that there’s more to life than just work meetings. The solution is both deeply analog and deeply Icelandic.

Knitting is a big part of everyday life in Iceland, according to Visit Iceland, and is a common hobby for relaxation and socialization. Icelanders are often knitting lopapeysas, Iceland’s distinctive patterned jumpers made of lopi wool, in public and even during meetings. By joining the work call, the AI Knittakers will give you a glimpse of their culture and stunning surroundings, reminding you of how good life can be when it’s not dominated by work and technology.

“It’s easy to assume that every modern problem needs a technological answer,” said Sigríður Dögg Guðmundsdóttir, spokesperson for Visit Iceland. “In Iceland, we’ve found that some of the best answers are the simplest ones: a little more time, a little more nature and people who really listen to each other.

“With AI Knittakers, we’re sharing a little of that Icelandic perspective with the world, and we hope it inspires people to step away from their screens and perhaps come and experience Iceland for themselves,” she added.

#3182. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

#3181. Samsung adds better sleep tracking to Galaxy Watches – here’s what to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The FDA-approved sleep apnea tracking feature will first come to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Watch 9, and Ring.

Samsung’s sleep-tracking feature has been around on the Samsung Galaxy Watch for a few years now, but it recently got an upgrade: A new AI algorithm, that can deliver more detailed sleep reports than Samsung’s previous sleep apnea detection technology.

Users can see the insights behind their breathing disorders each hour. Prior to this update, the smartwatch would simply detect whether or not a user had sleep apnea but would not provide details on the condition’s specifics or timing.

Users wear a Galaxy Watch to sleep for a few nights, and the sleep apnea results are divided into three stages: mild, occasional, and frequent. Samsung says this classification allows for greater specificity in condition management.

Many smartwatch and health tracker companies have implemented some sleep apnea detection features on their devices. The often underdiagnosed condition impacts around 30 million Americans, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). It’s a condition with gateway effects: if it goes untreated, it can lead to high blood pressure, heart disease, and impaired focus, according to the AMA. Despite sleep apnea’s prevalence, it’s highly treatable — and a great example of wearables passively detecting conditions at home.

Of course, the Galaxy Watch can’t aid in the treatment plan of a sleep apnea diagnosis.

The feature will be available in Korea first, starting in November, with no confirmed date for when it will arrive on US Samsung watches and smart rings. The FDA-cleared feature will first come to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Watch 9, and Ring. Samsung says an update will bring the advanced sleep apnea detection to Galaxy Watch 7 and 8 through future software updates.

To use the feature, a Galaxy user will need to record two nights of sleep within a 10-day period to learn details about their condition.

#3180. Jean-Luc in Blue Jeans: Picard Cosplay Taught Me How Much Patrick Stewart Is Loved

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

My husband was assimilated at an Emerald City Comic Con, and even the Borg adored him. Thank you, Patrick Stewart.

Star Trek fans never doubted the amount of love the community had for Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at age 86. But I experienced that love firsthand. Back in 2021, my husband, Rob, dressed as Captain Jean-Luc Picard for Emerald City Comic Con in Seattle, and the adoration he received, simply for cosplaying Stewart’s beloved character, was overwhelming.

Our planning wasn’t complicated. Looking for a costume that would go with his shaved head, and being a big fan of the show, it made sense for him to put on a red and black Star Trek uniform shirt, pin on a combadge and four pips to denote the Starfleet rank of captain, and step into some black shoes. Except for his glasses (and mask since this was 2021, the second year of the COVID-19 pandemic), it was an eerily accurate look.

Read more: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

Once we walked into the Seattle Convention Center for the con, it was as if the real Patrick Stewart had shown up. The respect Stewart had built up for Picard transferred seamlessly to his lookalike. Just walking around with Rob made me feel like a celebrity escort. We couldn’t travel more than a few feet without someone noticing and calling out to him, always with glee, always with respect.

“Hey, Captain! Captain!”“Jean-Luc!”“Make it so, sir!”“Engage!”“Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!”

Rob didn’t even wear costume-authentic black pants. In a hurry to get out the door and not expecting this level of attention, he had just pulled on his jeans. That led to a few of the funnier comments.

“Hey Captain! Was it casual day on the bridge?”

Comic Con attendees go all out. There were eerily realistic characters from Star Wars, Pokemon creatures, groups of friends dressed as The Incredibles, at least five Spider-Men, the Doctor from Doctor Who and exquisite, elaborate characters from anime. Many, many people had put more time, money and sweat equity into their costumes than we did, but few received such a universally awed reception.

Read more: Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles

Other Star Trek characters were also portrayed, for sure. Two separate Will Rikers, Picard’s trusted “Number One,” raced up to us at different times to take photos with their captain. One woman cosplaying as Kathryn Janeway, captain of the USS Voyager from Star Trek: Voyager, also posed with Rob for a two-captain photo.

And then, they saw us. A group of Comic Con attendees dressed as the Borg, the villainous cyborgs who take Picard hostage to assimilate him and temporarily turn him into Locutus of Borg.

These Borg did not throw their costumes together last-minute. They could have walked off a Hollywood set. They had working lights on their outfits, ocular and cranial “implants,” corpse-like face makeup, arms built into cybernetic tools. Of the Borgs, three were towering men and one was a woman. The woman played the Borg Queen, her bald head covered in white makeup, elegant and terrifying.

The minute the Borg saw Rob’s Picard in the convention center crowd, they came after him. Resistance, as they say in the show, was futile.

Thankfully, they were a jollier sort than the television Borg, and after one joke about his casual-day jeans, they whisked him away to stroll around as a group and snap photos.

These Borg were so realistic that I felt a bit unnerved the entire time he was gone — and relieved when they returned him unharmed, thanked us, waved and headed on their way. I’m sure there were other serendipitous meetups between cosplayers at the convention, but this one was amazing to see and even more so to be even a small part of.

We’ve been to Emerald City Comic Con other times. Our daughter has cosplayed a variety of characters, and Rob once went as Dr. Stone, a science prodigy with green-tipped white hair (which required a wig). People in the know enjoyed that cosplay, too, and he was similarly asked to pose for photos.

But the sheer love we experienced when he dressed as Captain Picard was like nothing I’ve ever felt. Since his death, I’ve seen Stewart called a generation’s space dad, and there’s truth in that. People at the convention were delighted to see their space dad, even if just a doppelganger. It buoyed us along on an unexpected high on that cold December day in 2021.

In the famous Star Trek: Next Generation episode Darmok, Picard is trapped on a planet with the Tamarian captain, Dathon. They can’t understand each other. The entire Tamarian language is constructed out of mythological and historical metaphors, none of which Picard knows

Slowly, Picard begins to comprehend. He figures out that one of the most frequent phrases, “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!” references Darmok and Jalad, warriors who united on the island of Tanagra and eventually became friends, just like he and Dathon.

But there’s another phrase I’ve been thinking of lately. “Kiazi’s children, their faces wet.” An online Tamarian dictionary translates it as “downplaying the severity of a perceived injury.”

There’s no downplaying this loss. We’re all Kiazi’s children today. Our faces wet.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

You could see these shoes the same day Rockstar releases the long-awaited game.

Rockstar Games is releasing the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 in just a few weeks, on Nov. 19, and rapper Travis Scott and Nike are reportedly getting in on the game’s hype. According to Sneaker News, Nike, Rockstar Games and Travis Scott are working together to release a set of Nike Air Force 1 ’07 sneakers themed around the upcoming game. Reports suggest the shoes will retail for $130 and be available on Nov. 19, the same day as the game’s release.

The shoes will reportedly be available in three colorways. Those palettes are supposedly “White/White/Fire Pink,” “Black/Black/Fire Pink” and “Multicolor/Pale Ivory/Black/Bold Berry/Fire Pink.” The sneaker account prm.stocks.01 shared images of what the black pair would look like if you want to take a peek.

The shoe will reportedly have the reverse swoosh logo traditionally seen on other Travis Scott sneakers, and the leather appears to feature a grid that looks like city blocks.

The shoes have six stars on the heels, the report says, a nod to the six-star wanted level, which makes its return to the Grand Theft Auto series in the upcoming game. Grand Theft Auto 5 replaced the six-star system with a five-star system.

The sneakers will also supposedly come with a $100 GTA-branded money band around the shoe’s toe box. Other Nike shoes, like the different colors of the Concepts x Nike SB Dunk Low Lobsters, have had removable rubber bands, too.

And the shoe’s midsole reportedly replaces the “AIR” lettering normally on all Air Force One models with the letters “GTA.” There are likely more details that reference the game hidden throughout the shoe.

Neither Nike nor Rockstar Games immediately responded to my request for comment.

While there will reportedly be three colors of this shoe available, I think Nike, Rockstar and Travis Scott could have stopped at the black pair. I’m sure the other two colorways are fine, but it’s a joke that black Air Force 1 sneakers are used in various criminal and illegal activities, making that pair a perfect representation of the Grand Theft Auto series.

I appreciate the six-star and money band details we see in the photos, and the pink gives the pairs a nice hint of Vice City-coded color without being too much. The black pair of these shoes reportedly comes with black and pink laces, and I’d lace up the pink ones if I ever got these shoes.

However, since these are a collab between Nike, Rockstar and Travis Scott, I’m not expecting to see them on my feet. Travis Scott and Nike collaborations usually release in limited quantities, so it’s difficult to get a pair. You could always buy the shoes on eBay, StockX or a similar marketplace, but some Travis Scott and Nike collabs sell on the aftermarket for more than $1,000, depending on your size. And I’m not spending that much on a single pair of shoes. I’ve got a mortgage to pay, thank you very much.

#3176. Android 17 adoption hits a staggering 1% – why you really should update now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Only a quarter of Android phones have even made it to Android 16.

Android 17 adoption hasn’t been speedy. According to the most recent data from heise.de via Android Studio, as reported by Android Authority, Android 17 has reached just 1% of active devices since its release in June 2026.

While Android 16 is finally the most used Google OS for Android devices, at 25.4% of active Android devices, these distribution figures indicate that getting users to upgrade to even newer software is an uphill battle.

It’s true that Android 17 has had less time to reach devices than Android 16 did when the previous distribution snapshot was published, but the minuscule adoption rate underscores how slowly the latest release is infiltrating the Android ecosystem.

Also: How Android 17 stops network snoops and SMS blasters now

Plus, the data show that more Android users than not are running versions that are many years old. I’m all for not fixing what’s not broken, but when Android 14 is the second most widely used version (15.% of devices are still running it), while Android 15 trails not far behind at 14.7%, there’s a pretty large chunk of individuals who may be putting themselves (and their data) at risk.

And it doesn’t end there. Android 13 and Android 11 are still on the table for 11.8% and 10.1% of users, with almost another 10% still using Android 12. That’s about another 30% of users still running Android 13 or older.

Though the numbers indicate that almost 60% of active Android devices are running Android 14 or newer, about 40% of users haven’t even upgraded to Android 14 or later.

Also: This Android 17 setting logs suspicious activity on your phone for troubleshooting

While the numbers are staggering, they’re not surprising. Android updates typically lag behind iOS updates. While the iPhone and its software are both designed, controlled, and distributed by Apple, Android updates must roll out from a single starting point to a wider array of mobile devices and systems to reach users. While Google is responsible for the core of the Android system, those updates must then be curated, reviewed, and pushed to every device that uses Android. This includes phones from Google, Samsung, Nothing, and more, which usually requires adaptations from each manufacturer. Apple’s updates are often adopted faster because there’s no middle entity between iOS and the user, while Android’s process is rather fragmented.

Keep in mind that Google no longer publishes a regularly updated public distribution chart, so this data isn’t from a real-time survey of every Android device. There’s only cumulative adoption data through Android Studio, and these estimates are derived from those figures and cover devices that contacted the Google Play Store during a seven-day period.

It’s always good practice to keep your device updated to the latest available software that your system allows. There are a few great reasons why those eligible for Android 17 should upgrade, including improved features — like the ability to “bubble” apps and stop network snoops and SMS blasters.

Also: I enabled Android’s new security feature that detects fake cell towers – here’s why

Plus, it’s the most proactive thing you can do for your device. Software updates usually include improvements to your phone’s operation, speed, security, and more, and it’s an easy (and free) way to keep your phone healthy.

#3174. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

Once these settings are enabled, users can configure HomeView to detect motion, stream real-time video, and record video. These strings appear in HomeView software version 27.2, suggesting that Apple will wrap this feature into an upcoming software update. Via HomeKit Security Camera, only users registered to the home can view HomeView’s video streams and recordings. Additionally, a green status light will appear, and a chime will sound to alert house dwellers that HomeView is recording or someone is starting a camera stream.

Finally, all members registered to the Home app will receive a notification when someone else changes HomeKit Secure Video settings, such as allowing HomeView to detect motion or record video.

HomeView may have four video options: Off, Detect Activity, Stream, and Stream & Allow Recordings. With Detect Activity, home members would be alerted to motion but won’t be able to rewatch who or what triggered the notification.

Stream would allow users to stream video from HomeView in real time, but the home hub won’t record the livestream. Finally, Stream & Allow Recordings would allow home members to stream video from HomeView in real time, with all members able to access its recordings.

Code strings also point to customization options, such as allowing HomeView to detect motion, stream, or record video only when you’re home, away, or asleep, using home members’ iPhone or other device locations to determine proximity.

Apple’s bottom-up ecosystem control gives it an advantage over competing home security brands like Ring, Nest, and Wyze. Users can easily access their HomeView camera stream without a third-party app or delayed notifications.

#3165. Anthropic Addresses Video Game Cloning With Minor Claude Update

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

There's a fine line between AI creations inspired by video games and those that are infringing copyright.

One of AI’s biggest selling points is its ability to build things quickly. AI models can help users sort through mountains of files, generate videos that have Hollywood studios worried, and create everything from websites and businesses to custom video games. With what’s called vibe coding, ordinary people can build playable video games in minutes using simple text prompts in popular AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

But the AI company Anthropic appears to be drawing a line in the sand about what kinds of games its AI model Claude can make. If a Claude user is trying to recreate someone else’s intellectual property, the AI tool will decline to build it.

That’s according to Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic who posted on X. He was responding to concerns that Anthropic had changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games, which could violate copyright rules and the company’s usage policy.

“Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working,” Osmani said. “We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to…

He offered to review cases where amateur game developers believe Claude wrongly refused their requests.

A representative for Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic’s stance, as expressed by Osmani, acknowledges that using AI to try to clone a video game, even a simple one, could constitute intellectual property infringement, an issue that predates the rise of AI tools like Claude.

Even with the change, Claude will still generate video games that resemble popular hits from the past few decades. A CNET request to build a game “that resembled Breakout but with the word Claude on each brick” yielded a playable web version of the arcade classic, but not one that any video game fan would mistake for the original.

The same thing happened after Flappy Bird became a hit in 2014, spawning a wave of copycat games in app stores. Copyright infringement of games is complicated, said David Kocan, an intellectual property lawyer at Nixon Peabody who co-leads the firm’s esports and gaming team.

“This is something courts have wrestled with long before AI came along,” Kocan said. “The basic distinction has always been that copyright protects a game’s original creative expression, but generally not its underlying ideas, rules, or gameplay mechanics. Copyright protects the game you created, not the genre you helped popularize.”

You can’t copyright the concept of, say, a battle royal game or a side-scrolling platformer, which is why when a new type of game emerges as a hit, you’ll see many similar games.

“That distinction may sound straightforward in theory, but in practice, the line between borrowing an idea and copying someone’s creative expression can be blurry,” Kocan said. “That’s particularly true in gaming, where so much of the experience combines functional mechanics with creative expression.”

RTB Ruhan, founder and CEO of Null Station, an animation and video game art studio, said that AI has made it”fast and cheap” to cross the line into infringement, allowing people with no art or design skills to clone a popular game. But that doesn’t mean someone can publish or sell a cloned game without running into trouble.

“‘(Claiming) AI made it’ won’t protect them,” Ruhan said.

“Remove the title and logo and ask whether a player could still tell the two games apart,” Ruhan said. “If they can’t, you’ve crossed the line.”

Legal experts CNET spoke with said there are no laws requiring AI companies to outlaw game clones on their tools. But adding those guardrails could prevent trouble down the road, said Eric Blatt, a corporate, securities and intellectual property lawyer at Scale and a former examiner at the US Patent and Trademark Office.

“Anthropic is prudent to tap the brakes here,” Blatt said. “If Claude — Anthropic-owned software operating on Anthropic servers — receives an instruction to copy a game, and if Claude then copies the game, there is a facially plausible argument that Anthropic performed the copying. The chat logs would be a gold mine for the plaintiff’s counsel.”

Blatt said that litigation hasn’t kept pace with AI’s growth, but he thinks lawsuits could quickly follow if a rebuilt game made with AI directly threatens a company’s business model.

But some of those attempts could be stopped before they start if AI models refuse to make exact copies.

“Ultimately, copyright law draws the legal boundaries,” Kocan said. “But AI companies have to decide where they’re comfortable drawing their own. And those aren’t necessarily going to be the same thing.”

#3164. Firefox’s new Mini Window is every multitasker’s dream – Chrome can’t do this

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The open-source browser's newest feature lets you pop out a page - or part of a page - into its own mini window. See why this is incredibly cool.

The developers at Mozilla are always hard at work to make Firefox the most useful browser on the market. To that end, they’ve added a new feature (still in beta), called Mini Window. I started using Mini Window as soon as it appeared in Firefox Nightly, and I’ve been very happy with how it performs.

Also: Why I’m sticking with Firefox as my browser

The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window. Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app. Essentially, I can move a page (or section) into what looks like a browser window, minus the browser bits. At first blush, there’s no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it.

However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/foward/reload buttons, and the window close button– and that’s it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.

Also: Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined

On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I’m working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy.

Using the Firefox Mini Window feature is quite simple, but until the feature comes out of beta, it can only be found in Firefox Nightly. I’ve been using Nightly as my default browser on both Linux and MacOS for some time now and have yet to run into a problem (YMMV).

For those who don’t want to risk using a potentially less-than-stable alpha version of Firefox, know that the Mini Window feature is slated to move to stable on November 10. Update Firefox on that day and can start enjoying the feature without upgrading to Nightly.

Until then, you can test Mini Window by installing Firefox Nightly, which can run alongside the stable Firefox release.

Also: Firefox just fixed my biggest annoyance with web browsers

Once I installed Nightly, there was nothing more to do. I didn’t have to enable Mini Window, as it’s already there. I simply had to right-click on an open tab and select Move Tab > Move to Mini Window.

Once I did that, the mini window popped out and hovered over Firefox. If I hovered my cursor over the mini window, the address bar and title bar for the window appeared, so I could drag the pop-up to wherever I needed.

I could also open a specific section of a tab in a Mini Window. To do that, I highlighted the section in question, right-clicked the section, and then clicked Move Section to Mini Window.

Let’s say I’m writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them — even when working on a smaller display.

Here’s another use case I’ve found: When using MacOS’s Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window.

Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

The closest thing Chrome has to Mini Window is Picture-in-Picture mode and the Mini Player. The caveat to Chrome’s feature is that those two options are only used for video and media playback. The next closest thing Chrome has is the ability to save a website as a web app, which you could then open alongside the main Chrome window. That feature, however, isn’t nearly as flexible as Firefox’s Mini Window option, and it’s not guaranteed to always hover over the main window.
