#3162. Starbucks Drive-Thru AI Could Know What You Want Before You Do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The company will begin testing AI for some orders, including using a form of customer recognition.

Could an AI barista know you’re craving an iced caramel macchiato? Starbucks says it will begin testing artificial intelligence for drive-up ordering — including recognizing customers as they approach — as the company focuses on integrating more automated tech, CEO Brian Niccol said on last week’s fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call.

The idea is to make ordering “faster, more convenient and more personal” for drive-up customers, which account for roughly half of all Starbucks patrons, according to Niccol. The company would begin testing background AI models for drive-thrus sometime during fiscal year 2027, which ends Sept. 28, 2027. There were no specifics as to where the testing would take place or how it would affect food and drink prices.

Niccol said AI would help input orders “more accurately and efficiently” while the baristas talk to drive-up customers to increase personal connection and speed up service.

The AI could also know what you want, or might want, before you even engage with the human barista. Niccol said the company is exploring ways for automated systems to recognize repeat customers as they drive up and offer “personalized digital menus,” possibly including suggested purchases.

While the exact kind of systems that would be tested to recognize customers weren’t specified, possible methods could include facial recognition, license plate reading or perhaps mobile app detection. It also remains to be seen which methods would require explicit customer consent or offer an opt-out mechanism. In an email to CNET, a Starbucks representative did not confirm which specific technology would be employed.

The representative said that Starbucks is already using AI in its operations through Green Dot Assist, which helps workers look up drink recipes, troubleshoot equipment issues and coordinate staffing. The company also uses Smart Queue to figure out sequencing of orders that come in via in-store, drive-thru, mobile app or delivery.

Several major fast-food chains are using or testing AI to process drive-thru orders, including McDonald’s, Taco Bell, KFC, White Castle and Wendy’s. Customer reviews have been mixed so far, with the main problems being botched orders, lengthy processing and the inability of bots to answer questions, according to customer research from restaurant tech website Canopy.

Burger King, meanwhile, decided to pull back on using AI for drive-thru because some customers drove off rather than place their orders with a bot. The company is still testing AI but said it wants to give people the option of ordering from a human.

It’s unclear what Starbucks’ goal is or what customers the company is trying to appeal to, said Uttara M. Ananthakrishnan, AI researcher and associate professor at the University of Washington. But there’s plenty to be skeptical about.

“AI in face-to-face customer service will fail in many edge cases and has many potential PR problems with no clear benefits,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “It is better to defer until there is a broader general acceptance among the public.”

Ananthakrishnan said one flaw of using bots is voice recognition — many AI models are trained on general US accents and don’t perform well with non-native speakers or international accents. Surrounding noise from vehicles and weather can also affect how well the bot understands the customer through a kiosk microphone. That could pose health risks, Ananthakrishnan said, if, for example, someone is allergic to nuts and the AI misinterprets the request as “no nuts.”

McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru experiment with IBM in 2024, when bots were unable to understand various accents and dialects. The fast-food giant recently launched a new experiment with AI bot Archy as part of an $8.5 billion modernization plan. There was also a fake order that went viral when someone ordered 18,000 waters at a Taco Bell, and the AI processed it.

Most of Ananthakrishnan’s students have said they don’t want to talk to AI during their customer service interactions. However, more people might accept drive-thru AI if they know that mistakes will be rectified quickly, Ananthakrishnan said.

Starbucks has said it doesn’t use surveillance pricing, a discriminatory method that’s been increasingly used by hotels, airlines and retailers. Still, a 2025 report in The Washington Post indicated that loyal customers using the Starbucks app more often might be getting fewer promotional deals.

In a 2026 statement on the use of AI, the company says: “Our business is rooted in human connection — and our technology is designed to strengthen it, not replace it.” But Starbucks’ human connection with its workers has been problematic, and AI isn’t known for improving labor relations.

Since initiating a major organizing blitz starting in late 2021, Starbucks employees have formed unions at nearly 700 stores in the US, demanding higher pay and more robust staffing levels. Workers say they are not given enough hours so the company can avoid providing benefits, and are often given very short notice about shift changes. Last year, the NLRB said Starbucks “engaged in a scorched earth campaign and pattern of misconduct in response to union organizing.”

Since taking over as CEO in September 2024, Niccol has cut more than 2,000 employees as part of his Back to Starbucks strategy, which has resulted in simplified menus, reduced wait times and the closure of some shops.

In August, Starbucks Workers United, which represents 12,000 baristas, announced an open-ended national consumer boycott against corporate-owned Starbucks locations. The call accused the company of violating US labor law and attempting to break up the union, while also criticizing the corporate push for AI. “Starbucks has repeatedly demonstrated a lack of care for the workers who fuel the company’s profits by wasting millions of dollars on AI and technology that doesn’t work, launching countless gimmicky drinks designed to distract from real problems, and inventing pointless policies that do nothing but make workers’ jobs harder,” the call read.

In a 2025 interview with Current Affairs, union organizer Jason Woods said the company was trying to use AI to place orders but couldn’t handle staffing when an employee calls out. “They want to use algorithms to deploy our plays,” he said. “It’s inhumane. It’s anti-worker, anti-labor.”

Starbucks Workers United didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Apple's pricey and intricate folding phone could lead to a costly repair if something happens to it.

The first iPhone Duos are now in customers’ hands, and we’re seeing in real time what happens when years of confidential Apple design meets the real world for the first time. Although reports still seem limited, several just-unboxed units are suffering from dramatic cracks on the inner screen. CNET is doing our own testing of the phone’s hinge by continuously opening and closing an iPhone Duo — which is now up to more than 200,000 times.

Apple has already promised to replace cracked units, a repair that also falls under the phone’s one-year warranty, but what if a crack or some other defect appears outside that window of time? Should owners and potential buyers add AppleCare Plus for their new Duo? (Or at the very least, an iPhone Duo case?) Based on Apple’s repair prices, it might not be a bad investment — unless you’re JerryRigEverything, whose warranty is most definitely voided.

After all, the iPhone Duo starts at expensive and goes up to exorbitant for its higher-capacity configurations. If something happens and you need a repair, the costs could be substantial without AppleCare coverage.

The base 256GB storage option is priced at $1,999, but if you want to max out Apple’s new foldable phone with 2TB of space, it’ll cost $3,199. That’s pricey by iPhone standards, compared to the iPhone 18 Pro that begins at $1,199, though in line with the retail prices of Android folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Adding AppleCare coverage on top of the iPhone Duo’s price is an ongoing cost in addition to the price of the phone, but in terms of potential repairs, it does make sense. Because if you don’t fork out for a plan, and the inner display of your iPhone Duo gets crunched, expect to pay $999 to get it replaced, according to Apple’s support documentation. These are prices for repairs made directly by Apple, not third-party services.

The range of repairs starts at a modest $49 for “cover layer damage” and jumps all the way up to $1,499 for “other damage,” though it’s not clear what the latter entails. Here’s the breakdown:

AppleCare Plus with Theft and Loss is priced at $20 per month or $200 per year until canceled and includes “unlimited repairs for accidents like drops and spills” and theft and loss coverage for up to two claims every 12 months. It also features Express Replacement Service, which gets you a new iPhone Duo instead of waiting for a repair.

Alternatively, the AppleCare One service costs $20 a month until canceled and applies AppleCare Plus to up to three devices. It also adds a third theft-and-loss coverage event in the 12-month span.

If something happens to your iPhone Duo under AppleCare, the repair pricing ranges from zero for battery service to $149 for theft or loss. The list of repair services doesn’t match up exactly to the ones noted without coverage. Here’s what Apple details as estimated costs:

Keep in mind these are the amounts provided by Apple’s services. If you’re purchasing the iPhone Duo through a wireless carrier, it might have different warranty options.

We’re looking forward to testing not just how well the iPhone Duo works, but how resilient Apple’s most complex iPhone will be. In the meantime, be sure to check out our review of Apple’s first foldable and ask yourself if the iPhone Duo is really for you.

#3158. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

#3156. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

October was a rocky month for readers of the fan-run fiction site Archive of Our Own, popularly known as AO3. Now, a routine disruption has escalated into a crisis. What began as an estimated 12-hour unplanned outage has ballooned into a multiweek shutdown, leaving millions of users locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout the month. An outage of this magnitude hit readers out of nowhere, landing with all the subtlety of a Looney Tunes anvil.

The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works. An update posted Thursday to the site’s status page and shared via Bluesky and Tumblr said that service restoration will take at least two weeks, possibly four.

“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner,” the update said. “If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved.”

That update followed an initial notification, 12 hours earlier, with the announcement that “AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer.”

A post on Nov. 1 said the site had no further updates beyond what had already been shared.

In response to a CNET request for more information, an OTW representative pointed to a status update, saying, “The statement confirms that the downtime is a security incident, the scope of which is still being assessed. I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”

[update] Identified: Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been fou…

According to the update, “Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far.”

It emphasizes that no data has been deleted, and while they don’t think user data was compromised, they can’t rule it out and recommend you change your password if it’s not unique to AO3. (It should be if you practice safe password practices.) Donor information resides in a separate, unconnected database.

If you need a stopgap for your fanfic needs, you can try Wattpad or FanFiction. The r/DeletedFanfiction Reddit, Bluesky members and other communities have stepped up to offer copies of works they’d already downloaded and to crowdsource alternatives.

#3153. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3152. iOS 27.2 Draining Your iPhone Battery? Don’t Panic, That’s Normal

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

Apple said faster battery drain after an update isn't unusual, so it's nothing to worry about.

Apple released iOS 27.2 on Monday, Oct. 26, and the update brings Siri AI to more languages as well as hundreds of bug fixes. After you download the update, it might seem like your iPhone’s battery is draining faster than usual, but don’t worry. Apple wrote online that this is normal and — most important — temporary.

Apple released a statement in July 2026, saying if your iPhone battery drains quickly after downloading an update, it’s nothing to worry about.

“This is normal, because your device needs time to complete the setup process in the background, including indexing data and files for search, downloading new assets, and updating apps,” Apple wrote in a support page. “Immediately after completing an update, particularly a major release, you might notice a temporary impact on battery life and thermal performance.”

But your personal iPhone use could be contributing to battery drain, too. Apple said some features might need more resources to function, so depending on how much you use your iPhone, you might “notice a small impact on performance or battery life.”

So while your device might experience some additional battery drain at first, it should be a temporary issue after you download iOS 27.2. If you find you’re using your iPhone more after downloading iOS 27.2, that could be contributing to your battery drain, too.

My Amazon smart display has been filling with AI garbage. Here's how to clear it out if you're struggling.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

With Amazon announcing a new Echo Show 16 to square off with Apple’s upcoming HomeView, the smart displays are having a moment, but I’ve noticed something seems off. In the past week or two, my Echo Show has started showing me a lot of lazy, annoying AI-generated ads under a playback feature called Created For You. So I figured out how to improve my experience with a few settings changes.

Not only is this AI slop vague and accompanied by poorly generated images, but it also doesn’t seem to have anything to do with my recorded interests or personalization, either. Basically, it’s very general content I don’t really care about and don’t want showing on a central display at home.

I suspect Amazon is pushing its AI podcasts and similar chatty content with this latest round of generated ads, but if you’re not interested in viewing any of these canned clips, they can come across as irksome. So I reviewed my settings options and found out how to push my Show display away from these creations and toward more interesting content.

The good news is you can control what your Echo Show, well, shows you — but you have to know what settings to change. This isn’t very easy through the Alexa app, but I found a better way using the Show’s own touchscreen controls. Here’s what to do when you have a minute.

First, when an AI slide like this appears, tap the three-dot menu button and tap the thumbs-down option to indicate your dislike. It’s not a perfect solution, but it should help start weeding out these types of ads.

Next, swipe down on your Echo Show device to access the main menu, and choose Settings. Then choose Display & Appearance, and head to Content Categories.

Here you have two options. You can manually turn off all the categories you don’t want to see, especially those connected to the AI slop that you’ve been seeing. Keep focus on topics that you’re interested in if you still want to see other related content. You can also toggle the Rotate Once setting on, which will show you Amazon’s slides only once, my preferred option for handling this kind of unwanted content.

As an alternative, you can switch your Echo Show to show only a photo album of your choosing. I like getting some Alexa recommendations like recipes and updates, so this option isn’t for me, but if you have a good photo album to share with Alexa, you can limit your slides to only your own content.

With these settings adjusted, you should see far fewer AI-generated images and more slides tailored to your own interests. I’ll keep an eye on my Echo Shows and let you know if anything changes, but this has worked well for me so far.

#3146. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

#3145. The Bambu Lab H3C Is Here and It’s Powerful and Uncompromising

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bambu Lab H3C is a large-format 3D printer with nine printheads, and it's available now.

Multicolor 3D printing has been around for many years. Like all technologies, manufacturers are constantly looking for ways to push it further than ever before. Bambu Lab announced today the H3C, a large-format 3D printer that uses nine separate nozzles to print not only different colors or types, but also different-sized filaments. It’s designed to allow you to mix and match as you see fit, expanding your creative options beyond the standard.

The Bambu Lab H3C starts at $2,500 and comes with the nine-filament system and Automated Material System. I’ve spent the last few weeks using it, and while I haven’t finished my review yet, I already have quite a few thoughts.

This is not a small machine by any measure. I originally had it on my workbench, but the H3C sits so tall that opening the lid and loading the filament was arduous, even for a 6-foot-1 person like myself. Bambu Lab also sent me a metal rolling cart, sold separately, that lowers the machine to a usable height. That said, it still stands 63 inches tall on the cart, so yeah, it’s a big’un.

Despite its size and complex design, setting it up was simple. I would recommend having a second person around to do it, as it’s cumbersome — but not difficult to plug in all the parts. The AMS 3 that sits atop the machine is different from most of the best 3D printers because the H3C requires it operate. It’s not a separate add-on but an integral part of the machine.

You can tell from every metric that the H3C is designed to be a Bambu Lab flagship. It has all the top-of-the-line hardware, including a heatbed that can reach 120 degrees Celcius and an optional but very cool bird’s-eye camera to monitor prints from above. It’s fast, too, with a top toolhead speed of 1,400 mm/s. Of course, that isn’t the print speed, but it does show you the type of speed it could reach if you pushed it to the max.

Printing at high speed does have some disadvantages, though. I have had several print failures on tall prints where the supports or purge tower have fallen due to accidental touches or vibration. The H3C moves fast, prints fast and fails fast if you aren’t careful. Most of those failures occurred at 125% speed, but that’s the standard setting I use for large prints on other machines, and they handle it just fine.

Bambu calls its nine-nozzle system, which heats using conductive heating, the Swaptek system. This isn’t to be confused with another nine-nozzle system you may have heard of: INDX, which uses conductive heating. INDX and Swaptek are extremely similar in execution but differ in a few areas. INDX is purely mechanical, whereas Bambu says its Swaptek system supplies data and power to each tool, allowing the nozzles to start heating faster than those in a standard INDX system — in around 6 seconds per nozzle.

In practice, there isn’t a huge difference between what I’m seeing on the H3C and the Prusa Core One + INDX in terms of speed. The Core One has the advantage that it’s calibrated to avoid a purge tower, and it doesn’t purge as much waste as the Swaptek system. The H3C has its own neat tricks, though: Not only can it print with different nozzle sizes and materials, but it can also print with materials of different diameters.

One of the biggest roadblocks with printing TPU — the very soft, rubbery material that 3D-printed shoes are made from — through an AMS is that it’s too soft to push through the AMS feeder. To combat this, you have to use a harder TPU that isn’t nearly as flexible as you would need for shoes or things that bounce. Adding toolheads capable of printing 2.85mm-diameter materials lets Bambu create TPU that’s more flexible after melting but thicker and easier to feed in the AMS. It works really well.

And it doesn’t stop at TPU, either. You can use 2.85mm PLA with a 0.8mm nozzle to print the infill of a model, while using a 0.2mm nozzle and 1.7mm PLA to print the detailed outer walls. It gives you so many options. The AMS even has two material slots with active heating chambers, so you can print materials that need to be warm and dry, along with other, more shelf-stable materials.

Given the $2,500 price and the H3C’s flagship status, it would be shocking if the print quality were bad. All of the models that didn’t fail due to purge tower collapse look great, and the nine separate nozzles make light work of just about any color project. I love watching this machine print as it swaps across the nozzles at blistering speeds.

Some of them did fail, though, and the H3C was good at catching the errors, pausing the print and letting me know. I chose to keep one of them going despite the failed tower, and it turned out fine, though a little damaged. I had some fun 3D printing my scanned head at life size, using silver for my greying beard — and I love the way it came out.

The CNET test print wasn’t nearly as good as the one the H2C produced, which pretty much maxed out every test, but it wasn’t the worst either. Accuracy was good, and despite the printer’s speed, ringing was kept to a minimum. It struggled on the 0.2mm tolerance test, but it did well on bridging and overhangs, showing that its temperature control is excellent. I still have more of these to do before I’m ready to give a complete score, but so far, I’m happy with the result.

In video games, there’s a concept called endgame content: the harder challenges you tackle after completing most of the story. It’s not for the faint of heart. The H3C is endgame content. It isn’t hard to use, but it’s designed for someone who has gone as far as possible with machines such as the P2S and A1 combos of the world. If you’re looking to go beyond what you thought you could do with a 3D printer, the H3C is the machine to get you there.

Swaptek, INDX and multi-toolhead printers are here to stay. And, like all 3D printers, they can come in many sizes and budgets. The Core One INDX is smaller but cheaper, but the H3C has a lot of options right out of the box to make some incredibly complex models. We live in interesting times and the landscape can only get better.

#3144. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

Typical signs of a bank phishing email include:

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

#3142. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

#3141. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3140. I tried Sonos’ latest app features – these 2 small upgrades fix big annoyances

New Sonos software and firmware updates are rolling out. Here's what you can expect.

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

#3139. After 120 Hours of Testing, This Phone Had the Longest-Lasting Battery Life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

We benchmarked the battery life on nearly three dozen smartphones from companies like Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google.

A shiny brand-new phone might not have a longer battery life than your old phone.

The phones that CNET tested in 2026 had, on average, the same battery life as models we tested in 2025 and in 2024. That doesn’t mean that we didn’t have standouts. Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max top our testing results, along with foldable phones like the Motorola Razr (2026) and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, each of which has a silicon-carbon battery and offers increased capacity without requiring a larger physical battery. The most recently released device we tested, the iPhone Duo, tied for the top spot in one of our tests.

Late-2025 models like the iPhone 17 and OnePlus 15 (RIP OnePlus) are among the best values for getting the most time between charges.

Having your phone run out of battery is extremely frustrating, especially when it happens at an inconvenient time. No one wants to be seated on the floor of an airport terminal with their phone plugged into an outlet.

Battery life is affected by several factors. If your phone is 2-3 years old, the battery capacity is likely less than when it was fresh out of the box. How much you use your phone affects how long you have between charges. Are you a Light Lift Lisa and rarely on your handset? Or are you an Obsessively Online Oliver and your phone never leaves your hand?

While it seems that companies add larger batteries to new smartphones, those same phones come with new power-hungry features like brighter screens, more powerful processors and AI tools that gobble up that “extra” battery life. And CNET’s phone battery testing shows just this.

CNET tested the battery life of 28 phones in 2026 so far, and our results continue to show that a higher capacity (typically measured in milliamp-hours or mAh) doesn’t always mean the longest-lasting battery throughout the day. These devices, along with four handsets that didn’t get updates this year, are included in our results. Each phone was put through a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute anecdotal stress test, both with the battery at 100%. The results show the remaining battery percentage – the higher, the better. We averaged the results to determine our rankings. 32 phones were each tested for 3 hours and 45 minutes, meaning CNET has spent 120 hours testing smartphone battery life over the past year.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is our overall winner for having the longest battery life. Apple gave the 18 Pro Max a larger battery compared to the equally impressive 2025 iPhone 17 Pro Max. That increased capacity which along with iOS 27 optimizations and the efficient Apple A20 Pro chip, gave the 18 Pro Max an edge over last year’s model and every phone that we’ve tested in 2026.

Most phones sold in 2026 were hit with a price increase due to US tariffs and higher RAM and component costs driven by demand from AI data centers. That doesn’t mean you can’t find an affordable phone with great battery life. Notably, the $500 Motorola Moto G Stylus (2026) and the $600 Motorola Edge (2026) both rank in our top 10. Interestingly, while Motorola incorporated silicon-carbon batteries into its Razr phone line, these two budget handsets lack them. It’s like that the screens and processors on the Stylus and Edge don’t consume as much power as a $1,000 flagship phone with all the bells and whistles.

If you’re looking for an affordable iOS phone, you might need to adjust your definition. The cheapest phone Apple sells is the $699 iPhone 17E, which I’d argue isn’t what’s considered a budget device. However, the 17E lasted a long time in our tests and its performance tied with phones that are nearly twice and three times its $700 price: the $1,400 Motorola Razr Ultra (2026) and the $1,999 Apple iPhone Duo – both foldable phones.

We tested a variety of phones from brands you know well, like Samsung, Google and Apple, to handsets you likely never heard of, like Xiaomi’s wonderful photography-centric Leica Leitzphone, or the controversial “gold” T1 Phone from Trump Mobile (a rebranded 2024 HTC U24 Pro nicknamed the “Trump Phone”) that scored toward the bottom of our ranking.

We run two battery-life tests on all the phones we review at CNET: one that stresses the phone and the other for video streaming. In our 45-minute stress test, during which we stream videos, make a video call, play games and scroll social media, and with the battery starting at 100%, the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo took the top spots, only dropping 1%. Google’s Pixel 11 Pro XL deserves a shoutout for tying for third, losing only 3%. Compare that with the 2025 Pixel 10 Pro XL, which dropped by 7% in the same test.

In the 3-hour video battery test, where a video is streamed over Wi-Fi for 3 hours with the screen at full brightness and the battery starting at 100%, the smaller iPhone 18 Pro took the top spot, losing only 6%. The iPhone 17 deserves your attention, as it scored among the top results for both tests, as did the Motorola Razr (2026) and (more expensive) Razr Ultra (2026) flip phones.

If you’re wondering how to remember all these model names and qualifiers like Pro, Ultra, XL and Max, we also looked at how all the models from a specific brand did by averaging the results. We only did this for companies where we tested more than one model. So if you’re looking for the brand that sells phones with the best battery life, go with Apple.

This is the second year in a row that the iPhone lineup has performed better in our battery life tests than other brands. OnePlus, a subsidiary of the Chinese brand Oppo, came in second but sadly announced that it will stop releasing phones in the US after the OnePlus 15 series. So if you see a great deal on the OnePlus 15 or budget OnePlus 15R, they are both excellent options for amazing battery life.

This year we saw Motorola and Samsung begin adopting silicon-carbon batteries in some models, mostly foldable phones. But I imagine in 2027 and beyond that we’ll see more companies using that type of power cell.

Lastly, if you’re happy with your current phone and your only complaint is that it doesn’t hold a charge like when you first got it, don’t buy a new phone. Instead, replace the battery, either yourself or have a service do it for you. If you’re an iPhone owner, the Apple Store will do this for $80-$100, depending on the model and how much your battery has degraded. Replacing the battery will save you hundreds of dollars and add a few more years to your phone’s life-span.Of course, there are always power banks to help keep your phone’s battery topped off, too.

Black Friday is just weeks away and there are already deals on power banks, including this one specifically designed for Apple’s iPhone Duo foldable.

#3137. Firefox’s Built-In VPN Hides Your IP Address at No Cost. What You Should Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Firefox’s built-in VPN masks your IP address while you browse, gives you 50GB a month, and only requires a free Mozilla account.

Firefox comes with 50GB of free VPN browsing every month, and all it asks for is a free Mozilla account. Mozilla added the built-in VPN to desktop Firefox in March, then brought it to Android in July. It routes your browser traffic through a proxy server, hiding your IP address and location from the sites you visit, and you can choose which server location to use. It doesn’t protect other apps on your device, but for everyday browsing, it covers a lot without a subscription.

Keep in mind that free VPNs can be dangerous. If they’re not from a trusted provider, they can put your data at risk or include vulnerabilities you wouldn’t find in some of the more popular paid VPN services.

In CNET’s tests, among VPN services that offer a free tier, the best free plan on the market is Proton VPN’s free service. (It’s the only free VPN CNET currently recommends.) But the free Proton VPN service is missing some features found in the company’s premium plan, such as the ability to choose a server manually or connect multiple devices at the same time.

Mozilla’s overall VPN technology has undergone independent audits from Cure53, has resolved security issues over its history and uses WireGuard, which gives it a good security foundation.

The browser-based free version may give the impression that it offers the same level of overall protection as a stand-alone VPN. However, it only protects web traffic viewed through the Firefox browser.

“The fundamental limitation is scope,” said Jacob Kalvo, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of Live Proxies, which provides technical services to businesses and individuals. “[The free Firefox VPN] only protects browser traffic, not apps, system processes or other network activity. That creates a false sense of ‘full protection’ for less technical users.”

That could make it a useful feature for casual use while browsing the web for those who don’t already have a VPN service. And Kalvo says the 50GB data limit is generous for a browser-based VPN.

But, he said, for anything involving “sensitive data, competitive intelligence, or large-scale operations,” he doesn’t recommend it.

Van Leeuwen noted that AI is rapidly changing how software companies function.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced.
