Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

#3132. Why Intel Stock Collapsed 23.4% Last Month

The semiconductor giant is seeing weakness in the PC market.

Shares of Intel (INTC +0.69%) fell 23.4% in October, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The semiconductor giant has seen its share price begin to slip due to weak demand in the PC market, its second-largest revenue generator after artificial intelligence (AI).

There are also doubts about the future of its outsourced manufacturing foundry business. Here's why Intel stock collapsed in October, and why it is now down over 50% from its highs.

Intel is trying to build three business lines for the future of computing. First, it is selling computer chips for personal computers (PCs). Second is its own data center and AI computer chips. Third, it manufactures computer chips for third parties, a process called a foundry.

The second line is doing quite well at the moment, with Intel's data center and AI segment posting 78% revenue growth to $7.3 billion last quarter. However, it is the traditional PC business that is showing signs of strain, with revenue down 5% last quarter and guidance for weak upcoming quarters. This is due to rising costs for computer chips around the globe, which is putting a dent in demand for people to buy their own computers.

Third is the foundry business. Its revenue grew 58% to $6.7 billion, but investors are expecting much more for a business that is backed by the U.S. government and important to the AI trade. Its largest competitor, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, grew revenue by 41% year-over-year, on a much larger revenue scale of $47 billion. Intel's foundry business is also losing money at over $1 billion per quarter.

Investors have made large bets on Intel as the United States' champion in AI chip manufacturing. The stock is still up 57% over the past year, even after this drawdown.

However, when you look at its guidance vs. the stock's valuation, it is hard to make a case for owning shares today. The stock trades at a market cap of $329 billion. Over the last twelve months, Intel's revenue was $60 billion, or a price-to-sales ratio (P/S) of 5.3. The business is growing again but will face headwinds from the PC market and is not as well positioned to capitalize on the AI boom as investors would have liked.

For that reason, the stock is likely one to avoid for the time being.

#3131. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously records audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

#3130. How AI Data Centers Became a Central Issue in Today’s Midterm Election

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Server farms for AI have become a uniting issue for voters and a bipartisan headache for candidates.

For years we’ve heard concerns from residents near hyperscale data centers at city council meetings and other public hearings in towns across the country. Now, those fears — about the environment, rising electric costs and general quality of life — are playing a big role in voters’ decisions as they head to the polls to vote in Tuesday’s midterm election.

Recent polls show majorities of Democrats and independents, along with a sizable share of Republicans, oppose new data centers in their areas. That leaves candidates in both parties answering questions about projects once courted by state and local leaders. Supporters say the facilities bring jobs, tax revenue and an advantage in AI development.

Further, a new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community.

Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.

Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.

Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue.

As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.

The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026.

A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room.

According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide.

“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.

Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.

The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

#3128. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3126. Warren Buffett Has 1 Simple Rule for Investing During Bear Markets. History Says He's Right.

Take a lesson from Buffett's experience in 2008.

Warren Buffett picked a tough time to tell people to buy stocks. On Oct. 16, 2008, with the financial crisis in full swing, he wrote his famous op-ed in The New York Times, "Buy American. I Am." In it, he announced that he was buying stocks again.

Unfortunately, that call came way too early in the bear market. From the time this piece was published to the March 2009 low, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.58%) fell by more than 30%. It was one of the few times in his career where investors thought he might have finally lost his magic touch. While the timing of his buying proved to be incorrect, there were a couple of Buffett principles that proved to be right.

It's easy to look at the 30% loss figure from this example and presume that this trade was a disaster. But it wasn't completely. In fact, history would go on to show that it eventually became a really good trade.

The reason is that by October 2008 when Buffett announced that he was buying U.S. stocks again, the S&P 500 was already down roughly 40% from its high. He was actually fulfilling one of his other investing tenets: "Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful."

Many investors had long since abandoned their equity positions and moved into cash. With the entire U.S. economy looking like it was on the brink of collapse, there was little demand for stocks while prices were still falling.

But Buffett viewed it as an opportunity to buy stocks at discounted prices. He finally found value after the S&P 500 fell by 40% and acted on it. He didn't care what anybody else in the market was doing. His investing process told him that it was time to buy -- which is one of Buffett's key investing principles: Keep investing even when short-term conditions turn rough.

That means continuing to make monthly periodic investment plan contributions into brokerage accounts and 401(k)'s. It also means putting the process on autopilot so you don't accidentally miss an investment or are tempted to avoid it because stock prices are down.

Imagine a scenario where someone invested right at the market peak before the financial crisis. But they held on throughout the bear market and rode it out all the way back to its previous high. Granted, that would have been a six-year journey from start to finish. But a full round trip would have resulted in a total return of 0%.

Now imagine that person continuing to make monthly investments from the pre-crisis peak in late 2007 to the new high in early 2014. They would have spent over six years picking up additional shares at prices below their previous highs. At the bottom in March 2009, they would have bought at nearly 60% less than the price a year and a half earlier. That's a heck of a deal!

Any initial investment made at the pre-crisis peak would have earned a 0% return, just as in the example above. But all of those incremental purchases along the way would have produced a positive return once the S&P 500 finally got back to its previous high. Buying as share prices are falling or well below their previous high can actually enhance your portfolio's long-term returns. Bear markets are essentially sales that don't get advertised.

In his op-ed, Buffett explained that he wasn't trying to pick the market's low. He was simply trying to invest at the point where the value was attractive enough to invest.

That's good advice to heed. You'll drive yourself nuts trying to find the absolute market bottom. And there's a good chance that stocks will keep falling after you buy. But if you find requisite value at some point, it's a good enough time to buy. And just as Buffett found out, the long-term boost to your returns can be substantial.

Keep investing during those bear markets. So many people are tempted to run to the sidelines when conditions get bad. In most cases, those are the best times to pick up shares on sale. Keep your focus on your long-term goals and take advantage of the sales along the way!

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

During its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call, Apple execs covered supply chain struggles, high memory costs and the role AI will play in future financials.

John Ternus led his first earnings call as Apple's new CEO this week.

Leading his first earnings call at the helm of Apple this week, CEO John Ternus announced strong revenue growth, but acknowledged that the ongoing chip shortage could make things difficult for the foreseeable future.

For the last quarter of fiscal 2026, revenue was up 12% year over year, capping what Ternus called the company’s “best fiscal year ever,” with $418 billion in revenue. The growth comes despite “unprecedented” supply chain constraints and rising memory costs limiting the availability of iPhone, iPad and Mac hardware. Warning that shortages could continue through next year, Ternus didn’t rule out future price increases for affected Apple products.

Monday’s earnings call comes as Apple ranks as the world’s most valuable company, overtaking Nvidia last week, and on the heels of a string of high-profile product debuts: the brand’s first foldable iPhone, its first touchscreen MacBook Pro laptop and the new HomeView hub at the center of its renewed smart home ambitions.

At the center of Apple’s ecosystem sits the iPhone, which Ternus described as an “intelligent personal hub.” Despite supply chain limitations, Apple saw iPhone sales grow to a record $57.6 billion in revenue for the quarter, accounting for the lion’s share of the brand’s total quarterly revenue. Sales were spurred by the launch of the new flagship iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, as well as early adopters of the iPhone Duo.

Apple executives didn’t comment on reports of cracked screens on some early examples. Apple announced and released the iPhone 18 Pro with its variable aperture camera at an event last month, but the standard (and more affordable) iPhone 18 was notably absent from any mention. Staggered releases for the two tiers aren’t unprecedented, but Apple usually announces the standard and Pro phones together, at least.

Like the rest of the computing world, Apple has faced tariffs, supply chain shortages and rising memory costs for some time, hampering its ability to meet demand for its most popular products. Apple Chief Technology Officer Sadih Khan says that the availability of memory and storage will increasingly limit the supply of iPhones, iPads and Macs.

Apple’s Mac Mini and Mac Studio have been especially hammered by the AI boom. On one hand, the components they require are being slurped up by AI data centers. On the other hand, they’re wildly popular among home AI enthusiasts and developers running local agents like OpenClaw.

In the past, the company has been able to somewhat offset memory shortages by relying on stockpiled components and compensating with price hikes for the Mac and iPad in June and the iPhone in September. But there doesn’t appear to be much relief from the component crisis on the horizon.

Ternus said there’s room to expand Siri and Apple Intelligence capabilities over time, growing to include more sophisticated capabilities that take advantage of server-side horsepower in the cloud: iCloud horsepower that Apple can begin charging for.

Apple is a hardware company, as its record revenue confirms: The iPhone is still its cash cow and largest revenue stream. But Apple’s services revenue is also booming, accounting for an increasingly large share of the revenue pie, and the company is leaning more heavily on subscriptions and ads. As Apple continues to evolve its AI ambitions beyond what can be reasonably handled by on-device silicon, there’s bound to be a paid tier for Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, bundled into an iCloud or iCloud Plus tier.

Executives made it clear that memory costs and supply constraints will continue to weigh on iPhones, iPads, Macs and MacBooks through the winter holidays and beyond. Though they declined to say whether further price increases are coming, there’s a high probability of more hikes hitting consumers next year.

#3124. 2 Monster Stocks to Buy and Hold for the Next 20 Years

Alphabet and Amazon both sold off on AI spending fears, but that spending could also make them AI winners.

Great companies will sometimes see their stocks fall. But what truly makes a monster stock is a business with excellent growth characteristics, built on durable competitive advantages, or moats, that can keep earnings growing for decades through rough patches.

Alphabet (GOOG +0.03%) (GOOGL +0.13%) and Amazon (AMZN +2.15%) fit that description. These monster stocks have slightly outperformed the Nasdaq-100 -- an index that includes the best of breed in the tech sector -- over the last 10 years.

Both just dropped after earnings amid worries about heavy artificial intelligence (AI) spending, providing investors a more attractive entry point to buy and hold these monster stocks for the next 20 years.

Alphabet's moat is built on its ownership of every piece of the artificial intelligence (AI) puzzle: its own chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs); its Gemini models; its cloud business; and products used by billions of people. CEO Sundar Pichai said this full-stack approach "drives a lot of efficiency" and gives Alphabet options across a wide range of opportunities. That's a combination few companies can copy.

The third-quarter report showed that advantage paying off. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to about $31 billion, and its operating margin jumped to 36% from 24% a year ago. In other words, the cloud business is growing fast and getting more profitable at the same time.

Still, the stock fell about 13% in early trading the day after earnings on Oct. 30. Wall Street didn't seem to like the continued heavy spending on data centers, which pushed free cash flow negative in the quarter.

But the sell-off leaves the shares trading at a more attractive 17 times 2026 earnings estimates -- a discount to the Nasdaq-100 average forward earnings multiple of 21. That valuation looks too modest for one of the leading AI companies whose finance chief expects returns on that spending to be "meaningfully above our cost of capital." For a 20-year investor, that dip looks like an opportunity.

Amazon's moat is huge in two giant businesses: Amazon Web Services (AWS), its cloud computing arm, and a retail network that keeps getting faster at delivering packages and cheaper to run. CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon is "on a path to have two" businesses with a trillion dollars in annual revenue, AWS and its online store. That kind of scale is hard for rivals to match.

Q3 results showed AWS revenue surging 39% year over year, marking its sixth straight quarter of faster growth and its fastest pace in nearly five years. Jassy believes the industry is in a "10-to-20-year cycle" of companies moving their computing to the cloud.

Even so, shares slid about 7% in pre-market trading on Oct. 30 as investors focused on the company's heavy AI spending. That puts the stock at about 30 times 2026 earnings estimates and about 23 times 2027 estimates.

Wall Street may not like the heavy capital spending and negative free cash flow. Still, Jassy called AI "a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity." The post-earnings sell-off is a chance to invest in that opportunity at a discount.

The risk for both is that massive AI spending continues to weigh on free cash flow. If AI demand cools before those data centers pay off, profits could fall short, and the stocks could go through a stretch of underperformance relative to the broader market.

Still, for patient investors, businesses that can afford to spend the most will have the most compute capacity and may be best positioned to win in AI. That opportunity is why Alphabet and Amazon are quality tech stocks to hold for the next 20 years.

#3122. Why Shares of AST SpaceMobile Slipped 27% Last Month

The satellite internet provider is coming back to Earth.

Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS +3.70%) fell 26.8% last month, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The potentially disruptive satellite internet operator has slipped because it is falling behind in getting satellites into orbit and faces a threat from SpaceX.

The stock is now down 71% from its highs, and fell a further 27% in October. Here's why, and whether now could be a good time to buy the dip.

With large-array satellites, AST SpaceMobile believes it has developed the capability to beam satellite internet directly to mobile devices from low Earth orbit. The technology has been validated with numerous tests, which is why investors have bid the stock up so much from the lows.

However, even if the technology works, it still requires numerous satellites in orbit to provide fully functional satellite internet coverage. According to management, it will need at least 45 in orbit, up from only 13 today, for the service to begin working in the United States and a select few other markets. To do so, it needs to hitch a ride on a rocket launch service, specifically SpaceX.

The problem is, there is a huge bottleneck of satellites waiting to get deployed into orbit, including from its launch provider SpaceX and the Starlink satellite internet service. Elon Musk says Starlink will start providing direct-to-smartphone service, which could compete with AST SpaceMobile before it even gets off the ground.

For the time being, AST SpaceMobile is generating little revenue and has heavy cash burn. Last quarter alone, it had negative free cash flow of $719 million.

After this stock price collapse, AST SpaceMobile trades at a market cap of $15 billion. This is still a significant premium over its trailing revenue, which isn't much.

In theory, AST SpaceMobile will be able to quickly scale revenue when its satellite internet service is operational, which it plans to sell through telecommunications providers. However, not everyone in the world will want or need extra satellite internet coverage beyond what they get from mobile and at-home providers.

For this reason, it is likely that AST SpaceMobile will be a niche offering. Even if it can start scaling revenue, the stock looks overvalued today. At $1 billion in revenue, it would have a price-to-sales ratio (P/S) of 15, and likely a high price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) once you account for its heavy cost base. For this reason, investors should avoid buying AST SpaceMobile stock right now.

#3121. Siri Is Getting Ears on the Apple Watch: Here’s What That Means for Your Privacy

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Two controversial new features arriving in beta this week will let the Apple Watch rewind and recap conversations.

Your Apple Watch is about to start listening a little more closely (if you want it to). A beta rolling out this week gives Siri ears on the Series 12 and Ultra 4, with new features that can recall what was said in the last 15 seconds and summarize conversations throughout your day.

Audio Intelligence, as the new set of perks is called, consists of four audio-related features: music recognition, sound recognition, Siri rewind and Siri recap. The first two, which have been available since launch, include a faster Shazam that can recognize songs without even opening the app.

I’ve been testing it in beta and noticed it responds much faster, especially since I don’t even have to open the app to identify a song. Songs now appear automatically in my watch’s Smart Stack. This even includes the lullabies I sing to my toddler at bedtime, though understandably, it hasn’t been able to identify those.

Sound Recognition can alert people who are deaf or hard of hearing to sounds such as a crying baby, barking dog or doorbell.

How to access: You have to enable the feature on your iPhone, under Settings > Accessibility > Sound and Name Recognition and toggle it on. You can even select which sounds you want it to identify.

In my testing, it successfully identified my fake cough, the doorbell and the car horn. But then it spent the rest of the day gaslighting me, telling me there was a dog barking or a car honking when there clearly wasn’t, which made me question both my own reality and its listening range. But this may require further testing, since I’m still on the beta versions of all these.

The newest features, which are out now in beta, are the most controversial, and I’ll be testing them more this week.

At any point during the day, Siri Rewind lets you double-click the Digital Crown to pull up a text snippet of what was said in the previous 15 seconds, kind of like the audio version of Live Photos (which lets you see a few seconds of video before and after you pressed the shutter).

How to access the transcribed text? If you do nothing after seeing it on screen, it disappears. You can also ask Siri about it, or save it to the Siri app to view later on your phone. Old audio is continuously replaced by new audio and then deleted, so if you don’t trigger the feature to recall the last 15 seconds, it’s gone.

This is for unplanned moments where you need to revisit information without having to ask the speaker to repeat themselves. Apple’s keynote example showed someone reviewing the specials menu at a restaurant after the waiter had already walked away from the table. Whether you want to look away from the person speaking down at your watch instead of just asking them to repeat what they said is more of an etiquette question, but it could be helpful during large presentations.

Siri Recap can listen in the background while enabled and generate high-level summaries and key points of conversations throughout your day. This can be anything from a parent-teacher conference or work meeting to spur-of-the-moment conversations or brainstorming sessions with coworkers that you wouldn’t go out of your way to record with Voice Memos.

How to access it: Similar to Siri Rewind, the notes from these recaps can either be saved in the Siri app and exported to the Notes or Journal app, or deleted. They automatically delete after seven days if you don’t delete manually.

Both features are opt-in, meaning you have to go out of your way to enable them during setup for them to work.

Once they’re on, Siri Rewind requires you to manually double-tap the digital crown to activate it. Siri Recap is completely customizable.

You can leave it on at all times and let Siri decide what counts as important conversations to recap, set it to on a schedule based on important meetings for the day, or enable it manually via the new Siri Recap icon in the Control Center on your Apple Watch like you would Focus mode or Do Not Disturb.

If you forget to turn it off, you’ll get a reminder in the morning telling you it’s on. You’ll also get reminders to check your recaps throughout the day and notifications when schedules start or stop, so you’re aware when it’s active.

And it won’t work for conference calls or FaceTime, if you have your AirPods or headphones in. It only works with audio it can pick up through the speaker.

Even if you do decide to leave all four on all day, Apple says they won’t ding your battery. The Apple Watch Series 12 gets around a day and a half of use (in my real-world testing), while the Ultra 4 gets anywhere from two and a half to three days of use.

This is possible because of Apple’s new S11 chip and its dual architecture in which one part handles background tasks without draining the more power-hungry main processor.

The Audio Intelligence features won’t affect battery life.

The watch doesn’t save audio. It processes raw audio inside a hardware-isolated compartment on the S11 chip that Apple says even it can’t access, called the Secure Exclave.

Siri Recap doesn’t send a full transcript to the cloud, either. It condenses the text first, deletes the full transcript and sends only that condensed version to Private Cloud Compute. It omits financial data, authentication details, personal identifiers, language related to self-harm and government secrets.

Still, there’s something about explicitly giving the watch on my wrist the ability to listen to conversations that doesn’t sit right with me and many others. Especially when those conversations involve other people who may have no idea it’s happening.

There’s a chime that alerts people when Rewind is active, but to my knowledge, there’s no other warning when Siri is recapping a conversation. Smart glasses like the Meta Ray-Bans have an indicator light when they record video, though even that isn’t foolproof, since there are ways to get around it.

Maybe I’ll change my mind once I can actually test it. Apple has certainly given me reasons to trust how it protects data. I’m just not convinced yet that this is the intelligence I want my watch to have.

The features are rolling out in beta, with the update to iOS 27.3, initially in English, with additional languages planned later.

I’ll be testing over the coming weeks, so check back for more.

#3120. This Index Just Did Something It Hasn't Done Since 2009. Is It Time To Buy?

The current tech pullback has overshadowed the gains happening elsewhere in the market.

With tech stocks having fallen by roughly 10% from their all-time high in early October, a historic gap has opened between that sector and the rest of the market.

The equal-weight version of the S&P 500 just had its single best monthly outperformance of the traditional index in more than 17 years. It returned 5% in October, compared with a loss of around 0.8% for the S&P 500.

Obviously, this kind of dichotomy doesn't exist without a major shift in the U.S. equity market. The decline in tech and the "Magnificent Seven" stocks is the biggest catalyst. But more than 70% of S&P 500 components were actually up on the month. There's also a much larger rotation happening below the surface.

On October 7, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP -0.01%) was trailing the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF by nearly 4% on a year-to-date basis. As of the end of October, it's leading by roughly 3.6%. So this has been a significant shift away from big tech, which had accounted for around 39% of the S&P 500.

It'd be easy to see what's happening in tech and say that the U.S. equity market is selling off. But it isn't. You just need to see where the returns are coming from.

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF and the Vanguard Communication Services ETF, which includes NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Broadcom, were the only two S&P 500 sectors that were negative in October. The rest were positive, some significantly so.

I think the biggest story is what was leading last month. The top four performing sectors were energy, consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare.

Energy stocks continue to perform strongly, with Brent crude oil prices flirting with $120 a barrel. The other three sectors are all considered defensive equities. The positive overall performance of the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF shows that investors are still buying stocks. But they're unquestionably rotating into more conservative, non-growth areas of the market.

When this last occurred 17 years ago, the whole market was in the process of recovering from the financial crisis. The S&P 500 bottomed out one month earlier, and it wasn't surprising to see small-caps outperforming large-caps. It's a pattern we often see in the early stages of a recovery cycle. The turnaround from the COVID bear market in the latter half of 2020 is a good example.

We're not in a recovery cycle today. We're just in an environment where a handful of major tech stocks have been pulling the indexes higher. Whenever you have that kind of top-heavy concentration, the S&P 500 is vulnerable to a sharp pullback whenever the theme that's been driving them higher starts to cool. That looks like the point we're at now with the AI boom. The heavy capex spending that got investors excited about a year ago is raising investors' concerns now.

In terms of speculating about how the market could progress from here, I believe a 2009 environment would produce a higher likelihood of an extended run for the equal-weight S&P 500. It could still happen in 2026, but it just takes a change in investor sentiment to kill the rally.

Tech stocks have been leading the market pretty much non-stop since the beginning of 2023. It's not surprising that an eventual correction would happen.

But this is exactly why the argument for diversification is so strong. Whether it's just a modest addition of smaller companies via the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF or a more dramatic shift with the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF, taking some tech exposure off the table probably isn't a bad idea.

Plus, consider how equal-weight tends to outperform cap-weight in a recovering market or economy. The better long-term play right now could be going with the equal-weight option.

#3119. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

#3118. Taiwan Semi or Broadcom: If I Could Only Own 1 for the Next 5 Years, It Would Be This

Both stocks have more than tripled in three years, but only one of them gets paid no matter which AI chip designer comes out on top.

If you own stock in Broadcom (AVGO +3.28%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +1.82%), you have to be pretty happy about your returns over the last three years. Broadcom stock is up nearly 300% over the last three years, and Taiwan Semiconductor has done even better, gaining 370%.

Both play critical roles in the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI), but their businesses are very different. Broadcom designs custom AI accelerators and networking chips that help technology companies build powerful AI systems. Taiwan Semiconductor, better known as TSMC, manufactures the advanced chips that companies like Broadcom design.

And that distinction is why, if I could own only one of these semiconductor stocks for the next five years, I'd choose TSMC stock.

There's plenty to like about Broadcom. The company has become a major player in AI infrastructure, supplying custom accelerators and networking technology to some of the world's largest technology companies.

Broadcom makes custom chips, called application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Rather than relying entirely on general-purpose graphics processing units (GPUs) from Nvidia, hyperscalers can work with Broadcom to develop processors designed for their specific AI workloads.

That can deliver better performance and efficiency for certain applications. And as companies spend billions building AI infrastructure, even modest efficiency improvements can translate into substantial savings. And Broadcom has revenue streams beyond AI, including semiconductor products and infrastructure software.

But there's a catch. Broadcom's custom AI chip business depends on customers continuing to invest in their own processors, and it faces competition from Nvidia and other chip designers. Its growth opportunities are substantial, but so are the expectations surrounding its AI business.

TSMC offers a different way to invest in that same demand. Let's see how.

One of TSMC's most attractive features is that it doesn't need to predict which chip designer will emerge as the biggest winner in AI. That's because TSMC manufactures chips for Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Apple, and Broadcom, among others. These companies compete in different semiconductor markets, but they all depend on TSMC's manufacturing capabilities.

And TSMC has an extraordinary competitive advantage. Manufacturing advanced semiconductors requires enormous capital investments, sophisticated equipment, and years of experience perfecting production processes. Developing a chip design is difficult enough. Manufacturing millions of those chips with consistently high yields is an entirely different challenge.

TSMC has spent decades building that expertise, and its dominance in the pure-play foundry market demonstrates just how difficult it is for competitors to catch up. TSMC produced more than 12,600 different products in 2025 and used more than 300 separate process technologies.

The company's manufacturing leadership is particularly valuable as chip designers move toward smaller, more advanced process technologies. TSMC's ability to manufacture leading-edge chips at scale makes it an essential partner for companies pursuing faster and more power-efficient processors.

Broadcom may win new customers for custom AI chips. Nvidia may maintain its dominance in AI accelerators. AMD could gain market share. TSMC stands to benefit from all three outcomes.

TSMC isn't without risks. The company needs to spend enormous amounts of money to expand capacity and develop new manufacturing technologies. And while its international expansion, including its massive investments in Arizona, should help it diversify production geographically, those facilities come with higher costs.

Still, I believe TSMC has the more attractive long-term business position. Broadcom's success depends partly on its ability to win custom chip designs and maintain relationships with major customers. TSMC, meanwhile, benefits from demand across a much broader group of semiconductor designers.

That doesn't make TSMC immune to an AI spending slowdown. Lower demand for advanced chips would affect both companies. And a great business isn't automatically a great stock at any valuation. But over a five-year holding period, I'd prefer to own the company that manufactures the chips rather than bet on which designer will capture the most business.

Broadcom is an outstanding semiconductor company with considerable growth potential. Yet even if Broadcom becomes one of AI's biggest winners, it will still need someone to manufacture its advanced chips. And there's a very good chance that someone will be TSMC.

#3117. SpaceX Just Delivered a Monster Quarter, but the Stock Is Still Down 38% From Its High. The Reasons Are Obvious.

Space Exploration Technologies' third-quarter earnings report demonstrated impressive growth from Starlink and artificial intelligence (AI) services.

When Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +3.68%) made its stock market debut in June, investors rushed in to participate in what some considered a once-in-a-generation investment opportunity.

SpaceX stock reached an all-time high of $226 on June 16, briefly propelling its valuation above those of Microsoft and Amazon. However, enthusiasm has cooled quite a bit.

As of this writing (Nov. 2), SpaceX stock traded at roughly $140, representing a staggering 38% decline from its peak. Let's assess why Wall Street is punishing SpaceX right now and determine if this sell-off represents a buying opportunity for long-term investors.

SpaceX's third-quarter financial report proved that its transformation into a diversified technology company is gaining momentum. The Starlink connectivity business generated $5.2 billion in revenue, representing 69% year-over-year growth. Operating income from this segment doubled to $2.4 billion.

Meanwhile, SpaceX's Super Intelligence (SI) division generated $7.6 billion in revenue, up 830% year over year. This business is benefiting from growing demand for computing capacity, including agreements with major AI developers such as Anthropic and Alphabet. Moreover, SpaceX is also developing its Grok AI model while pursuing longer-term opportunities involving orbital data centers.

Perhaps the most encouraging part of the earnings report was that SpaceX's consolidated operating income reached $2.8 billion, compared with an operating loss of $273 million last year. Even so, robust earnings don't always translate into strong stock performance. Sometimes, investors are more concerned about what lies ahead than what a company has already achieved.

I see three reasons for the decline in SpaceX stock.

First, the expiration of IPO lockup agreements is introducing selling pressure. Lockup agreements temporarily prevent certain employees, executives, and early investors from selling shares following an IPO. As these restrictions expire, previously unavailable shares become eligible for trading.

According to its IPO prospectus, SpaceX established a staggered release schedule, allowing up to 59.1 million shares to become eligible for sale after 91 days, followed by three additional releases of up to 328.4 million shares each. Furthermore, up to 1.3 billion additional shares became eligible for sale following the company's third-quarter earnings announcement.

Becoming eligible for sale doesn't mean every shareholder immediately sells. However, the idea of additional supply can weigh on investor sentiment, especially when early shareholders are likely sitting on life-changing gains.

Second, SpaceX's valuation was arguably stretched from the get-go. At its June peak, SpaceX boasted a market capitalization of more than $2.6 trillion. Even after its sell-off, the company remains valued at $1.9 trillion. Based on Wall Street's expected 2026 revenue forecast of $48.9 billion, this represents a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 39. That's a hefty premium for a company operating several capital-intensive businesses.

Third, SpaceX's ambitions require enormous capital expenditures (capex). During the third quarter, the company spent $19.6 billion on capex. For perspective, that investment exceeded SpaceX's entire revenue for the quarter.

While operating profitability is improving, the company's aggressive spending plans will pressure free cash flow. As a result, SpaceX is turning to debt financing to support its infrastructure expansion, including a reported $40 billion offering to buy GPUs.

This creates another layer of risk. Building AI data centers requires substantial capital outlays up front, but the returns on these investments are entirely dependent on customer demand, pricing dynamics, and utilization rates.

The recent sell-off underscores an important distinction between business performance and stock performance. SpaceX can continue delivering robust financial results while its stock declines if investors think they are paying too much for future growth.

While this doesn't necessarily mean the underlying investment thesis is broken, it also doesn't automatically make the stock cheap. SpaceX still carries a premium valuation, and its expansion plans will require meaningful additional financing. At the same time, the payoff from these infrastructure investments is far from guaranteed.

Nevertheless, I think SpaceX's decline could be an opportunity to begin gradually accumulating shares. Rather than attempting to identify the exact bottom, building a position over time will help manage the risks associated with additional lock-up expirations and valuation adjustments.

All told, SpaceX's sell-off is a mixture of technical selling pressure, elevated valuation expectations, and concerns about accelerating capex. While its latest earnings report suggests the business is strengthening, the stock will likely remain volatile as Wall Street reassesses the company's ability to generate cash flow consistently. For patient investors willing to tolerate that uncertainty, I think SpaceX is a compelling long-term opportunity.

#3116. Another child dies of measles as CDC reportedly holds up health alert

NY gov. pointed to Kennedy’s long-standing anti-vaccine work as spurring outbreaks.

A child in New York has died of measles, health officials in the state announced late Monday. It marks the first reported measles-associated death in New York in more than 30 years. It is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the US this year; all six of the other deaths were reported in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing a dramatic measles outbreak that has stricken over 1,430 people this year. Prior to the deaths, Pennsylvania hadn’t seen a measles-related death in 35 years.

The boom in vaccine-preventable outbreaks, cases,  and tragic deaths is being fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. One of the most prominent anti-vaccine activists in the US currently serves as the US health secretary; Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent decades prior to taking office attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation. He and his anti-vaccine organization, Children’s Health Defense, have been one of the most prolific sources of anti-vaccine content.

Since taking office, Kennedy has waged a multi-front war on vaccines that has included dismantling and obstructing federal vaccine recommendations; launching dubious studies to look for alleged, unspecified harms of vaccines; promoting alleged vaccine injuries; and continuing to spread misinformation about vaccines and vaccine-preventable illnesses.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul directly tied the state’s death to Kennedy’s policies and anti-vaccine activism. She called the child’s death “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” She also said she was “heartbroken” by the death, sending her condolences to the family. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through,” Hochul said. Overall, New York has reported 170 measles cases in over a dozen counties.

Days before the seventh preventable measles death, The Washington Post reported on Kennedy’s latest push to thwart public health efforts: Career scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention—which is under Kennedy’s control—were blocked from publishing an urgent health alert to clinicians regarding the risk and management of measles cases during pregnancy.

Given the previous success of vaccines and vaccination campaigns, many clinicians have never seen such cases in their careers. But measles infections during pregnancy pose severe, life-threatening risks to both pregnant people and fetuses. As such, CDC scientists wanted to issue an informational advisory through the CDC’s Health Alert Network.

But the CDC Director’s Office declined to provide the required approval for the alert, sources told the Post. The scientists have since moved to trying to publish the information in the CDC’s publication, The Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). But the peer-review process for the publication is longer than that of an advisory. Further, vaccine-related studies already approved for publication in MMWR have been suspiciously delayed, the Post reported. The scientists are now considering publishing the information outside the agency to avoid onerous clearance. Health officials in Pennsylvania, meanwhile, released their own alert on measles in pregnancy and congenital measles on October 19.

New York has not released the age of the child who died or any other details about the case. The other sixth deaths reported this year have included babies, including one with congenital measles. The six deaths in Pennsylvania included a newborn with congenital measles, whose mother was severely ill at the time of birth; a 6-week-old who was too young to be vaccinated; a “perfectly healthy” 18-year-old; a 20-year-old with leukemia; a 40-year-old with underlying conditions; and a 39-year-old with underlying conditions. All the deceased were unvaccinated.

Pennsylvania’s health department is currently only reporting five deaths; the department confirmed to Ars Technica on Monday that its investigation into the sixth death, reported by the Franklin County coroner on October 12, is still pending. A Franklin County judge has ordered that information about the death be sealed from public review, and The Philadelphia Inquirer has taken legal action to obtain certain death record details.

The CDC, meanwhile, has reported only three of the seven deaths this year. Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to delete some of the early deaths and has since changed how the CDC counts deaths. Instead of the long-standing practice of relaying reports from states, the CDC now relies on federal death records, which can take weeks to come through and are not designed to capture the real-time data needed to respond to an active outbreak.

Overall, the CDC reports over 4,850 measles cases across 47 states and jurisdictions. At least 511 people have been hospitalized. This year’s tally is more than double the total from all of 2025, which was 2,289 cases with three deaths. The 2026 tally is also the largest the country has seen since 1991, prior to measles being declared eliminated from the US in 2000 amid high vaccination rates.

#3115. Why Anthropic's IPO May Have Just Gotten a Whole Lot Riskier

The tech stock may end up going public at a very inopportune time.

Chatbot maker and leading artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic plans to go public later this month, potentially at a higher valuation than even Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SPCX +3.68%), which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it went public in June. Anthropic's valuation might top $2 trillion out of the gate.

That high a valuation creates risk for investors, as it means expectations will be enormous right away. While the business is certainly growing fast, it's still unprofitable and full of uncertainty. What's worse is that the risk related to buying the IPO may be even higher now.

In recent weeks, there have been significant sell-offs taking place in the tech sector, as lofty expectations weigh on many high-profile companies. The State Street Technology Select Sector SDPR ETF has declined by about 13% over the past month as market apprehension about tech has grown more pronounced.

Anthropic's ability to simply soar in value, and for it to command a high price simply because of a high growth rate or because it makes the popular Claude chatbot, may not be enough. The company's growth rate has been exceptional, coming in at a whopping 1,200% during the first nine months of the year, totaling $33.2 billion. However, with a net loss of $104 billion during that stretch, which includes changes in fair value and non-operating items, investors may be more likely to think twice about the stock now than even a month or two ago, when there wasn't so much of a spotlight on highly valued tech stocks.

Even SpaceX, which surpassed a $2 trillion valuation in its early trading days, has been falling of late to around its IPO price. It's struggled to get back to its early highs, in large part because its valuation is incredibly high and its fundamentals don't support such an elevated price.

Hype can have a significant impact on stocks, sending their valuations to inflated levels for long periods. But inevitably, they'll come crashing down to reality.

That's what I believe will happen with Anthropic. It might get close to $2 trillion in market cap when its IPO hits, but even if it does, it may ultimately fall significantly lower as the excitement fades, as more competition emerges, and the company's results simply don't look as impressive anymore, which can happen if the losses pile up and its growth rate slows down.

Anthropic isn't an IPO I'd consider buying, as it was already a risky investment to consider before the recent softness in the tech sector. Now, it could be going public at a very inopportune time, when the market is growing bearish on tech stocks as a whole. This is why I believe investors are likely better off waiting rather than rushing to buy the new IPO.

JetBlue's seat selection policy is based on the type of fare, so include the selection fee when comparing prices.

Airline miles, hotel points, travel insurance

JetBlue Airways charges more for seat selection than any other major U.S. airline, according to a NerdWallet analysis, so it pays to know when you can pick a seat for free.

The airline offers several seat options, including standard economy seats, extra-legroom seats and lie-flat Mint suites. But whether you can select a seat for free depends on the type of seat and fare you book, as well as whether you have Mosaic elite status.

Here’s what to know about JetBlue seat selection, including the different seat types, how much seat selection costs and when you can choose a seat for free.

JetBlue offers several onboard experiences, ranging from standard economy to lie-flat business-class seats.

JetBlue’s standard economy product is called Main, and there are three types of seats in this cabin.

Main: Economy seats throughout the Main cabin. These seats may be complimentary, depending on the fare type chosen.

Main Preferred: Economy seats located closer to the front of the cabin. They cost extra.

Extra Legroom: Seats with additional legroom that are located over the wing, in front of the Main Preferred seats. These seats also cost extra.

All Main cabin passengers receive complimentary snacks, drinks and Wi-Fi. Each seat also offers an entertainment screen with live television and movies.

EvenMore is JetBlue’s premium economy experience, and the seats are located in front of the Main cabin. These seats offer up to 38 inches of legroom and include priority boarding, priority security (at select airports) and dedicated overhead bin space.

Travelers receive three complimentary alcoholic drinks, unlimited nonalcoholic drinks and snacks, along with free Wi-Fi and a seatback entertainment screen with movies and live TV.

BlueFirst is JetBlue’s new domestic first class, which is expected to start flying on Dec. 8, 2026, on non-Mint aircraft and routes.

Adding a domestic first class product allows JetBlue to better compete for travelers who prefer to fly first class within the U.S., a market currently served by American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.

JetBlue’s premium business class experience is called Mint, and it is available on select domestic and international routes.

The front row of the cabin also includes Mint Studios, which offer even more space than a standard Mint Suite. Mint Studios also have a large 22-inch television screen, a mirrored vanity, additional storage and a guest seat that can accommodate another Mint passenger during flight.

If a Mint Studio seat is available, it will be displayed on the airplane seat map.

The Mint travel experience also includes a dedicated check-in desk, lounge access (except with Mint Base fares), priority boarding, priority baggage and two checked bags (one with Mint Base fare).

» Learn more: JetBlue boarding groups explained

JetBlue offers three fare categories: Base, Standard and Flex. The table below shows how the categories compare in terms of flexibility.

Base fares are the most affordable but the least flexible.

Main Base fares do not include complimentary seat selection, but travelers can purchase a seat at any time. Those with an EvenMore Base fare can select a seat for free, but only at check-in. If a seat isn’t chosen, JetBlue will assign one automatically before departure. (BlueFirst Base fares include free seat selection only within 24 hours of departure.)

Comparatively, Standard and Flex fares include complimentary seat selection. This also applies to Mint, except for the new Mint Base fare, which charges for advance seat selection; complimentary seat selection is included only with Mint or Mint Flex tickets. Passengers who want to select a Mint Studio will need to pay extra, and the cost of the seat varies. In an October 2026 sample search for a flight from New York to Paris, a Mint Studio upgrade cost an additional $299 on top of the Mint fare.

Seat selection fees vary among airlines. To get an idea of what passengers can expect to pay, NerdWallet analyzed seat selection fees across major U.S. airlines and found that JetBlue had the highest average one-way seat selection fee at $73.

» Learn more: Airlines with the best (and worst) fees in 2026

JetBlue’s elite status is called Mosaic, and there are four tiers, ranging from Mosaic 1 to Mosaic 4. Mosaic members receive complimentary access to certain upgraded seats, with the benefits depending on their status level.

All Mosaic members, plus JetBlue Premier Card holders who book with their card, can get complimentary space-available upgrades to BlueFirst for themselves and one companion. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares aren't eligible.

Main Base fares are excluded from complimentary seat selection benefits, regardless of Mosaic status.

All Mosaic members receive complimentary access to Main Preferred seating, but EvenMore benefits vary by status level. Mosaic 1 members can select EvenMore seats for free starting 36 hours before departure for themselves and up to two companions, while Mosaic 2 and above can select them at booking. Mosaic 3 and 4 members can extend this benefit to up to four companions.

Mosaic 3 and 4 members receive Premium Upgrade Certificates, and starting Feb. 1, 2027, Mosaic 2 members can choose one through Perks You Pick. Mosaic 4 members earn 2 additional certificates for every 100 Tiles earned beyond the Mosaic 4 threshold. Certificates can be used to upgrade eligible Main or EvenMore fares to Mint or BlueFirst (once it starts flying).

» Learn more: JetBlue Mint: your guide to flying business class

You can select a seat during the booking process, or after, through JetBlue’s website or mobile app. During booking, you’ll first choose your fare type (Base, Standard or Flex), which determines whether complimentary seat selection is included.

After you’ve selected the flight, you’ll see a seat map displayed with the available seats and any applicable fees. For example, passengers who purchase a Main fare can choose eligible Main seats for free but will see prices for upgraded seats.

If you purchase a Main Base fare, all advance seat selections will include an additional fee. Mint passengers can select an available Mint Suite at no additional cost or pay extra for an available Mint Studio.

» Learn more: How to navigate costly airline seat selection fees

#3113. I Just Invested $4,700 Into 4 Dividend Stocks. Here's Why I'm More Excited About Their Potential Returns Than Their $59 in Annual Income.

Brookfield, Prologis, Chubb, and Kinsale don't pay much today, but their earnings growth could do the heavy lifting over the next decade.

I recently invested roughly $4,700 in four dividend stocks: Brookfield Corporation (BN -1.50%), Prologis (PLD -0.83%), Chubb (CB -0.23%), and Kinsale Capital (KNSL +1.95%). At their current yields, this combined investment should generate about $59 a year in dividend income. That 1.3% current yield might sound disappointing, especially when plenty of stocks yield more than 5%.

However, I'm more interested in what these four companies could do for my wealth over the next decade than in how much passive income they'll produce next year. Here's why I bought them and what they could be worth in 10 years.

I bought 50 shares of Brookfield, investing about $1,900 to add $14 in annual dividends. That's less than a 1% yield. However, the income isn't the main point. Brookfield combines alternative asset management, insurance, and operating businesses that generate growing fees, insurance investment income, and operating cash flow. Brookfield also carries real risks, including a complex corporate structure and growing exposure to the AI and private credit markets. However, my conservative base case assumes 11% annual earnings growth -- well below the 17% compound annual growth rate Brookfield expects to deliver over the next five years.

Prologis is the income workhorse of the group. I invested over $1,000 in the leading industrial REIT, which should generate $34.24 in annual dividends at its recent yield of more than 3%. The logistics landlord expects to deliver high-single-digit annualized growth in the coming years, driven by rising rents, development projects (logistics properties and data centers), and its growing asset management business. Meanwhile, there are headwinds worth noting, including higher interest rates and weaker tenant demand, which could slow growth. That's why I think 5%+ annual core FFO per share growth over the next 10 years is a very reasonable assumption, which combines well with its higher-yielding payout.

Chubb is a bet on underwriting discipline. I bought two shares of the insurance giant for around $700, adding $8.16 in annual dividend income. Profitable underwriting, a growing investment portfolio, and buybacks all compound shareholder value, while catastrophe losses, softer pricing, and reserve surprises are the main threats. While the company has delivered robust 24.5% growth in core operating income per share through the first nine months of this year, that rate isn't sustainable over the long term. I think a more reasonable baseline is around 8% annual normalized EPS growth.

Kinsale is the riskiest of the four. The specialty insurer has historically delivered exceptional underwriting profitability and growth, but rising competition is beginning to put pressure on its business. Despite that, I invested about another $1,100 in a company that I expect will produce only $3 in annual dividend income. What appeals to me is its potential for high returns on equity, which it can reinvest to grow shareholder value. I think Kinsale can deliver 8%+ annual earnings-per-share growth with a widening valuation multiple as its growth rate reaccelerates.

The roughly $4,700 I invested in these four dividend stocks isn't buying me much dividend income. However, dividends aren't the only way a company can reward its investors. It can also grow its earnings and cash flow per share through business growth and value-enhancing share repurchases. Faster growth can earn the stock a higher valuation in the market. Add in dividend income, and these three return drivers can really add up over the long term.

To test that idea, I built a preliminary valuation model. My base case is that these four companies can deliver an average annual total return between 9% and 12% over the next decade. Here's a look at what I expect these investments will be worth a decade from now:

That's a roughly $8,400 gain, which is quite a bit more than the $59 in dividend income I expect to receive each year. I think these are very reasonable assumptions. They don't require rapid growth or a significant expansion in their valuation multiple. These companies simply need to continue paying their dividends while growing their earnings at solid rates to compound shareholder value.

None of this is guaranteed. Growth could disappoint, valuation multiples could shrink, or dividends might get cut. However, I think those are lower-probability outcomes, as they are financially strong companies with long histories of growing shareholder value.

I love collecting dividend income, but I don't pick stocks on yield alone. These four purchases show why. They'll initially pay only about $59 a year. I'm more interested in their ability to compound earnings and grow shareholder value, and potentially turn my $4,700 into over $13,100 over the next decade. That's the kind of long-term wealth creation I'm after.

#3112. Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too

Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don’t give away the answers.

While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks, the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools. Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom. However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.

Google’s new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months.

When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.

This is actually consistent with Google’s approach in the consumer space. Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search. Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function. Google sees this as the future.

In a statement to The New York Times, Google education VP Chris Phillips reiterated this approach to web search. “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” he said, adding that if a school chooses not to enable AI, the students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google could make a version of search for schools that doesn’t have AI tools, but it’s not doing that. Instead, it’s creating two different versions of AI in search. When schools enable AI for student accounts, they’ll have two options: the standard Gemini-based AI and the new “Guided Learning” version. The latter, available in Classroom as well as search, is supposed to provide one-on-one tutoring and assistance without giving away all the answers. Google notes all of its generative AI products can make “mistakes,” though, so it may not be difficult to talk the chatbot into doing your homework.

Google is betting that schools won’t want to give up Google Search and will therefore accept AI tools. This will expose students to AI early and often, possibly changing the way they interact with technology. Schools that don’t like Google’s approach could switch to alternatives like DuckDuckGo, which lets you disable AI features. But will Google’s new Guided Learning be enough to assuage their concerns?
