#3110. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3109. Costco Hasn't Split Its Stock Since 2000. Here's Why 2027 Could Be the Year.

Costco's long-term potential extends well beyond a stock split.

Costco Wholesale (COST -1.54%) hasn't split its stock in nearly 27 years. Its last split occurred on Jan. 13, 2000, when the company executed a 2-for-1 split. Since then, Costco's share price has climbed from roughly $40 to more than $1,000, rewarding long-term shareholders as the company built one of the world's most successful retail businesses.

As of Oct. 30, shares were trading around $1,012, giving Costco a market capitalization approaching $450 billion. The stock has also traded as high as $1,096 over the past 52 weeks.

With shares firmly in four-digit territory, a stock split in 2027 is certainly possible. And while a split wouldn't make Costco fundamentally more valuable, it could attract additional attention to a company that already has plenty going for it.

Costco executed a 2-for-1 split in May 1991, followed by a 3-for-2 split in March 1992. Its most recent split came in January 2000. Since then, management has allowed the share price to climb without another split, even as Costco expanded into one of the world's largest retailers.

Today, the company operates 939 warehouses across multiple countries, with a lot of opportunities for additional domestic and international expansion. And with shares now trading above $1,000, another split could make practical sense.

Consider what would happen if Costco announced a 10-for-1 stock split in 2027. At a hypothetical pre-split share price of $1,000, each share would become 10 shares trading at approximately $100 apiece. So if you're holding 10 shares worth $10,000, you would own 100 shares worth the same $10,000.

A 5-for-1 split would produce a $200 share price, while a 4-for-1 split would bring shares down to $250. None of these scenarios would change Costco's underlying value. However, a lower share price could make the stock more accessible to individual investors who prefer purchasing whole shares.

Granted, fractional-share trading already allows many investors to buy Costco with relatively little money. Still, a lower nominal price could broaden the stock's appeal and potentially encourage additional retail participation.

Costco reported fiscal 2026 net sales of $297.2 billion, up 10.1% from the previous year. Net income increased approximately 14% to $9.23 billion, while diluted earnings per share climbed from $18.21 to $20.76.

Those results are particularly impressive considering Costco operates in an industry known for thin profit margins and intense competition. But unlike traditional retailers that rely primarily on merchandise markups, Costco benefits from recurring membership fees. Customers pay for access to its warehouses, and those fees help support the company's low-price strategy. The model has proven remarkably effective.

Membership renewals provide a relatively predictable source of revenue, while Costco's purchasing power helps it negotiate favorable prices with suppliers. Its limited product selection also contributes to operating efficiency. Meanwhile, international expansion offers another avenue for growth.

Costco generated $15.8 billion in operating cash flow during fiscal 2026, providing significant financial flexibility to open warehouses, invest in its business, and return capital to shareholders. These are the characteristics of a business that can continue compounding earnings for years.

At approximately $1,012 per share, Costco trades around 49 times trailing earnings. That's expensive compared with many traditional retailers. But Costco isn't an ordinary retailer. Its membership model, customer loyalty, operating efficiency, and consistent expansion help explain why investors have historically been willing to pay a premium for its shares.

Of course, you still need to pay attention to valuation. Even exceptional businesses can deliver disappointing short-term returns when investors pay too much. And a stock split wouldn't change Costco's valuation.

If the company executed a 10-for-1 split, its share price would fall to approximately $101, but earnings per share would decline proportionately. Its price-to-earnings ratio would remain unchanged. Still, if you plan to hold shares for a decade or longer, Costco's ability to grow earnings and cash flow could matter far more than the price paid for any individual share.

Costco hasn't announced a split for 2027, and there's no guarantee one is coming. But with shares trading above $1,000, management has a reasonable opportunity to make the stock more accessible through a split. For long-term investors, though, Costco's business remains the bigger attraction.

The company has demonstrated that it can consistently grow sales, expand its warehouse footprint, generate substantial cash flow, and retain loyal customers. Those advantages aren't going away simply because the stock trades at a four-digit price.

TL;DR: Average mortgage interest rates jumped today.

If you're here looking for lower mortgage interest rates, today is definitely not your day.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.32% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 22 basis points higher than yesterday and 24 basis points higher than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This comes after the Federal Reserve announced central bankers’ decision to hold the federal funds rate steady yesterday. While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, the federal funds rate is one factor that moves them. Last month, when markets began pricing in a possible federal funds rate increase, mortgage rates spiked.

The next Fed meeting isn’t until December, so any rate movement in the next week will likely stem from other factors, like the upcoming jobs report. For more on that, read on.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Traders expected that the Fed would vote to hold the federal funds rate steady yesterday, so that wasn’t much of a factor for mortgage lenders as they set rates.

In his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that September’s rate increase is “starting to work some” toward moving inflation down to the Fed's 2% goal, but that central bankers don't have any firm conclusions yet. He also acknowledged that the Fed’s monetary policy actions hadn’t achieved price stability yet, but that they’re “working on it.”

This hints that if inflation data continues to trend upward, central bankers might raise the federal funds rate again at their December 8-9 meeting.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, dropped this morning — a day too late for central bankers to consider it in their decision-making process.

The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on November 25.

Next week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out Friday, Nov.6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build an even stronger case for the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again in December, because it would suggest that the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.82% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3107. Buttons are back and storage is king when it comes to car interiors

We talk with Nissan designer Hiren Patel about how vehicle interior designs are changing.

As with interior design for houses, interior design for vehicles is also subject to fashion trends. And like any fashion trend, even the best ideas can become stale and played out with overuse. Some ideas weren’t the best, either, like demonstrably worse human-machine interfaces that add to driver distraction; yet, they still proliferated throughout the industry and across the cars offered for sale. But the good news is that the pushback seems to be working.

“When the trend of the Piano Black and the switchless interior was happening, it was during a time when designers and companies and engineers and everybody were thinking that, ‘Hey, we can just get rid of all these switches on the interior. We can put it all in the software. It’ll save money. It’ll save us tooling up all these extra parts for unique cars and all this stuff and make the interior more like a software experience.’ And it was done with those intentions,” said Hiren Patel, senior design manager at Nissan.

That resulted in cars with minimalist interiors that looked good in the dealership. But people drive their cars on roads; they don’t just sit inside them, parked inside a dealership. “So lots of people were complaining about it and saying, ‘Hey, it takes my eyes off the road to change the temperature or to adjust my seat or do whatever.’ It’s not as easy as doing something on your phone where it’s just right at your fingertips and intuitive,” Patel said.

In part, blame the increasing complexity of modern cars, which have multiple subsystems that need to be controlled. “It’s really like I’ve got to go in all these menus and do stuff, and all the car companies have a different way of doing it, too. So maybe nobody’s really figured out a great way of doing it.”

Most recently, Patel was responsible for the new Rogue, Nissan’s bestselling family SUV. And its interior is a good one. Less minimalist than the all-electric Ariya, the new Rogue Hybrid has buttons and switches for most of its controls and a useful amount of storage built into the interior. Yet it’s not a boring design—the seats are a standout, taking inspiration from puffer jackets. And no, there’s no Piano Black in sight.

“People want easy, intuitive controls,” Patel said. “They want wireless charging. They want surfaces that are easy to manage and clean, keep clean and clutter-free, and they want lots of places to store things. Oh, and the last thing is, they want easy access.” So the new Rogue’s rear doors were engineered to open to 90˚ to make it easier to put in a kid’s car seat or help an elderly parent into the back. That would be less of a priority for a sedan being marketed at a more image-conscious customer, but vitally important for this segment.

“The target customer for this product… they have families and they have a lot of stuff. So you’ll notice that you open the door, and immediately there’s places to put stuff,” Patel said.

Utilitarian need not mean prosaic, however. As designers since the Bauhaus movement have proved, “everyday” doesn’t have to be ordinary. Patel shared that sentiment. “One of the exciting things and one of the really big challenging things of doing a car or doing design for a product that is a usable everyday product is when you can make that product beautiful,” he said. “There’s so much more that goes into our everyday usable products in terms of cost, engineering, usability, feasibility, everything. And then on top of that, we’re struggling and really trying our best to fight for every little millimeter that we can get that we feel is important to making sure that that product is appealing from a visual standpoint.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#3106. Why Palantir Technologies Stock Crashed Today

The data mining and AI specialist delivered record-setting results. It wasn't enough.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.28%) tumbled out of the gate Tuesday, falling as much as 7.3%. As of 11:32 a.m. ET, the stock was down 3.5%.

The catalyst that sent the data mining and artificial intelligence (AI) software specialist lower was investor reaction to its better-than-expected quarterly financial report, which some viewed as a mixed bag.

For the third quarter, Palantir delivered record revenue of $2.3 billion, an increase of 96% year over year and 20% quarter over quarter. This marked the 13th successive quarter of accelerating growth. This drove earnings per share (EPS) of $0.44, up 144%. Analysts' consensus estimates called for revenue of $2.2 billion and EPS of $0.41, so Palantir cleared both hurdles with ease.

The company's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) was the catalyst that drove Palantir's impressive growth. While U.S. government revenue of $953 million climbed 96%, U.S. commercial revenue -- which includes AIP -- soared 148% to $984 million, overtaking government contracts as the company's largest growth driver for the first time.

There's more. Palantir's gross profit margin climbed to 83.4%, up from 82.4% in the prior-year quarter, while its net profit margin rose to 49%, up from 40.3%. This illustrates how efficient the company is at sending more of its revenue to the bottom line.

Management raised its full-year guidance for 2026, forecasting full-year revenue of roughly $8.53 billion, representing 91% growth and well ahead of Wall Street's consensus estimates of $8.22 billion.

That all sounds like good news, so why is the stock falling? Palantir's contracts and the resulting backlog appear to have decelerated. The company's total contract value (TCV) climbed 6% year over year, down from 49% growth in Q2. This fueled concerns that Palantir's hectic pace of growth may finally be moderating.

Moreover, Palantir is selling for 147 times earnings, a premium valuation to be sure. That, combined with fears that the company's future growth may be slowing, was enough to tank the stock today. It's important to remember that Palantir's sales can be lumpy, which can lead to variations from quarter to quarter. While this trend is certainly worth watching, I don't think the sky is falling.

Danny Vena, CPA has positions in Palantir Technologies. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Palantir Technologies. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3105. Should You Buy Sandisk Stock Before Nov. 20?

The company recently announced a stock split that will go into effect later this month.

Shares of tech company Sandisk (SNDK +3.66%) have been red hot this year, rising by more than 350% thus far. The business has performed exceptionally well, as the memory shortage has unlocked some tremendous opportunities for the company, which spun out from Western Digital back in February of last year.

Its stock price is well over $1,000, but that's going to change soon, as the company has announced an 8-for-1 stock split, and it will begin trading on a split-adjusted basis on Nov. 20. Should investors buy the tech stock before then?

The big benefit of a stock split is that it brings a company's share price down. Theoretically, if an investor couldn't afford to buy full shares and fractional shares weren't available through their brokerage, a lower price would make the stock more accessible to them, as it would be easier to buy full shares of the business.

But many brokerages do allow investors to buy fractional shares, and the overall incentive to conduct a stock split just isn't significant, since it doesn't result in better per-share earnings numbers or make the stock look any cheaper. While the share price does come down as a result of a stock split, everything else adjusts accordingly. If a stock's earnings multiple was high before the split, it'll remain high afterward as well.

Even an investor's position in the business will remain unchanged. They will own more shares in the business following a split, but they'll also be valued at a lower price to adjust for the split; the valuation will be unchanged directly after a split. Many stocks trade at well over $1,000 and never do stock splits. It's a discretionary move that doesn't make a stock any better or worse of a buy.

A stock split isn't a huge catalyst for a stock. It might go up afterward, but it may just as easily go down. A bigger factor for Sandisk investors to consider is how long the shortage in memory and storage products will last. That's what's weighing on Sandisk and similar stocks these days -- not knowing how long demand will remain excessively higher than supply, and how long the impressive growth will last.

Sandisk looks like an incredibly cheap stock to own, with its price-to-earnings multiple being in single digits, but that's due to some exceptionally strong quarters of late. If that changes, the stock suddenly becomes much more expensive.

For investors who believe the shortage in memory and storage products could last years, as some analysts think it might, then Sandisk could be a great buy right now. But it's that outlook that is going to have a greater impact on the stock and its future returns than the stock split itself.

#3104. VanEck Just Launched a Diversified ETF Holding Stocks, Bonds, and Bitcoin. Is This the Best Way to Get Exposure to Crypto?

The VanEck Wealth Builder ETF livens up the multi-asset ETF concept by adding Bitcoin to the mix.

Thanks to exchange-traded funds (ETFs), investors have a variety of options for accessing Bitcoin (BTC +0.84%), the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

An ETF segment that began with futures-based products and later evolved into pure spot funds has grown to include income-generating funds as well as ETFs that "buffer" against Bitcoin downside in exchange for capped upside participation.

This new ETF has some Bitcoin exposure, but maybe not enough for some risk-tolerant investors. Image source: Getty Images.

A growing number of other ETFs that aren't crypto-dedicated are also including a sprinkling of Bitcoin. Add the newly minted VanEck Wealth Builder ETF (WBMO +0.04%) to that list. Put simply, this rookie ETF provides exposure to many asset classes, including Bitcoin, under one roof. So it checks the convenience box, but whether its Bitcoin exposure is enough is a matter of individual investors' taste.

The famous Bitcoin white paper just turned 18 years old, so if it's an "adult" now, 18 in investing terms is still really young. Likely due to that youth, professionals are mixed in their opinions regarding how much Bitcoin investors should hold in their portfolios.

After allocating to the building blocks of broad-based equity funds and individual stocks, it's recommended that new investors direct 1% to 2% of their investable capital to Bitcoin. On that basis, the new VanEck ETF is worth examining because it devotes 1.9% of its roster to the VanEck Bitcoin ETF (HODL +1.34%), which provides spot exposure to the cryptocurrency.

Although the wealth builder ETF is actively managed, investors shouldn't expect its Bitcoin sleeve to grow much beyond 2%, as the issuer notes that 2% is the target. There's nothing wrong with that. Plenty of investors are likely to be happy with a Bitcoin "flirtation," not a full-fledged committed relationship.

It also pays to note who this new ETF is most likely to appeal to. That audience is likely to be inexperienced investors, those apprehensive about conducting their own research, those seeking convenience, and market participants who simply want to keep things simple. In those contexts, modest Bitcoin exposure is applicable.

The VanEck Wealth Builder ETF is definitely a nifty addition to the ETF space, but it's not the best fund for risk-tolerant investors who want a bigger helping of Bitcoin. Some experts say that if an investor can handle the risk, a portfolio allocation of up to 10% Bitcoin could pay off over the long run.

Obviously, the wealth builder ETF doesn't meet that demand, and it's not intended to. Then there are market participants who simply want to own Bitcoin directly, whether through a digital wallet, on an exchange, or through a pure-play spot Bitcoin ETF. Those investors shouldn't lean on the rookie VanEck fund for Bitcoin exposure, either.

Putting it all together, the Wealth Builder ETF is a great tool for Bitcoin exposure for some investors, but those willing to take on more crypto risk and who expect larger Bitcoin allocations should look elsewhere.

Todd Shriber has positions in Bitcoin. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Bitcoin. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3101. NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms

Lawsuit calls Brave “supplier, dealer, and distributor” of stolen news content.

The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.

“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”

The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index [and use that content] to train their own AI models, or to access content they use to respond to specific user queries… or both.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website, which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”

The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”

The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.

“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.

When testing the Brave browser for Mac today, we found that the optional “paywall blocker” feature made it possible to read a paywalled New York Times article. The feature was enabled in the default settings and can be turned off.

The NYT asked for a permanent injunction to stop Brave from continuing the allegedly illegal conduct. The lawsuit seeks statutory damages, actual damages, restitution of profits derived from alleged copyright infringement, and “restitution and disgorgement of all revenue and profits Brave obtained through its ad-substitution scheme.”

A similar lawsuit was filed against Brave in the same court yesterday by the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel companies. We contacted Brave and will update this article if it provides a response.

Perplexity, which is not a defendant in the Brave lawsuit but is facing a different lawsuit filed by the NYT, accused the news organization of “disinformation” in a statement provided to Ars and other news outlets. Perplexity’s statement did not identify any specific inaccuracies in the lawsuit against Brave.

“The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.),” Perplexity’s statement said.

The NYT sued Perplexity in December 2025, alleging that its AI tool gives users “outputs that are identical or substantially similar to” NYT articles, including “verbatim or near-verbatim reproductions, summaries, or abridgements of the original content.” Perplexity’s response to that lawsuit said its answer engine only fetches content from copyrighted articles in reply to user queries. Perplexity argued that “developing an AI tool that can allegedly automatically fetch and provide specific content in response to user requests based on its pre-configuration and access to materials available on the Internet” is not “volitional conduct.”

The NYT also sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023 in a lawsuit alleging that OpenAI trains its AI with stolen news content. The lawsuit is heading toward a trial, with OpenAI arguing that its use of news articles is fair use under copyright law.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#3100. Meet the Dividend Stock That Warren Buffett Backed for Decades. Here's Why Greg Abel Is Still Holding.

This fantastic stock is beating the market this year.

Warren Buffett has left a legacy as one of the greatest investors of his generation. He's also one of the best-known investors, and there are reams of shareholder meeting transcripts and letters available for review from Buffett with smart, sound investing advice for anyone from the professional to the layman.

Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.35%) (BRKB +0.47%) stock gained 5,502,284% in value during Buffett's 56-year tenure, versus a 39,054% rise for the S&P 500. Buffett grew the company by holding on to his strong principles about business and investing. He loves dividend stocks because they demonstrate commitment to creating shareholder value. They also bring in lots of cash for the holding company, which it uses for many purposes.

The longest-held stock in Berkshire's portfolio is Coca-Cola (KO -0.42%), which has one of the best dividend-raise streaks on the market. Here's why it's one of the foundations of the equity portfolio.

Berkshire Hathaway CEO Greg Abel. Image source: Getty Images.

Coca-Cola has raised its dividend for the past 64 years straight, through every kind of economy and market, without missing a beat. That makes it about as reliable as it gets, and it has one of the best track records of any Dividend King (stocks that have raised their dividend for at least 50 consecutive years).

Buffett said that Berkshire Hathaway spent $1.3 billion buying Coca-Cola stock over several years ending in 1988. It owns 400 million shares and has never sold any; the stock accounts for 10.4% of the whole portfolio, making it the third-largest position.

Coca-Cola pays an annual dividend of $2.12 as of February, which means that this year, Berkshire Hathaway is on track to make $848 million just from the dividend alone. Aside from price appreciation, the company has made back its initial investment several times over.

Coca-Cola stock is demonstrating unusual market outperformance this year, up 37% vs. 12% for the index. Investors are loving its resilience under pressure, as it's the anti-artificial intelligence play. Revenue increased 7% year over year in the third quarter, and operating income was up 12%. That, of course, leads to a wider operating margin, and it increased to 33.4% from 32% last year, despite inflation and higher costs.

That's right up Buffett's alley. He has praised the company time and time again for its products that everyone needs, which is why it can outlast trends and technological changes. He also loves its brand name, which draws sales from engaged consumers even through challenging times.

These are the reasons the company is performing so well today and why the stock is likely to remain a foundational holding for the foreseeable future.

#3099. Netflix Trades at a Discount to the S&P 500's Valuation. Is It Deserved?

Netflix is now trading for less than 17 times next year's earnings.

You can buy Netflix for 19 times trailing earnings and less than 17 times -- 16.5, to be exact -- next year's profit target. In the other corner, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.58%) is trading for 25 times trailing earnings and 18 times next year's net income expectations.

Is this an opportunity for investors in the streaming company that has been a 520-bagger since going public 24 years ago? Is this one of the few times that someone has mentioned Netflix and "value trap" in the same sentence? Let's take a closer look at how we got here, before wondering if Netflix merits a rare market discount.

As a longtime Netflix shareholder, I have tasted the highs. I have swallowed the lows. This is one of the swallows. Shares of Netflix hit another two-year low last week. The stock has fallen 54% from the all-time high it reached in June of last year.

Revenue growth has decelerated for three consecutive quarters. Its top-line guidance suggests the streak will extend to four when it reports again in January. Perhaps the most disheartening run is that Netflix has initially moved lower after each of its last six earnings reports.

The first few times, it was a matter of a richly priced stock posting good rather than great financial results. Lately it's been a string of disappointing guidance updates. Last month's update was particularly toasty, with layoffs announced just ahead of the report. You could say the company that inspired binge viewing isn't exactly binge hiring these days.

There's some good news as you walk through the ruins. Netflix stock has been through this before. The 54% peak-to-trough investors are experiencing today pales in comparison to the drawdowns following the 2011 Qwikster fiasco and the 2022 growth-stock sell-off.

The stock fell roughly 80% in both cases, only to soar more than fivefold to make that back -- and then some -- in just a couple of years. This doesn't mean that Netflix doesn't need to earn this recovery. The marketplace has evolved amid stronger, now-profitable streaming competition.

Naturally, I still like Netflix's chances here. I'm still a shareholder. The valuation is near historic lows. Analysts see Netflix continuing to post revenue growth in the low double digits. Margins will be pressured next year, but looking out to 2028 and 2029, the stock is now trading for less than 14 and 12 times earnings, respectively.

I understand why Netflix has fallen out of favor. Do I think the discount to the S&P 500 is warranted? No. I do not.

#3098. How to Make a $50 Holiday Gift Feel Like $100

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3097. CoreWeave's 15% Bond Yield Is a Warning for AI Debt. Here Are the Stocks Most Exposed.

The neocloud leader is paying billions in interest on its double-digit-yield bonds.

CoreWeave (CRWV +5.40%), a "neocloud" provider of AI infrastructure services, is one of the tech sector's fastest-growing stocks. At the end of 2022, it only operated three data centers. Today, it operates 51 data centers with over a quarter-million Nvidia (NVDA +2.80%) GPUs.

From 2022 to 2025, its revenue surged from $16 million to $5.13 billion as more companies adopted its dedicated cloud-based GPUs, which can train AI models roughly 35 times faster and at 80% lower cost than larger cloud infrastructure platforms. But its net loss widened from $31 million in 2022 to $1.17 billion in 2025 as it leased more data centers and bought more GPUs.

To fund that expansion, CoreWeave issued more shares and took on more debt. It's increased its share count by 19% since its IPO in March 2025, and it ended the second quarter of 2026 with $72 billion in total liabilities and an alarmingly high debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3. The average yield to maturity on its senior unsecured bonds also ranges from 14.1% to 15.6%. Let's see why those high yields are a bright red flag -- and what they might mean for its neocloud peers.

CoreWeave's senior bonds will start to mature in 2030. Let's see how much it owes on each of those tranches, their yields, their maturity dates, and current market prices.

CoreWeave has already been issuing its debt at high yields, but it will likely need to issue even higher-yielding bonds if the Federal Reserve keeps raising its benchmark rates. That's bad news for a company that spent roughly a quarter of its revenue on interest payments ($1.23 billion in 2025 and $1.18 billion in the first half of 2026) for its outstanding debt.

To tread water, CoreWeave has been issuing more convertible debt with lower cash coupons (1.75%-2.875%) to reduce its dependence on bonds. But its $10.8 billion in convertible debt could be converted into new shares upon maturity, diluting its existing investors.

Most of CoreWeave's senior notes are still trading at about $0.80 on the dollar, which implies the market hasn't lost faith in its ability to pay off its debt. But that 20% discount suggests investors are fully confident it will remain solvent through the early 2030s.

From 2025 to 2028, analysts expect CoreWeave's revenue to surge from $5.13 billion to $43.55 billion -- but its net loss could barely improve from $1.20 billion to $1.09 billion. That pressure will make it tough for CoreWeave to expand without issuing even more debt.

Most of CoreWeave's direct competitors will face similar headwinds if interest rates continue to rise. However, CoreWeave remains more leveraged than many of its industry peers.

Nebius (NBIS +6.66%) and IREN (IREN +10.13%), which are both growing faster than CoreWeave, ended their latest quarters with debt-to-equity ratios of 1.7 and 2.8, respectively. Over the past two years, Nebius' share count rose only about 15%, while IREN's surged 78%.

Nebius' senior notes only have an average coupon rate of 1.7%-2.2%, while IREN's convertible senior notes were issued at 1%-3.5%. While CoreWeave's soaring bond yields might be a red flag for other expanding neocloud companies, it's much closer to walking off the end of the plank than its closest competitors.

CoreWeave is much bigger than Nebius and IREN, and it could still have plenty of room to grow as it converts its massive backlog (at $104 billion in the second quarter of 2026) into revenue. But if interest rates keep rising, it could struggle to fulfill its debt obligations in the early 2030s. That pressure could make it tougher for smaller players like Nebius and IREN to secure more financing at reasonable rates -- so investors in neocloud stocks should recognize these long-term risks.

#3095. Intuit vs. Palo Alto Networks: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2027?

Intuit trades at a 14x forward P/E versus Palo Alto Networks' 88x, but their growth rates and profit margins tell a starkly different story.

As businesses and individuals move financial and security needs to the cloud, choosing between steady software staples and high-growth defense matters. Investors are weighing Intuit (INTU -0.78%) against Palo Alto Networks (PANW -0.48%).

Intuit leads the financial management landscape for small businesses and consumers through its ubiquitous tax and accounting tools. Conversely, Palo Alto Networks provides a comprehensive cybersecurity platform designed to protect large organizations from evolving digital threats.

Both offer essential software services but follow different growth trajectories and valuation profiles in today's tech-heavy market.

Intuit provides a global financial technology platform for consumers and small businesses. It is a leader among tech stocks that provide mission-critical accounting and tax tools.

According to its annual report, the company serves about 93 million customers worldwide through its QuickBooks and TurboTax brands, while expanding into mid-market services with Intuit Enterprise Suite, introduced in 2024.

In its latest annual report for fiscal 2026, which ended July 31, Intuit reported revenue of about $21.4 billion, up roughly 13.9% year over year. Net income reached nearly $4.6 billion, yielding a healthy net margin of about 21.3%.

This performance continues an upward trend from the 20.5% net margin recorded in the prior year. Management guides for fiscal 2027 revenue of $23.3 billion to $23.5 billion, or growth of 9% to 10%.

The company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.4x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. Its current ratio of approximately 1.5x measures its ability to meet short-term liabilities with liquid assets. Free cash flow, operating cash flow minus capital expenditures, reached roughly $8.7 billion, though stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 23.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

Palo Alto Networks secures the digital infrastructure of more than 70,000 customers, including enterprises, service providers, and government entities worldwide.

It uses an indirect fulfillment model with more than 8,700 channel partners to deliver its network, cloud, and security operations services. No single customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in fiscal 2026, limiting the risk of individual client concentration.

For fiscal 2026, which ended July 31, the company reported nearly $11.5 billion in revenue, up 24.5% from the prior year.

Next-Generation Security annual recurring revenue ended the year at $9.1 billion, up 63%. Net income was about $307.0 million, for a net margin of about 2.7%, down from 12.3% in fiscal 2025.

The bulk of that decline stems from a $620 million non-cash loss on the fair value of convertible notes assumed in the CyberArk acquisition, along with higher operating expenses and deal costs from a year of acquisitions, rather than weaker demand. On a non-GAAP basis, management reports net income of $2.9 billion.

The balance sheet shows a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.1x and a current ratio of nearly 0.9x. Free cash flow for the year was approximately $4.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 39% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Intuit faces competition from business software providers, from platform companies offering general-purpose AI, and from potential government-funded tax software options.

The company also faces risks related to its rapid integration of artificial intelligence and the management of sensitive financial data.

Additionally, it must integrate pending deals, such as Sequence, the revenue management platform it agreed to acquire in October 2026, to realize the expected benefits.

Palo Alto Networks operates in a crowded field against large providers like Microsoft (MSFT +2.77%) and Cisco Systems (CSCO +2.21%). It also addresses risks from the complex integration of recent acquisitions such as CyberArk and Chronosphere, and in October 2026 it patched a PAN-OS flaw that it said had seen limited exploitation targeting firewall management interfaces.

Furthermore, the company faces geopolitical instability and trade regulations that particularly affect its operations and employees in Israel.

Intuit currently trades at a significantly lower valuation multiple than Palo Alto Networks, based on both revenue and forward earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Intuit gets my pick, with the caveat that the stock is cheap because investors are asking whether general-purpose AI erodes the tax and accounting franchise before Intuit finishes putting AI to work inside it.

Shares have lost more than half their value in a year, leaving a company that just grew revenue 14% and guides for 9% to 10% growth in fiscal 2027 trading at a mid-teens forward earnings multiple.

Add a 21% net margin and a dividend raised again in August, and the business looks better than the chart suggests.

The pending Sequence deal extends the mid-market push, and the free Credit Karma Tax launch in October opens a new front against the government-filing threat the 10-K keeps flagging.

Palo Alto Networks has the stronger growth story. Next-Generation Security ARR climbed 63% last quarter, and management's fiscal 2027 outlook calls for revenue growth above 20% with CyberArk folded in.

The headline collapse in net income looks worse than the business does, since the bulk of it traces to a paper loss on CyberArk's convertible notes and a year of deal costs rather than a weaker core.

What's holding me back is a share price up more than two-thirds in a year and near 90 times forward earnings, while the company digests two large acquisitions and a string of smaller ones.

If those integrations go cleanly, Palo Alto could keep compounding for years, and anyone already holding it has little reason to sell.

#3093. 3 Double-Digit-Yield Stocks to Buy That Earned Their Dividends Last Quarter

There's a catch with double-digit stocks like mortgage REITs, but that doesn't necessarily mean income investors should skip the space entirely.

With the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.59%) yielding around 1%, double-digit percentage dividend stocks stand out in the eyes of income-focused investors. However, as the saying goes, "There's no such thing as a free lunch." There's a reason these super high-yield dividend stocks exist: The market has slept on their fundamentals.

Double-digit yields can often serve as a red flag, signaling stocks at risk of a dividend cut or, worse, deteriorating fundamentals that lead to significant stock price declines that outweigh the juicy payouts. However, in the case of these three, all of which are mortgage real estate investment trusts (REITs), dividend coverage is not an issue, at least for now: AGNC Investment Corp. (AGNC -1.15%), Annaly Capital Management (NLY -1.22%), and Rithm Capital (RITM -2.09%).

On Oct. 19, AGNC Investment, one of the largest mortgage REITs, and perhaps regarded by its fans as one of the best monthly dividend stocks, released its latest quarterly results. Although AGNC reported comprehensive losses of $1.28 per share, its net spread, or the difference between the yield on its mortgage portfolio and its short-term debt financing, was $0.37 per share, just above the stock's quarterly dividend of around $0.36 per share.

In other words, as with other mortgage REITs, rising interest rates negatively affected the value of its portfolio, even as it continued to generate positive interest income. The "comprehensive losses" were largely due to mark-to-market write-downs of its portfolio. Yet while this may explain how AGNC can, for now, maintain its 16.7% forward dividend yield, if rates keep rising from here, it could bode badly for it in two ways.

First, if AGNC's book value continues to decline, expect the stock price to follow. That's what has happened in the past, especially since a rising-rate environment first emerged. Over the last five years, the stock has fallen by around 45.7%.

Second, if the rising rate trend persists, AGNC could have to temporarily slash its monthly dividend again, as it did in 2022. Although investors in this stock since 2021 are still ahead, given the dividend, AGNC's total return is less than 10% over the five years and pales in comparison to the S&P 500's 76.7% total return during this same time frame.

Annaly Capital Management is the largest residential mortgage REIT, with a total portfolio worth around $107 billion. Similar to AGNC Investment, last quarter Annaly reported significant generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) losses yet generated sufficient dividend coverage based on earnings available for distribution (EAD), using a metric that measures cash flow from its mortgage portfolio rather than including mark-to-market losses. EAD came in at $0.80 per share, while Annaly currently pays a $0.75-per-share quarterly dividend.

Similarly, this suggests that Annaly could be subject to the same risks as AGNC, such as a future dividend cut or an outsize share price drop due to a decline in book value. Yet while these are serious concerns with Annaly Capital Management, there could be a silver lining: management's optimism regarding future results. As CEO David Finkelstein noted on the REIT's latest earnings conference call, Annaly expects to "out-earn in Q4," although he remained vague about 2027 prospects

Although Annaly, like AGNC, has performed poorly since the 2022 interest rate hikes, the coming five years may not necessarily be a repeat of the past five. At the very least, if interest rates hold steady, there may be a path for Annaly to continue out-earning its dividend, and for its book value to stabilize. That's not to say this stock could hold steady while paying its current 16.5% forward dividend, but it could create a scenario in which the stock generates more satisfactory total returns for investors.

Rithm Capital has a far lower forward dividend yield than the two aforementioned mortgage REITs, 10.7%. However, this lower yield, plus Rithm's diversification beyond mortgages, may be what gives it greater dividend safety than AGNC or Annaly.

Calling itself a "global alternative asset manager," Newrez, Rithm's mortgage origination and servicing business, operates two separate asset management companies and a construction lending segment. Rithm also owns several office buildings in New York and and San Francisco.

Although macro factors like interest rates affect its business across the board, this diversification, with much of its income derived from fees and other streams rather than net interest margins, signals an even higher level of dividend security. The figures and facts back this up as well. Last quarter, for instance, Rithm reported $0.55 per share in earnings available for distribution, or more than 2x coverage for its $0.25-per-share quarterly dividend.

Going back longer term, in contrast to AGNC and Annaly, Rithm Capital maintained this payout since before the 2022 rate hikes. Don't get me wrong: Rithm Capital comes with its own set of risks. Total returns for this stock, although far higher than with AGNC and Annaly, are still relatively weak compared to the S&P 500. Still, if portfolio income is your goal and you're looking to add a mortgage REIT with a double-digit yield into the mix, Rithm Capital may be your best option.

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3089. Why Did Bloom Energy Stock Jump 10% Today?

Bloom Energy signed a new agreement to evaluate its fuel cell systems for power generation in California.

Increasingly negative sentiment toward data center growth has weighed on the shares of many AI infrastructure stocks. Bloom Energy (BE +9.28%) is a prime example, as its backlog of business is heavily reliant on data center projects. That helps explain why Bloom stock has declined about 25% in just the last month.

Investors are pushing past that negativity today, after word that Bloom signed a new memorandum of understanding (MOU) that could expand the use cases for its fuel cell technology. The news had investors bidding Bloom shares up more than 12% this morning. As of 12:12 p.m. ET, Bloom stock was still up 9.5%.

The agreement seeks to evaluate the possibility of Bloom providing at least 1 gigawatt (GW) of solid-oxide fuel cell power generation for California Resources Corporation (CRC), to be combined with carbon capture and storage, to power California data centers, and to supplement the power grid for other needs.

California Resources is an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company focused almost entirely on California. It is the largest in-state producer by volume. Combining Bloom's scalable and clean energy source with CRC's carbon capture and storage expertise could lead to additional business for Bloom.

Aman Joshi, Bloom's Chief Commercial Officer, stated, "Our non-combustion technology makes carbon capture more efficient and economically viable at scale, opening a new path to carbon-neutral power generation and addressing the decarbonization needs of large critical infrastructure."

It's another reason for investors to see a long growth path for Bloom Energy, helping push shares higher today

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.57% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

#3087. Here's the 1 Thing I'd Wait to See Before Buying Plug Power Stock

Plug stock has failed to make it to one buy list, but that could change if the company achieves a certain feat.

While Plug Power (PLUG +6.49%) stock has captured growth investors' hopes and dreams for over two decades, I've consistently preferred a bearish stance. My icy feelings toward the fuel cell stock, however, have recently started to thaw with the company's improving financials and a change in management.

But the thought of clicking the buy button on Plug stock remains unlikely for the time being. This could certainly change, though, after the company reports third-quarter 2026 financial results in the coming days.

Let's give Plug Power credit where credit is due. The company has excelled at growing sales over the past decade. From 2015 through 2025, Plug has seen sales rise at a 21.3% compound annual growth rate (CAGR).

The company's achievement on the income statement hasn't translated to the cash flow statement. Over the past decade, Plug has consistently reported negative cash from operations -- a troubling sign in and of itself but especially concerning when juxtaposed with the success that fuel cell peer Bloom Energy (BE +9.28%) has demonstrated. In the first half of 2026, Bloom Energy has reported $300 million in operating cash flow, while Plug has reported negative $244 million in operating cash flow during the same period.

PLUG Cash from Operations (Annual) data by YCharts

While both companies have struggled to generate operating cash flow for years, Bloom has blossomed in this regard over the past two years.

Due to its inability to generate organic cash flow, the company has resorted to raising capital through equity issuance, thereby subjecting investors to shareholder dilution. From March 2016 to February 2026, Plug's outstanding share count grew from over 180 million to about 1.4 billion.

It's likely that Plug will continue to post sales increases in the coming quarters, but it's all for naught if the company can't generate organic cash. Until it can achieve this feat, Plug Power stock is essentially a sinkhole for shareholder value -- not a sound investment.

#3086. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

Mortgage rates are continuing to cool off as we head into November.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 6.93% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

A significant drop is eye-catching, but bear in mind that you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. Since September, mortgage rates have been hovering around 7%. That’s a full percentage point higher than they were at the beginning of 2026.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.
