#3083. Realty Income Has Paid 676 Consecutive Monthly Dividends. Here’s How Its Earnings Results Fit the Bigger Picture.

Realty Income’s latest results show the cash flow behind its payout and how modest its growth really is.

There's no question that Realty Income (O -0.23%) is my favorite dividend stock. I appreciate the consistency and convenience of a monthly dividend, and I love the company's commitment to dividend growth.

And now that Realty Income reported its third-quarter earnings report on Nov. 2, I see no reason to change my mind.

The real estate investment trust recently declared its 676th consecutive monthly dividend, a track record that stretches back more than 56 years. But the real story isn't how long the company has been paying dividends. It's how Realty Income continues to generate the cash needed to keep those payments coming.

Its third-quarter earnings report offers some encouraging evidence.

Realty Income's third-quarter revenue was $1.62 billion, up 10.3% from a year ago. Net income was $403.9 million and $0.43 per share versus $315.8 million and $0.35 per share last year.

But for mortgage REIT investors, adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) may be even more important. This metric adjusts earnings for items such as real estate depreciation, providing a better picture of the cash-generating performance that supports dividends.

Realty Income's AFFO was up 3.7% year over year to $1.12 per share, up 4 cents a share from a year ago. That might not sound particularly exciting, especially when compared with the growth rates of high-flying technology stocks. But Realty Income isn't supposed to be exciting. It's supposed to produce dependable income, and that's exactly what its business continues to do.

Management raised its AFFO guidance for the full year to a range of $4.45 and $4.46 per share, while reaffirming its $10 billion investment target for 2026.

Realty Income's business model is fairly straightforward. The company owns about 15,500 commercial properties and leases them to tenants, typically under long-term net leases that require tenants to cover many property-related expenses. It has clients in every U.S. state, the U.K., and eight other European countries.

Its diversified client base spans nearly 100 industries, including grocery stores, convenience stores, home improvement retailers, pharmacies, and other businesses that serve everyday consumer needs. Dollar General, its largest tenant, accounts for just 3.3% of annualized contractual rent, while 7-Eleven accounts for another 3%.

Realty Income has also demonstrated remarkable consistency in maintaining occupancy across its properties. Its year-end occupancy rate hasn't fallen below 96% since 1992, including during the financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Meanwhile, the company continues to expand. Realty Income invested $2.6 billion during the third quarter, with its proportionate share totaling $2.2 billion. Those investments had an initial weighted-average cash yield of 6.8%.

The company also expanded its private capital business into Europe through a joint venture with KKR. These arrangements can provide an additional source of capital for investments without relying exclusively on Realty Income's balance sheet.

The appeal of Realty Income has never been the prospect of explosive share-price appreciation. Investors can find plenty of other companies offering faster growth.

What makes Realty Income special is the combination of recurring rental income, a diversified property portfolio, and a long history of rewarding shareholders.

During the third quarter, the company paid $0.813 per share in dividends, compared with $1.12 in AFFO. That's a payout ratio of roughly 73%, leaving room to fund other needs while continuing to reward shareholders.

And that's why the latest earnings report fits so neatly into the bigger picture.

Realty Income doesn't need spectacular earnings growth to deliver on its investment proposition. It needs dependable tenants, disciplined acquisitions, and enough cash flow to keep increasing its dividend over time.

After 676 consecutive monthly dividends, that approach has a pretty convincing track record. And it's why Realty Income remains my favorite dividend stock.

#3082. The New Leadership Equation: Why AI Makes Judgment More Valuable Than Speed

Deepali Kaushik, executive at NBCUniversal, is an Amazon bestselling author and writes about technology, leadership and transformation.

AI is changing the scale of this challenge because it can analyze enormous amounts of information, identify patterns and recommend actions in seconds. But it creates a leadership question I believe we aren’t asking often enough: When technology can move faster than human beings, what should leaders still be responsible for?

In my work, I’ve learned not to treat a dashboard, report or automated result as the decision itself. The data can tell me that something changed. It can’t always tell me why it changed or what the consequences of acting on it will be.

The Lesson: Before accepting an AI-generated recommendation, ask: What information is this based on? What might be missing? What would make this recommendation wrong?​

Sometimes, the right answer is to accelerate. Sometimes, it’s to run another test, involve another expert or add another control. And sometimes, the right leadership decision is simply to say no.

Technical solutions aren’t always the hardest part—it’s deciding what the technology should do in the first place. Ownership can’t disappear simply because a process becomes automated.

Consider an app store age-restriction decision. Deciding whether the product should be available to users aged 13 and older or restricted to those aged 18 and older is a different kind of challenge.

An 18+ threshold could simplify some aspects of serving younger users, but it could also exclude a generation of potential customers who might otherwise grow up using the product.

Neither option is just a coding decision. AI can analyze the trade-offs, but leaders must balance legal risks, costs, customer acquisition and long-term growth and own the consequences of their decisions.

The Lesson: For every AI-enabled process, identify three things before deployment: who owns the outcome, what decisions AI is permitted to make and when a human must intervene. That’s accountability by design.​

Technology leaders naturally measure efficiency, time saved, cost reduced, processes automated and capacity increased. When evaluating a technology change, I also ask what happens to the people around the process. Does the employee gain capability or simply lose a task? Does the customer experience actually improve? Does the organization reduce one type of risk while creating another?

A system can be technically successful and still produce a poor leadership outcome.

The Lesson: Add a human-impact question to technology reviews: Who’s affected by this change, and how might their experience change? It takes very little time to ask, but it can change the quality of the decision significantly.​

Organizations are understandably focused on AI adoption. Leaders are asking where AI can save time, reduce costs and increase productivity.

But capability alone isn’t a strategy. Instead, ask: Where should we use AI, and where should we deliberately keep a human in the loop?

That distinction requires experience. A leader who understands only AI capability may automate aggressively. A leader who understands only risk may avoid innovation. The better approach is to evaluate both.

The Lesson: Three questions help move AI enthusiasm to responsible adoption. What value will AI create? What risk could it introduce? What decision should remain human?​​

AI will continue to make organizations faster. It will make information easier to access and execution easier to automate. But those advances don’t make leadership less important. They make the quality of leadership more visible.

When a machine can generate 10 possible answers in seconds, the leader’s value isn’t simply producing an 11th answer. It’s knowing which questions need to be asked, which answers deserve to be challenged, what risks haven’t yet been considered and when decisions should remain human.

That’s why I believe the leadership advantage of the AI era won’t be speed alone. It will be the judgment to know when speed creates value and when wisdom requires a pause.​

#3081. Shopify Stock Just Plunged. Here's Why I'm Not Selling

Shopify's third-quarter results were better than you might think.

Shares of Shopify (SHOP -5.62%) fell by about 10% on Tuesday morning after the e-commerce platform reported its third-quarter results. The drop left the stock roughly 22% below its October record. As a Shopify shareholder myself, I obviously don't enjoy watching the stock price fall. But after going through the report, I'm not planning to sell a single share.

Here's what happened, and why I think the market's reaction says more about expectations than about Shopify's business.

Shopify's revenue grew 32% year over year to $3.74 billion. Merchant solutions revenue, which mostly comes from payment processing, rose 35%, and subscription revenue grew 20%.

The company's profits grew even faster. Operating income jumped 66% to $568 million, and free cash flow came in at $816 million, or 22% of revenue, up from 18% a year earlier. Shopify also spent $562 million buying back its own stock. On the bottom line, Shopify posted earnings of $0.49 per share (adjusted), which surpassed analyst estimates.

Based on the last section, you might be wondering why Shopify's stock is under pressure. And the reason is that two metrics came in a bit light. First, gross merchandise volume (GMV), the total value of sales on Shopify's platform, rose 29% to $119.1 billion. That's an impressive growth rate for a platform this size, but it was slightly below analysts' expectations and slower than the 32% growth rate Shopify reported in the second quarter. Subscription revenue of about $836 million also fell short of the consensus estimate of roughly $850 million.

Normally, misses this small wouldn't be that concerning. The problem is that Shopify's stock was priced for near-perfection. As of Monday's close, Shopify traded for roughly 64 times analysts' 2027 earnings estimates heading into the report. With that kind of valuation, investors tend to punish anything short of perfect. We've seen this with several other big-name tech stocks that have fallen after strong earnings and guidance.

Speaking of guidance, management expects fourth-quarter revenue to grow in the low thirties (percentage) and gross profit in the high twenties. It also expects operating expenses to fall to 29% to 30% of revenue, from about 32% in the third quarter, and it guided to a free cash flow margin in line with last year's fourth quarter. In other words, Shopify expects to keep growing at about the same pace through the holiday season while becoming more profitable.

On artificial intelligence (AI), Shopify's Harley Finkelstein said the company is building commerce "into every surface, every agent, and increasingly, everywhere."

I've owned Shopify since 2022, and my thesis rests on three things. I want rapid growth, expanding margins, and a platform that gets stronger as more merchants and shoppers use it. This quarter checked all three boxes. A company growing revenue by about a third while increasing its operating income by two-thirds is doing what I want it to do.

To be sure, the stock isn't cheap even after the drop, and the two metrics Shopify missed expectations on are certainly a concern worth keeping an eye on. If GMV growth continues to slow, the valuation could keep shrinking, and that's the main risk I'll be watching over the next couple of quarters. The same goes for subscription revenue.

Having said all that, I don't think a slight GMV miss in one quarter changes Shopify's long-term path, nor does it make the company 10% less valuable than it was yesterday. I'm holding my shares, and if the price keeps falling, I'm more likely to add than to sell.

#3080. Why Isn't Realty Income's Stock Taking Off After Strong Earnings Results?

Realty Income delivered another solid quarter, but its results also help explain why the dividend stock hasn't taken off.

Realty Income (O -0.22%) continues to deliver the results investors expect from one of the world's largest real estate investment trusts (REITs). Its properties remain nearly fully occupied, its dividend is well covered, and its investment program continues to generate attractive returns.

However, despite another solid earnings report, the stock hasn't generated much excitement. The reason has less to do with the company's real estate portfolio and more to do with how quickly it can grow earnings per share.

Realty Income just keeps getting it done. The REIT grew its adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) by 3.7% in the third quarter to $1.12 per share. That put its dividend payout ratio at a conservative 72.6% of its AFFO, despite continued dividend growth. It has now delivered 5% AFFO per share growth through the first nine months of this year compared to the prior-year period. Its existing real estate portfolio continues to provide steadily rising cash flow. Occupancy was 98.8% at the end of the third quarter, while its rent recapture rate was 103.5% (meaning new leases on the same property were, on average, 3.5% above prior rates).

Meanwhile, the REIT continues to find attractive investment opportunities. It invested another $2.6 billion during the quarter at an initial cash yield of 6.8%. That includes properties acquired in its U.S. Core Fund and through joint ventures, such as its recently established strategic joint venture with KKR in Europe.

The company remains on pace to invest $10 billion this year. That supports its guidance to deliver $4.45-$4.46 per share of AFFO this year, a $0.01-per-share increase from its prior range. That's a more than 4% increase from last year despite headwinds from higher interest rates.

Despite its solid quarterly results, Realty Income's share price isn't soaring. That's likely due to three factors.

Realty Income's growth remains modest. AFFO per share grew just 3.7% despite a 10.3% increase in total revenue. Meanwhile, it only increased its full-year guidance by $0.01 per share at both ends of the range. Due to its large scale and net-lease focus, the REIT isn't growing as quickly as others in the industry.

It also continues to face some headwinds from interest rates. Higher rates increase interest expenses when refinancing existing debt and also drive up borrowing costs for new investments. That's a headwind for AFFO per share growth. Higher rates also weigh on the value of commercial real estate. Realty Income's share price has fallen almost 15% from its peak earlier this year, coinciding with the recent spike in the 10-year Treasury rate.

Given its size, Realty Income requires significant external capital to fund its investment program. Even highly attractive acquisitions can have a modest effect on AFFO per share when accounting for financing costs.

Realty Income isn't going to grow fast, which is why we shouldn't expect its stock to surge, even with a solid earnings report.

The thing with Realty Income is that investors don't need rapid growth to earn an attractive return. At its recent share price of around $57.50, the REIT offers a 5.6% yield at its current monthly dividend rate. It would only need to grow its AFFO per share by around a 4% annual rate to produce an average annualized total return approaching double digits. That assumes no change in its valuation multiple, which is currently a very reasonable 12.9 times.

Meanwhile, there's the potential for additional upside. Falling interest rates and incremental earnings from its expanding private capital platform could drive faster AFFO per share growth in the future. That could also drive some multiple expansion.

Realty Income doesn't need explosive earnings growth to deliver solid returns for investors. With a dividend yield around 5.6% and the potential to grow AFFO per share by more than 4% annually, the REIT could generate double-digit annualized total returns. Those returns likely won't come in one big post-earnings move but should arrive steadily as it continues to grow its earnings and pay its monthly dividend.

#3079. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3078. Apple Stock Fell After a Record iPhone Quarter. Here’s the Margin Problem Investors Shouldn’t Ignore.

Investors are looking past iPhone growth to how much profit Apple keeps on each device, and rising memory costs are pushing that down.

Apple (AAPL -1.84%) just delivered the biggest September quarter in its history, with revenue jumping 12% to $114.5 billion. Its iPhone business performed even better, and earnings per share topped Wall Street's expectations.

So why did Apple stock fall about 2% on Tuesday?

The answer has less to do with how many iPhones Apple is selling and more to do with how much money it's making on each one. Rising memory chip prices are putting pressure on Apple's profit margins, and management doesn't expect relief anytime soon.

I'm still bullish on Apple, but investors shouldn't dismiss this problem.

Apple's iPhone revenue jumped 17.5% year over year to $57.6 billion, beating Wall Street's estimate of $56.5 billion. That's an outstanding result for a product line that already generates more than $200 billion in annual sales.

Not everything went Apple's way. Its iPad revenue declined 10%, while wearables revenue fell 8%. Management attributed those declines partly to difficult comparisons with last year's product launches and to supply constraints affecting the iPad.

But the iPhone remains Apple's biggest business, and its performance suggests consumers are still willing to pay a premium for the company's flagship products. The problem is that Apple is paying more to make them.

Apple reported a gross margin of 47.9% for its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026 (ending Sept. 26), although that figure benefited from roughly 1 percentage point of tariff refunds. Without those refunds, its gross margin would have been approximately 46.9%.

For the December quarter, management expects gross margins between 45% and 46%.

That might not sound like much of a difference. But every percentage point of gross margin on $114.5 billion in revenue represents roughly $1.1 billion in gross profit. And Apple expects its December quarter to be even bigger.

The culprit compressing margins is memory chips, which are becoming increasingly expensive as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure puts pressure on supply. CEO John Ternus described memory pricing as "unprecedented," while CFO Kevan Parekh said rising memory costs accounted for the entire underlying gross margin decline between the June and September quarters.

Apple has already raised prices on its iPhones, Macs, and iPads, but it's also benefiting from memory purchased earlier at lower prices. As those inventories are depleted, higher costs will increasingly affect profitability.

And there's another complication. Apple stock trades at roughly 35 times expected earnings, leaving less room for disappointing results.

I don't think rising memory prices fundamentally change Apple's long-term investment thesis.

For starters, Apple's services business carries a gross margin of approximately 76%, making it substantially more profitable than hardware sales. That business provides an important cushion against rising manufacturing costs, although management expects services revenue growth to slow to between 8% and 9% in the December quarter.

Apple also has the financial resources and purchasing power to secure memory supplies. Its manufacturing purchase obligations increased by $33 billion during the quarter, reflecting efforts to lock in future production.

That doesn't eliminate the margin problem, and Apple's Siri AI rollout will introduce additional costs. But memory prices are cyclical, and Apple has weathered component shortages and rising manufacturing expenses before. The bigger question is how much of those costs Apple can pass along to customers without hurting demand.

When Apple reports its Q1 2027 results, I'll be watching whether gross margins land within management's 45% to 46% forecast. I'll also be paying attention to services growth and whether supply constraints affecting Macs and iPads begin to ease.

Apple's iPhone business is performing exceptionally well, and I don't see any reason to abandon my bullish outlook over one disappointing margin forecast.

But at 35 times expected earnings, Apple needs more than strong sales. It needs to demonstrate that it can keep those sales profitable, even as the cost of producing its products increases.

#3077. Luka Dončić shows how unbeatable Lakers can be in rout of Heat

LOS ANGELES — Luka Dončić has had himself a day.

Dončić, over a 24-hour stretch, dropped a staggering 87 points in consecutive Los Angeles Lakers victories, the latest Monday, Nov. 2 in a 138-117 domination over the Miami Heat. In the process, not only did Dončić outshine Heat star Giannis Antetokounmpo, he's proving that Los Angeles is close to unbeatable when he's besieging opponents with buckets.

Case in point: entering the night, NBA teams were averaging 113.7 points per game; the Lakers, by the end of the third quarter, were already at 111. For reference, that was four points off from tying the most allowed by the Heat through three quarters in their history.

One night after he dropped 45 in a win over the Toronto Raptors, Dončić toasted the Heat to the tune of 42 points on 14-of-24 shooting, scooping 7 rebounds and dishing out 13 assists.

It didn't matter who Miami sent at Dončić. Versatile defensive wing Andrew Wiggins started the game on Dončić, but Pelle Larsson and Davion Mitchell each got their turn. Later in the third, after Dončić was creeping toward 40 points, Heat coach Erik Spoelstra dug deep in the bench and deployed defensive-specialist guard Dru Smith. The Heat threw double-teams at Dončić, but that didn't matter, either.

Dončić zipped and lofted passes to open teammates who had been left neglected because of those double-teams. By the end of the third, he had already posted double-digit assists.

This is the bewildering thing about defending Dončić: even when you try to rush him, he stubbornly plays at his pace, parries away the additional defensive attention – almost teasing blitzing defenders and daring them to get close – only to pinpoint passes right into his teammates' shooting pockets.

This was an efficient Dončić. He did not need to strafe the rim with shots. He was under control. He was never flustered. And, at least on Monday night, he made his teammates better.

Antetokounmpo, by comparison, finished with 30 points on 10-of-17 shooting, adding 12 rebounds and 7 assists.

The Lakers improved to 6-2 and Dončić is now averaging 38.3 points per game, which is a full 4 points greater than the next closest player. They wield one of the top 3 offenses in the NBA. And as injuries have plagued some of the top teams in the West, like the Oklahoma City Thunder, there could be an opening for the Lakers to blossom into a legitimate title threat with Dončić as the unquestioned anchor of the team.

#3076. Apple Just Stockpiled $10 Billion of Parts While Warning Memory Prices Are 'Unprecedented.' Should Investors Worry?

Apple's annual report shows it loaded up on components as memory costs soar. Here's what that means for its margins, and for the stock.

Apple (AAPL -1.84%) just revealed to investors that it's buying parts as fast as it can, and it is paying up big to do it.

The company's annual report, filed Tuesday, shows components inventory of $10.4 billion as of Sept. 26, up from $2.1 billion a year earlier. Meanwhile, finished goods, meaning iPhones and Macs sitting in warehouses, barely moved, rising to $4.1 billion from $3.6 billion. In other words, nearly all of the buildup in inventories is parts.

The filing came a day after John Ternus, on his first earnings call as CEO, said "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented" and warned that costs will climb further. Put the two together, and you get a clear picture of how the world's most valuable consumer company is handling a memory shortage.

The parts pile isn't the only sign. Apple had $89.7 billion in manufacturing purchase obligations at fiscal year-end, with $82.7 billion due within 12 months. A year earlier, that total was $56.2 billion. Ternus said those obligations rose by $33 billion in the September quarter alone.

Building that stockpile cost real cash. Inventory soaked up $8.9 billion of operating cash flow in fiscal 2026, after adding $1.4 billion the year before. Of course, Apple can afford it: The tech giant still generated $145.1 billion in cash from operations, and it spent $85.8 billion buying back its own stock.

The 10-K is blunt about why. Apple says it is facing supply constraints and rising costs for advanced chips, memory, and storage, and it "expects these trends to intensify for memory and storage components." It also warns that price increases "may not effectively mitigate these negative impacts, and may also reduce demand for the Company's products."

The cost is already hitting margins. Apple's gross margin was 47.9% in the September quarter, but that included about one percentage point from tariff refunds. Without those refunds, CFO Kevin Parekh said, margin fell about a point from the June quarter, "driven entirely by memory impacts."

The December quarter looks tighter. Parekh guided gross margin to 45%-46%, mainly due to higher memory costs and some spending to roll out Siri AI. Ternus added that memory prices should keep rising beyond December, while the cushion from cheaper parts Apple bought earlier shrinks.

Apple has already passed some of that on to customers. Parekh said the company "reluctantly" raised prices on iPad and Mac around June and on iPhone in September, and it's too early to say how buyers will respond.

Memory is also limiting what Apple can sell. Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan said Mac and iPad supply in the December quarter will be held back mainly by memory constraints, as demand has run ahead of expectations.

Despite the frenzy around memory, there's one big bright spot for Apple: Product demand is certainly not a problem. Revenue rose 12% to a record $114.5 billion for the September quarter, and iPhone sales jumped 17% to $57.6 billion. Meanwhile, services grew 10% to $31.6 billion. For the full year, revenue climbed 15% to $478.8 billion and net income reached $132.2 billion.

Apple also expects December-quarter revenue to grow 7% to 10%, which Parekh said would make it the biggest revenue quarter in company history.

And the stockpile cuts both ways. When memory is scarce, the company that can commit tens of billions of dollars to suppliers in advance gets served first. Smaller phone and PC makers don't have Apple's balance sheet, so the same shortage that trims Apple's margin could cost them sales outright.

The memory squeeze is also a signal about who's winning right now. When Apple, one of the largest buyers of memory chips in the world, says prices are "unprecedented," that's good news for the semiconductor companies selling them, including Micron Technology (MU +2.30%).

For Apple shareholders, an important number to track is gross margin. If it stays near the 45% to 46% range and revenue keeps growing, the memory hit is a speed bump. If price increases start to dent iPhone demand, as Apple's own filing warns they could, that's a bigger problem.

So, is Apple stock a buy? The company is choosing to protect supply and sales over a point or two of margin, and it has the cash to do it while still paying a $0.27 quarterly dividend and buying back stock. For long-term investors, that looks like the right trade. Just don't expect margins to look as clean as they did last year until memory prices cool down.

#3074. Amazon's Earnings Just Hit a Record. So Why Is the Stock Down 11% From Its Peak?

Wall Street is worried about the tech giant's cash flow and its slowing e-commerce growth.

The technology bull market is beginning to stagger just a bit. Amazon (AMZN +2.15%) stock fell again after it reported earnings last week, and while it has rebounded modestly, as of midday Monday, it is still down 11% from its peak.

Earnings came in at record levels, yet investors remain nervous about the technology giant in e-commerce and cloud computing. Understanding why could help inform your decision about whether or not you should buy Amazon shares right now.

In the third quarter, Amazon's cloud division, Amazon Web Services (AWS), was the star of the show yet again. Revenue was up 39% to $46 billion, one of its fastest growth rates in years, with phenomenal earnings of $17.8 billion, resulting in a margin of 39%. Management is guiding for year-over-year revenue growth of 40% in 2027 and 2028, which would essentially double AWS' sales in just two years.

The problem is that high revenue growth at AWS will require massive up-front capital expenditures. The company's free cash flow has been negative over the last 12 months due to its $220 billion capital spending plan for 2026. It's likely to increase its capex in 2027 and 2028.

Amazon has around $100 billion in cash on its balance sheet that it could put toward funding these data center investments, but it may need to raise additional funds to fully finance its artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. The amount of long-term debt on its books stood at $173 billion as of the end of last quarter. The combination of more debt on the balance sheet and negative free cash flow will make investors more skittish about the stock.

The other engine of Amazon's business is commerce. Its North American commerce revenue growth decelerated to 6% year over year in Q3, which may have concerned the Street as well. In the second quarter, North American sales grew 16% year over year.

Most of the deceleration was due to a simple and obvious reason, though: Amazon moved Prime Day from Q3 last year to Q2 this year, which shifted 400 basis points (4 percentage points) of growth from Q3 to Q2 in 2026. Normalizing this switch, North American growth last quarter would have been 10%, which is quite good for a mature business generating close to $500 billion in annual revenue.

Margins look great for e-commerce, too. Over the last 12 months, North American profit margins were at a record 8.2% and are likely to keep climbing in the near future.

Combined with AWS growth and margin expansion in North American retail, Amazon's consolidated EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) reached $98 billion over the last 12 months. Free cash flow has diverged from EBIT and turned negative, but this trend should reverse once Amazon stops investing so much in AI capital expenditures relative to its current revenue base.

Right now, Amazon's market cap is about $2.7 trillion. The stock trades at around 26 times its trailing EBIT figure, which does not seem dirt cheap in a vacuum. However, Amazon is poised to deliver strong earnings growth over the next five years. AWS is projected to have strong double-digit revenue growth, and its superior margin profile should help lift Amazon's overall profit margins.

The margins in its retail segment will continue to expand as Amazon gains ever more operating leverage from its fixed infrastructure investments in delivery and warehouses. Overall sales grew 12% last quarter, and operating margin was a record 13.9%. Assuming this overall trend continues over the next five years -- which is increasingly likely as AWS becomes a larger percentage of the business -- Amazon could grow its revenues from $775 billion to $1.37 trillion.

If its operating margin expands to 17.5%, that would result in overall EBIT of $240 billion, or roughly 10 times the current market cap, making Amazon stock a buy today.

#3073. Meeting AI Demand Starts With The Right Infrastructure

​Juan Font is President and CEO of CoreSite.

In the words of Benjamin Franklin: “Great haste makes great waste.” It’s an apt perspective for viewing the rush to AI deployment in the enterprise today, where organizational leaders race into AI deployment decisions without always having the infrastructure in place to support them.

For many enterprises, the default setting is to contract directly with major frontier labs such as Anthropic or OpenAI and big cloud providers such as Google or Microsoft. Effectively, they’re racing to allow employees to use tokens for almost anything—often without much oversight.

This rush is strikingly reminiscent of when the cloud was introduced in the 2010s, and employees opened public cloud accounts, running up very large tabs—again with very little oversight over the projects being undertaken.

Today, companies are rushing to consume tokens with relatively little thought given to how that consumption is supported. In many cases, the problem isn’t the AI deployment itself. It’s the infrastructure supporting it. And solving that problem is critical to developing and realizing a sound AI strategy.

At the innermost layer, AI requires compute. But compute in the form of GPU chips is extremely scarce. To deal with that scarcity, a whole new segment of companies called neoclouds that offer GPU as a service has emerged.

Enterprises that want to develop or train their own medium-sized models are renting or leasing compute infrastructure from these neoclouds. As that market matures, some companies are beginning to buy the hardware themselves, particularly in financial services, where firms require massive amounts of compute as well as real-time access to financial data and exchanges.

Companies developing their own models and doing their own inferencing require space, power and cooling for GPU clusters, along with connectivity to the models they use for other workflows. Less sophisticated companies are simply using the cloud, which can become increasingly expensive as usage grows. Running GPUs is extremely costly, and performance can degrade when long-haul fiber is used to connect to compute resources. You end up with chips waiting for data—resources you’re paying for but not fully utilizing.

That’s where colocation data centers come into the picture, particularly those close to population centers and network hubs. Using colocation data centers as inferencing hubs to manage the handoff between private and public infrastructure can improve performance by enabling direct connections.

Adjacency to where compute is performed is of vital importance, but so is being in an environment that allows you to future-proof your infrastructure as the mix of workloads changes. Getting there takes a partner who can help you step back and build the right infrastructure foundation before you scale your AI.

We’re also seeing a preponderance of multi-cloud and multi-model environments. Cloud providers are trying to become the entry point into the intelligence realm, and they want to connect you to everybody. But to operate in a multi-platform environment, you need the interconnection infrastructure to support it. The ability for huge models to connect is what ultimately drives their value.

From a cost perspective, it’s impossible to overstate how expensive it would be to transfer terabits per second of data across regions. And now, companies are releasing agents. Meta recently released Muse, an agentic AI personal assistant, and we see OpenAI and Anthropic moving in the same direction. Each of these applications requires dedicated compute, cybersecurity controls and tremendous amounts of bandwidth. That rise in agentic inferencing workloads will require inexpensive, high-speed connectivity to these models. Having compute in metro centers, adjacent to the clouds, will be vital from both a cost and speed perspective.

The enterprises that have the greatest need to place their digital infrastructure in a colocation data center—and gain closer proximity to inferencing—are not necessarily traditional brick-and-mortar hospitals and banks. They’re the AI models themselves: Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, CoreWeave, Microsoft and Google. These companies are deploying edge networking infrastructure to support data transfer because the focus until now has been on the compute layer primarily devoted to training those models. Only now is the interconnection layer requiring edge compute and network being built. Demand for this interconnection capacity is already outpacing supply. Existing data center inventory is extremely limited, and we’re racing to build incremental capacity to meet growing enterprise demand.

All that horizontal stratification between the different participants of the edge AI compute ecosystem is happening right now, and it requires multiple megawatts of capacity. That edge infrastructure must be built to support the exponential growth in demand that is coming. In essence, this is the “plumbing” that is going to enable the massive growth in agentic AI workloads by enterprises and individuals alike.

Ultimately, because the network was not designed for the projected explosion in bandwidth, leveraging colocation data centers becomes a matter of survival. You must colocate—ideally adjacent to the edge compute infrastructure hosted by hyperscalers, neoclouds and frontier labs—and cross connect directly to the infrastructure. That’s the edge compute and interconnection on-ramps we’re building right now, and we’re just scratching the surface. The companies that take the time to build that foundation, before they scale, will be better positioned to turn today’s rush into an AI strategy that is sustainable tomorrow.

#3072. Player Grades: Recapping the Mavericks’ embarrassing 115-110 loss to the Sacramento Kings

The Dallas Mavericks (4-3) were riding high after beating two previously undefeated teams, but followed that up with a loss to a winless Kings (1-6) team, 115-100. No Kyrie Irving (rest) didn't help the cause, but Cooper Flagg had a rough night, and the Mavericks simply could not connect from downtown as a team.

The silver lining? If the Mavs slept on arguably the worst team in the NBA, they've learned the lesson that you just can't do that in this league.

The good news is that hopefully Flagg got his worst game of the season out of the way. He had a dreadful shooting night (3-of-19) from the floor, didn't have much interest in taking available three-point shots and seemed frustrated to the point it threw his game off entirely. He chipped in little bits elsewhere and bolstered his scoring with excellent free throw shooting, but it wasn't nearly enough with the overall messiness of the game.

You never want to see a player get injured as happened to Christie (hip), but it's the only thing that spared him from a solid "D" grade. He was 0-of-5 – all from downtown – before the injury and sadly has brought very little to the team this season inclusive of Monday night's performance.

Martin wasn't on my starter Bingo card as the guy who would take Kyrie Irving's place in the starting lineup, but keeping the bench unit of Zaccharie Risacher, Morez Johnson and Marcus Sasser made sense. He was fine, but didn't play starter minutes and didn't contribute all that much. So, while he didn't necessarily hurt the team, he didn't quite help it in any appreciable way either.

Washington backslid a little from previous games, appearing a bit disengaged with a stat line to back that up. 2-of-9 shooting (with six misses from deep) and not nearly enough production for the amount of time he spent on the floor made for a bad night. This was a game Washington could have at least locked in on defense, but that is where the disengagement seemed to be apparent. Something was off in Dallas on Monday night, and it definitely got to Washington.

If not for Gafford, it's difficult to imagine how bad this game would have been. He was by far the best player on the floor for the Mavs. An offensive juggernaut hitting 9-of-10 shots and both of his free throw attempts. He made the absolute most of limited minutes and it's a shame it was largely a wasted effort.

Alongside Gafford, Clayton, Jr. was another bright spot. He was the only player on the team even remotely locked in from deep, hitting 4-of-5 three point attempts and 6-of-9 overall. In hindsight, he should have taken Irving's place as a starter, but who could have predicted that from the outset? This was a very nice night for Clayton, Jr. and hopefully something to build off as he will likely have opportunities on night's Irving rests.

This is simply a game you flush. Look around the NBA on any given night, and a team that has no business losing is getting waxed. Tonight it was the Mavs' turn. Almost to a man, they were completely off their game and plainly could not get anything going outside of a few bright spots. Learn from it and get ready for the next one.

#3071. Why Shopify Stock Dove Today

While the company beat on the top and bottom lines, investors still found cause for concern.

Shares of Shopify (SHOP -5.62%) were sharply lower on Tuesday, falling as much as 13.2%. As of 12:41 p.m. ET, the stock was still down 5.4%.

The catalyst that sent the e-commerce platform and tools provider lower was its financial results, which failed to instill investors with confidence.

Before the market open, Shopify reported its third-quarter results, but shareholders simply weren't inspired. The company reported revenue of $3.74 billion, up 32% year over year, which resulted in adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.49, up 44%.

To give the results context, analysts' consensus estimates called for revenue of $3.73 billion and adjusted EPS of $0.46 -- so Shopify cleared both hurdles with room to spare.

The strong top-line growth was fueled by a 29% increase in gross merchandise volume (GMV), or the total value of products sold on its platform. At the same time, monthly recurring revenue (MRR) of $230 million climbed 19%.

President Harley Finkelstein highlighted the company's strengths, saying, "Shopify is uncommonly good at operating in two realities at the same time: the world our merchants exist in today, and the one they are moving toward. Q3 is the perfect example. We powered $119 billion in GMV, while continuing to build commerce into every surface, every agent, and increasingly, everywhere."

For the upcoming fourth quarter, Shopify is guiding for revenue growth in the low-thirties percentage rate year over year, accompanied by gross profit in the high twenties and free cash flow margin similar to last year's rate of about 19%.

That all seems like positive news, so why is Shopify stock falling? Investors found nits to pick with some of the company's operating metrics. GMV of $119.2 billion fell short of the $120.1 billion analysts had predicted, while subscription revenue of $836 million was below the $850 million some expected.

At 99 times earnings, Shopify stock isn't cheap, so investors are more likely to nitpick its results. That said, the stock is valued at a significant discount to its three-year average multiple of 169.

Doncic leads the league in scoring with 37.7 points per game for the Lakers, and Antetokounmpo is fifth at 28.2 for the Miami Heat.

But this matchup didn't quite live up to the hype after Doncic continued his early-season dominance in the Lakers' 138-117 win.

Doncic was better, but he had more help. Austin Reaves scored 27 points on 10-for-15 shooting and Walker Kessler finished with 15 points and 15 rebounds for his third consecutive double-double.

"Yeah, he's a big piece for us," Doncic said about Kessler. "I think when he plays good, he gives us a way better chance to win. So, he just needs to keep going like this. Like we told him, we have his back. ... But what he's been doing, it's helping us win."

The Lakers (6-2) shot 57% from the field, including 44% (19 for 43) from three-point range. They also notched 39 assists on 51 field goals.

"The 39 assists, that's the most assists we've had since I've been the [coach]," JJ Redick said. "So, it's a really good offense that we're playing right now. And a lot of that, of course, is Doncic and what he's able to do and bend the defense. And his shot-making creates a lot of problems, and then he can make every pass."

Doncic has been on a scoring tear for the Lakers.

Miami Heat forward Giannis Antetokounmpo, right, scores over Lakers center Walker Kessler in the second half. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times)

In the third quarter, Doncic missed a three-pointer, but Jake LaRavia hustled to collect the rebound. He passed the ball to Doncic, who then made a three to give the Lakers a 93-74 lead. The play forced the Heat (2-5) to call a timeout as Doncic pointed at LaRavia in appreciation.

Doncic started strong like usual, with 16 points, five assists and four rebounds in the first quarter as the Lakers took a 37-30 lead. Doncic, who was called for a technical foul late in the first half — his second of the season — had 24 points by halftime.

In his previous four games, Doncic scored 45, 37, 41 and 52 points.

Lakers guard Austin Reaves shoots over Miami Heat guard Davion Mitchell in the first half. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times)

"Like the defensive mindset in me is always like, 'Why are they not blitzing him or why are they not doubling? Or why are they just letting him just walk to his spot and just do whatever he wants out there?' But they're trying," Williams said about defensive strategies Doncic faces. "He just is that good and he just makes it look that easy.

"He's unbelievable, man. Even a better person. And yeah, I'm happy to be on his side for sure."

#3068. Investors Are Asking the Wrong Question About Anthropic

The bull case for Anthropic is that AI use cases and adoption will expand, while the bear case is that businesses won't adopt AI as much as expected.

The Anthropic S-1 filing released on Oct. 26 held a wealth of information, and its updated filing on Nov. 2 provided even more recent data. In the first nine months of 2026, the artificial intelligence (AI) start-up generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from the $2.5 billion recorded in the prior-year period. It's also well funded, with cash and cash equivalents of $95.6 billion as of Sept. 30.

We also learned that losses are accelerating:

With that fresh round of information, Wall Street is fixated on whether Anthropic's valuation, expected to range from $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, is justified.

For long-term investors looking at the initial public offering (IPO) for its potential to create future meaningful wealth, the biggest concern isn't investing in a company with a perfect valuation. Instead, the question to answer is: "Will Anthropic become a more valuable company in the future because the AI market and use cases have significantly increased in size?"

Since Anthropic's rival, OpenAI, launched ChatGPT in November 2022, it feels as if AI is everywhere. It has been a boon for companies like Nvidia, which supply the chips needed to make the breakthrough technology run efficiently. That said, it's still mostly in its early stages of adoption.

In October 2026, the U.S. Census Bureau reported that 24.6% of U.S. businesses used AI, up from 3.7% in September 2023, according to research from The Motley Fool. While that percentage is up from September 2023, it means approximately 75% of U.S. businesses still aren't using it.

Breaking it down further, there is much higher usage across sectors: 46% of U.S. companies in the information sector, 44% in professional services, and 41% in finance currently use AI. Still, even within sectors with early adopters and more straightforward use cases, AI usage hasn't cracked the 50% barrier.

Also, between 42% and 63% of non-adopters, with the percentages varying by business size, cited AI as not applying to their company. That's an indication that the perceived use cases are just not there yet to add it to an everyday workflow.

For Anthropic, the bull case is that the adoption trend continues and the market size keeps growing, opening up new revenue opportunities. According to Statista, the global AI market is valued at $707.4 billion in 2026 and is expected to climb to $1.9 trillion by 2032. The bull case also involves the pure-play AI company expanding its products and offerings, winning over businesses that currently feel using the technology isn't relevant to their operations.

The bear case is that the AI market will grow slowly, or not much more from here, making it more difficult for Anthropic to bring in new customers, and it just keeps burning cash. In its S-1 filing, the AI start-up shared that its top five customers accounted for 25% of its revenue for the first nine months of 2026. To have real longevity, AI adoption will need to expand beyond a few early adopters.

That's why focusing on the expected future size of the AI market, what can go right, and what can go wrong, is more valuable for anyone considering investing in Anthropic than its valuation today.

#3067. Why Good Product Management Starts On The Factory Floor

Harmjan Derksen, Chief Product Officer, Ultimo. AI-augmented enterprise asset management (EAM) solutions for industrial businesses.

​At 6:30 a.m. on a weekday, a team lead at a manufacturing plant is already at work. She is cross-referencing overnight breakdown reports, shift logs and open notifications, building a mental picture of the equipment before her technicians arrive. It takes her 45 minutes every single day.

No analyst report ever told me about that morning ritual. I learned it by standing next to her and observing it.

As a chief product officer, I used to believe that strategy comes from market research, competitive analysis and analyst briefings. Although those inputs matter, years of building software for manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, energy and utilities companies have taught me there’s a different layer to strategy. Enterprise software teams should spend more time observing end users than reading analyst reports. And industrial executives should demand the same from every vendor who wants their business.

For industrial CXOs, introducing software that lacks operational reality creates a financial risk. Research from Splunk and Oxford Economics puts the cost of unplanned downtime at $400 billion a year across the Global 2000, roughly $200 million per company. And ABB’s 2025 research puts the average cost of a single hour of downtime anywhere from $10,000 to $500,000 across industrial sectors.

The workforce math is just as unforgiving. Deloitte and The Manufacturing Institute project that as many as 1.9 million U.S. manufacturing jobs could go unfilled by 2033 “if workforce challenges aren’t addressed.” Our own maintenance trend research found that 63% of industrial organizations are struggling with an aging workforce. Every experienced technician who retires takes decades of institutional knowledge with them—knowledge that exists in no system unless someone deliberately captures it.

Software built from a distance won’t solve problems that only reveal themselves up close.

Analyst reports tell you what the market is buying. The factory floor will tell you why products demand attention after they’re bought. Three lessons stand out from the time my teams and I have spent shadowing maintenance crews.

1. Workarounds are the truth. When a technician keeps a paper notebook next to a tablet, that’s unfiltered product feedback. The workaround shows you exactly where the software stopped fitting the work. You’re not going to find this often in a user satisfaction survey because people rarely report the friction they’ve already routed around.

2. Conditions change everything. A tool that demos beautifully in a conference room behaves differently at the top of a ladder, in gloves, next to a machine running at 90 decibels, in a corner of the plant with weak connectivity. If your product team has never watched software being used in those conditions, they’re designing for a facility that doesn’t exist.

3. Reality doesn’t care about your roadmap. I once presented AI capabilities at an industry conference, and a maintenance leader gave me candid feedback over dinner: What he needed was for his engineers to use their phones for work orders. Where I was talking about AI, he was still trying to solve mobile adoption. That gap between what vendors present and what customers are up against is where roadmaps go wrong, and it shaped ours more than any market forecast that year.

That dinner conversation is what listening looks like, but it’s not the whole roadmap. Innovation doesn’t always emerge from explicit user requests. The balance is staying grounded in what customers face, while still leading them toward what they haven’t asked for yet.

Observation also changes what you build. When our team watched that morning cross-referencing ritual up close at a European door manufacturer, the insight was humbling. The highest-value application of AI wasn’t an exotic prediction engine—it was automating the tedious assembly of information the team lead already trusted and giving her back nearly an hour a day. That priority came from the floor, not from a quadrant.

If you lead an industrial or healthcare business, you can turn this principle into procurement and operating discipline. Here’s my advice:

1. Ask every software vendor, “When did your product team last spend a shift with people who do this work?” Get specifics: which site, what they observed and what changed in the product as a result. Getting a vague answer can be just as telling as a fully detailed account.

2. Make a site visit part of your evaluation. Before signing, put the vendor’s product people, not just sales engineers, on your floor for a day. How they behave there tells you whether you’ve found a partner or sat through a pitch. A vendor confident in their product will welcome it.

3. Put frontline workers on the selection team. The technicians and operators who will use the software daily should have a real vote, not a courtesy demo. Systems chosen without them are systems worked around.

4. Measure adoption, not deployment. Go live isn’t success. Track whether people use the tool 90 days in and treat workarounds as defect reports. Usage data will tell you more than any steering committee update.

5. Apply the same discipline internally. Your IT leaders and digital teams should walk the floor regularly, observing and asking questions. The gap between IT strategy and operational reality closes one observed shift at a time.

“Go and see” is a well-worn idea in lean manufacturing, and industrial leaders have applied it to their operations for decades. What’s missing is applying the same discipline to the software those operations depend on, and to the people who build it.

The next time a vendor shows you a roadmap, ask where it came from. If the honest answer is a stack of reports, be cautious. If the answer involves worn safety shoes, you may have found a partner who understands that in industrial business, the truth lives on the floor.​

#3066. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3063. Chewy vs. Five Below: Stable Growth vs. Seasonal Revenue Spikes in Retail

Chewy's revenue runs 3x higher, but Five Below's growth rate tells a different story—especially during peak seasons.

Chewy Inc. (CHWY -1.37%) primarily generates its revenue by operating as a dedicated e-commerce retailer providing pet food, animal supplies, prescription medications, and general wellness items directly to domestic pet owners, maintaining an inventory of thousands of unique products.

It recently modified its paid membership program by lowering the annual subscription fee for new and existing customers, and it concurrently expanded the integration of automated self-service tools within its customer service and veterinary operations.

Five Below Inc. (FIVE -0.16%) earns the vast majority of its revenue by operating a widespread chain of specialty discount retail stores across the United States, selling a continuously rotating inventory of toys, games, beauty products, athletic apparel, and personal accessories.

It recently appointed a former Ulta Beauty Inc. (ULTA -0.88%) executive to its board of directors, while it simultaneously initiated an early holiday shopping campaign featuring a standardized assortment of toys, seasonal gifts, and home decorations.

Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item, and tracking this specific financial metric helps individual investors clearly understand the overall business size, the historical baseline growth trajectory, and the fundamental consumer demand for a given commercial enterprise before any operational costs, taxes, or basic administrative expenses are mathematically subtracted from the final total figure.

Chewy vs. Five Below Revenue over the last 8 quarters.

Normally, the first thing to note when examining a company's revenue trend is seasonality: some times of the year have stronger buying patterns than others. For most stocks, compare revenue year over year, by quarter. In retail, seasonality is well-known: with some exceptions, the bulk of retailers' revenue comes in the fourth quarter. Chewy has less seasonality, around the Christmas season, unlike most retailers. The strength of its autoship program mitigates seasonality; however, one would expect its growing focus on veterinary services to further smooth it out.

Five Below, meanwhile, would be expected to have strong seasonality, as a low-priced retailer of many gift-type items.

The chart shows the revenue trend. Even with some year-over-year comparable quarter variation, Chewy shows quite steady revenue, which is unusual for a retailer. Five Below shows that fourth-quarter sales spike each year. But looking at comparable quarters, the business is steadier than the chart may give at first impression: sales are rising comparable quarter over comparable quarter.

Revenue is perhaps the simplest metric investors have to judge a business by. As the chart shows, look for rising revenue, especially over similar periods of each year, and take comparable-quarter stagnation, or worse, declines, as a red flag. In the case of Chewy and five Below, investors should decide if they prefer sequentially steady revenue or more seasonally influenced growth.

Data source: Financial Modeling Prep. Data as of Nov. 2, 2026.

#3061. The Case For Pre-Breach Intelligence: Why Buying Access Before Attackers Do Beats Cleaning Up

Austin Berglas is Managing Director and Head of Cyber Operations at Nardello & Co. and the former head of FBI New York Cyber.

​For decades, enterprise security spending has followed one pattern: Detect the intrusion, contain it, investigate and recover. The breach occurs, and the security team responds as fast as it can.

That approach is expensive and increasingly avoidable.

IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report put the global average cost of a breach at $4.44 million and the average time to identify and contain at 241 days. Yes, this was a nine-year low, yet it still amounts to nearly eight months in which an attacker can sit inside a network, expand access and live off the land to conduct a larger-scale attack.

This is the limitation of post-breach incident response: It’s reactive. A SIEM can only correlate logs that exist, and an EDR platform can only flag malware after it’s been deployed. The industry has put enormous effort into faster detection and response and far less effort into stopping the incident from happening in the first place.

Most modern intrusions don’t begin with a zero-day exploit or custom malware. They begin with a transaction. Initial access brokers are criminals who specialize in breaching a network and selling that foothold to the highest bidder. These brokers supply a large share of the initial access used by ransomware crews and other individuals and groups conducting cyber-enabled crimes.

A gbhackers report noted that ​Rapid7 researchers tracked initial access listings across five major underground forums and found the average base price “rose from $2,726 in 2024 to $113,275 in the second half of 2025.” Additionally, Rapid7’s earlier dataset showed that more than 70% of listings “included some degree of privilege,” which means buyers were getting more than just a low-level login—they were purchasing a foothold from which to move laterally and expand access.​​​​​

Once access is listed, it doesn’t sit there for long. KELA Cyber research from 2022 found that access was often sold within one to three days of listing and that victims were listed on ransomware leak sites an average of 23 to 36 days later. This is a fairly significant window to conduct an attack.​

By the time the tech stack flags unusual activity, the access has already changed hands on a criminal forum. The attack that eventually triggers an alert is frequently the second or third step in a chain that began with a transaction on some dark web forum, completely unknown to the security team.

Pre-breach intelligence inverts the model. Instead of waiting for, and reacting to, a compromise, it involves direct monitoring of and, in some cases, legally acquiring access to the criminal marketplaces where access and credentials are bought and sold. In this way, an organization can learn if access to its own network is for sale before an attacker completes the purchase and exploits it.​

This changes what “detection” means. Pre-breach intelligence tells you that a specific method of access to your organization’s network is actively being marketed to buyers who intend to use it for a variety of crimes, such as ransomware, fraud or corporate espionage, while there’s still time to rotate credentials, patch the stolen access route and notify law enforcement before anything nefarious happens.​

Pre-breach intelligence is also significant for third-party risk. Vendors and partners are often the weakest link in an organization’s security posture and are frequently the last to know when their own access has been compromised. Monitoring the marketplaces where access to those vendors is sold can surface a third-party compromise weeks before the vendor discloses it or it becomes public.

None of this replaces traditional security operations and best practices. Endpoint detection, patch management and a competent incident response plan are still nonnegotiable. Pre-breach intelligence adds a layer that sits earlier in the attack chain. This is the difference between finding out your house key was copied and finding out someone already used it to get inside.

Insurers have started to take the approach seriously. In March 2025, Reinsurance News reported that AXA XL’s specialty risk division had partnered with DarkwebIQ, a pre-attack intelligence provider that intercepts access sales by infiltrating forums, marketplaces and private channels.​

Post-breach response has dominated budgets because its value is easy to explain. Here was the incident, here’s the cost and here’s what we spent fixing it. Prevention is a harder sell internally because success looks like nothing is happening. However, given how long it can take to remediate and recover from a data breach, and the significant cost associated, nothing happening is exactly the outcome worth paying for.

An organization that intercepts access before an attacker uses it avoids the costs that follow a breach. This can include months of containment, legal fees, incident response engagements, remediation and recovery, regulatory exposure and reputational damage.

Security leaders should ask whether access to their network is for sale today. If their current tools, vendors or partners can’t answer that, there’s no question that they’ll learn about their exposure on the attacker’s timeline rather than their own.​
