#3060. Game Recap: Booker fouls out as Suns fall short, 116-113

The Phoenix Suns fall to 1-4 on the season and have lost 3 straight games. There was progress overall, but the ultimate goal is to win games, and the Suns broke down late with key turnovers and missed free throws.

The Suns led by as many as 17 points, survived a Draymond Green ejection and a Stephen Curry heater, and still lost it at the free-throw line.

Golden State won 116-113, dropping Phoenix to 1-4. The Suns won the first half at the stripe 13-of-14 to 8-of-10, then watched the Warriors go 23-of-27 in the second half to their 9-of-16. Devin Booker fouled out with under a minute left and Phoenix down five.

Devin Booker led Phoenix with 26 points on 8-of-18 shooting, 2-of-4 from three and 8-of-8 at the line, with 5 assists in 34:58 before fouling out.

Miles Bridges added 21 points on 7-of-14 shooting, 3-of-5 from three, with 6 rebounds and 4 steals. Dillon Brooks scored 18 on 5-of-8 shooting with 8 rebounds and 4 assists. Oso Ighodaro was perfect at 6-of-6 for 14 points off the bench, and Jalen Green filled it up with 11 points, 8 rebounds and 8 assists. Luke Kennard finished +15 in 17:42.

Stephen Curry led all scorers with 34 points on 9-of-21 shooting, 5-of-13 from three and 11-of-12 at the line, with 7 assists and 6 rebounds. Brandin Podziemski added 20, Charles Bassey had 19 points and 8 rebounds off the bench, and Yaxel Lendeborg scored 16 with 8-of-9 at the line.

The Suns opened with Devin Booker, Dillon Brooks, Jalen Green, Miles Bridges, and Man Man, and the defense set the tone right away. Golden State's starting five went a combined 3-of-14 from the floor for 8 points.

The Warriors lived behind the arc and paid for it. Golden State went 2-of-15 from three, including Stephen Curry at 1-of-4, while Phoenix hit 2 of its 5 attempts. The Suns shot 60% overall (12-of-20) and turned Warriors mistakes into 9 points off turnovers and 8 fast-break points, compared to 3 and 2 for Golden State.

The bench kept the pressure on. Oso Ighodaro went a perfect 3-of-3 from the field and 2-of-2 at the line for 8 points, the most of anyone on the floor. Phoenix closed the quarter with Bridges, Luke Kennard, Jordan Goodwin, Collin Gillespie and Ighodaro, and Kennard posted a +9 in under four minutes without scoring.

The only area Golden State matched Phoenix was inside, where both teams scored 20 points in the paint. Charles Bassey led the Warriors with 7 points off the bench, and the Warriors won second-chance points 6-5. Booker led the Suns at +10 with 5 points and 2 assists, and Brooks added 5 points on perfect shooting.

Phoenix led after the first quarter, 31-19. A drastic first quarter improvement defensively from the opening 4 games.

After a 2-of-15 first quarter, the Warriors went 5-of-9 from three in the second and shot 50% overall (10-of-20). Yaxel Lendeborg hit both of his threes for 8 points in the quarter, and Brandin Podziemski added 6 on a pair of triples.

The Suns lost their grip on the paint. After winning the paint 16-12 in the first, Phoenix went 2-of-8 inside in the second for 4 points while Golden State scored 10 there. The Warriors also won the quarter on the boards 11-5.

Devin Booker kept Phoenix ahead. He scored 11 in the quarter on 3-of-4 shooting and a perfect 4-of-4 at the line, and the Suns went 8-of-8 at the stripe as a team. Luke Kennard knocked down two threes for 6 points off the bench, and Miles Bridges chipped in 7.

The Suns pushed the lead to 16 at 55-39 with 3:45 left in the half. Then the offense stalled. Golden State ripped off a 12-0 run over the next 2:42, cutting it to 55-51 at the 1:03 mark.

Golden State won the second quarter 32-26.

Phoenix led 57-51 at the break. Booker paced the Suns with 16 points on 5-of-8 shooting and 5-of-5 at the line. Bridges added 11 points and 5 rebounds, and Jalen Green posted a team-best +10 with four boards.

There was a huge blow to start the second half, as the Suns announced Jordan Goodwin would not return due to a calf injury.

As you'd expect, Dillon Brooks and Draymond Green got into it.

Draymond threw Khaman Maluach to the ground to start the altercation, and Dillon Brooks went to pull him back from heading towards Khaman who was on the ground. Green grabbed Brooks by his neck before the situation de-escalated.

Green was assessed a double technical and ejected, and Brooks received a technical.

Green played just two minutes in the third before his exit. He finished with 4 points on 1-of-2 shooting, 4 rebounds and 2 assists in 16:46.

Losing Green didn't slow Golden State. Quite the opposite, actually. Phoenix did not have an answer for Charles Bassey, who had 6 points and 4 boards off the bench in the quarter. Stephen Curry took over with 18 points in the quarter on 6-of-9 shooting and 4-of-5 from three. Brandin Podziemski added 10, and the Warriors shot 59.1% in the period.

The free-throw line flipped on Phoenix. After going 13-of-14 in the first half, the Suns went 6-of-12 in the third. Jalen Green missed all four of his attempts.

Brooks kept the Suns afloat with 9 points on 3-of-3 shooting, and Man Man went 2-of-2 for 5 points. Jalen Green dished 5 assists in the quarter. Devin Booker scored 8 but went 2-of-7 and picked up four fouls in the period.

Tied at 93, the fourth turned into a grind. Golden State made just 5 field goals in the quarter on 5-of-17 shooting, and Stephen Curry went 1-of-5. It didn't matter. The Warriors lived at the line, going 12-of-13 in the period while Phoenix went 3-of-4.

The Suns won the glass 13-8 and grabbed five offensive rebounds, but gave it right back with seven turnovers. Jalen Green battled for 7 points and 4 rebounds, three of them offensive, but had three of those turnovers. Phoenix went 1-of-7 from three in the quarter.

Booker fouled out on a flop from De'Anthony Melton, called for an offensive foul with under a minute left and Phoenix down 113-108. He finished with 26 points on 8-of-18 shooting, 8-of-8 at the line and 5 assists, but managed just 2 points on 1-of-3 shooting in the fourth.

Golden State won the fourth quarter 23-20 and the game 116-113.

The Suns will host the Blazers team that destroyed them on Opening Night on Wednesday in Downtown Phoenix.

#3058. Energy Transfer Just Delivered a Monster Quarter. Is Its High-Yielding Stock a Buy?

Energy Transfer delivered a monster quarter, boosting its earnings outlook while generating ample cash flow to support its high-yielding distribution. Here's whether its growth prospects make the MLP a buy.

Energy Transfer (ET -0.76%) delivered a monster third quarter. The energy midstream giant grew its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) by more than 30%, boosted its full-year outlook by $850 million, and generated enough cash flow to cover its high-yielding distribution more than twice. Meanwhile, the pipeline operator plans to invest even more money next year in infrastructure projects to capitalize on rising energy demand.

With its growth engine firing on multiple cylinders, is the 6.7%-yielding pipeline stock a buy?

Energy Transfer isn't your typical slow-growing master limited partnership (MLP). The energy infrastructure giant reported $5 billion of adjusted EBITDA for the quarter, a massive 31% increase compared to the prior-year period. Meanwhile, distributable cash flow surged 33% to $2.5 billion.

Three catalysts fueled the strong quarter:

The company had several positives come together in a single quarter, as strong market conditions, recently completed expansion projects, and acquisitions all combined to fuel a monster quarter.

Energy Transfer also increased its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance yet again. It now expects to deliver $19.7 billion–$19.9 billion in adjusted EBITDA this year. That's an $850 million increase (or about 4.5%) at the midpoint from its previous range of $18.8 billion–$19.1 billion. It's the third straight quarterly guidance increase. The company initially expected to deliver $17.3 billion to $17.7 billion of adjusted EBITDA. It now expects to deliver about 24% adjusted EBITDA growth this year.

That's not all organic growth. Sunoco's acquisition of Parkland and USA Compression's purchase of J-W Power have meaningfully boosted its share of income from these affiliated MLPs. However, Energy Transfer also benefited from robust market conditions, particularly higher export volumes driven by Middle East supply disruptions. It also completed Hugh Brinson ahead of schedule.

While Energy Transfer boosted its full-year earnings outlook, it lowered its 2026 growth capital spending range. The MLP now expects to invest between $5.4 billion and $5.6 billion this year. While that's down from its prior range of $5.6 billion-$5.9 billion, it's still at the very top of its initial capital spending guidance range ($5 billion-$5.5 billion).

However, investors shouldn't read that as a growth slowdown. Energy Transfer provided its initial outlook for 2027 growth capital spending, which it expects will increase to around $7 billion. That's due in part to the recent approval of the 215-mile Mississippi Pipeline Project. The company expects the project to cost $1.6 billion and to fund 51% of that cost. It's one of several new projects it has added to the backlog, adding to an already extensive list of growth capital projects that also includes the up to $5.6 billion Desert Southwest expansion project.

Energy Transfer also recently announced an acquisition of its own, agreeing to buy Vaquero Midstream for $2.6 billion. The company expects the acquisition to close in the fourth quarter. It will bolster its position in the Delaware Basin and should be immediately accretive to its per-unit distributable cash flow.

Energy Transfer has generated $7.8 billion of distributable cash flow through the first nine months of this year. That has covered its 6.7%-yielding payout by a very comfortable 2.2 times. This high-yielding payout provides a meaningful foundation for long-term total returns.

The MLP only needs to grow its distributable cash flow per unit by around 3% annually to deliver a double-digit total annual return, assuming no change in its valuation multiple. That seems very reasonable, considering its low valuation (around seven times trailing 12-month distributable cash flow) and all the growth it has coming down the pipeline. It has delivered a more than 20% increase in distributable cash flow per share over the last 12 months. While acquisitions and strong market conditions certainly enhanced growth over the past year, Energy Transfer recently secured an accretive acquisition and has several high-return growth capital projects in the backlog. That puts it in a strong position to continue growing its per-unit cash flow.

While there are risks, including cost and execution risks for its expansion projects and integration risk with Vaquero, the MLP looks like a buy for investors seeking income and solid total return potential. That assumes you're comfortable receiving the Schedule K-1 Federal Tax form the MLP sends investors each year.

#3056. Curry explodes after halftime to lead Warriors to 5th straight win

SAN FRANCISCO — The Warriors didn't have Steph Curry or Draymond Green when they visited the Suns on the second half of a back-to-back last weekend.

Hosting the Suns, again coming off a game the previous night, Golden State set things up to make sure its two veteran stars would be available for the rematch.

The training staff's best efforts ended up for naught.

After sitting out Sunday's win over the Clippers, Green spent most of the second half Monday night in the locker room. Green was ejected two minutes into the second half.

And that was precisely when the game turned for the Warriors, who pulled out a 116-113 win after falling behind by as many as 17 points and not holding a lead until the fourth quarter.

Golden State Warriors' Brandin Podziemski, left, and Stephen Curry celebrate during the first half of an NBA basketball game in San Francisco, Nov. 2, 2026. AP Photo/Jed Jacobsohn

The Warriors have won five straight since their 131-122 loss in Phoenix last Saturday.

When Green was tossed from the game, Golden State trailed 68-57. Immediately after play resumed, the Warriors' energy changed and they went on a 16-5 run to tie the score at 73.

Curry didn't exactly seem freshly rested as he struggled for nine points in the first half. But he exploded for 25 after halftime to lead the Warriors, finishing with 34.

After going off for 37 points without Curry the previous night and leading the Warriors with 26 the last time they faced Phoenix, Yaxel Lendeborg was contained to 16 on 3-of-10 shooting.

Stephen Curry of the Golden State Warriors shoots against the Phoenix Suns in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

But the Warriors didn't shy away from running their offense from the rookie with Curry off the floor, and his eight second-half free throws on nine attempts kept the Suns at bay.

With 44 and 31 his past two games, Curry notched the 25th streak of his career of three straight games with 30 or more in the scoring column. In six games this season, Curry has scored at least 20 in all of them, averaging 30.0, trailing only Anthony Edwards and Luka Doncic.

With Devin Booker pouring in 26 to lead the Suns and Mikal Bridges adding 21, Curry couldn't do it by himself. He got an unlikely assist in the form of center Charles Bassey, who picked up many of Green's second-half minutes to finish with a career-best 19 on 7-of-10 shooting.

Charles Bassey (28) of the Golden State Warriors drives to the basket against the Phoenix Suns at Chase Center in San Francisco on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Brandin Podziemski also contributed 20 points, including 14 after halftime. He tied the game at 93 on the Warriors' final possession of the third quarter on a kickout from Lendeborg.

A cutting Bassey converted one of Curry's team-high seven assists on the Warriors' first possession of the fourth quarter that gave them their first lead of the game, 95-93, and the margin never got wider than seven in either direction the rest of the way.

The Warriors followed in Curry's footsteps in the first half, knocking down just two of their first 17 attempts from 3. But the ball started falling for Curry and his teammates after halftime.

Golden State drained 11 of its final 25 attempts from 3, including five from Curry.

#3053. What Would Warren Buffett Do With Nike Stock Down 38% in 2026?

Whether or not you will conclude it's time to move on from the athletic apparel giant will depend on how much time you're willing to give its turnaround plan to pay off.

Nike's (NKE -1.96%) guidance for fiscal 2027 suggests things could get worse before they get better. The iconic athletic apparel company expects its sales to decline by a high-single-digit percentage, and there don't appear to be many catalysts on the horizon that could reverse the stock price's decline. As of this writing, the stock has fallen by 38% in 2026.

In times like these, it can be beneficial for a shareholder to take a step back and channel their inner Warren Buffett. He often offered valuable insights to retail investors, and there's one specific piece of his wisdom that Nike shareholders may want to consider as they weigh their next moves.

Buffett is known for making time an ally, preferring a buy-and-hold investing style. He's not quick to sell stocks, but one of his best investing lessons put him in a position throughout his career where he didn't have to make knee-jerk reactions during turbulent times.

"If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes," Buffett wrote in Berkshire Hathaway's 1996 shareholder letter.

For anyone who invested in Nike hoping for a quick turnaround, it hasn't materialized. And as more challenges lie ahead, this may be an ideal time for investors to evaluate their conviction in the stock.

If you don't believe the stock price can recover, or if you believe Nike management has had enough time to turn the business around, there's nothing wrong with considering whether it still belongs in your portfolio. Proceeds from selling Nike shares may be better used in a higher-conviction position.

On the flip side of that quote, those who believe brighter days are ahead for the company can give CEO Elliott Hill more time to revitalize the brand and, in turn, improve sales and profits. While Nike is becoming a more mature company and may not return to the days of 96% sales growth in a quarter (which it delivered in the fourth quarter of 2021), its sales can still stabilize, and renewed investor enthusiasm could provide some fuel for the stock price. Shareholders will also be rewarded with a dividend that yields 4.1% at the current stock price while they wait for the company's turnaround to show more signs of progress.

#3052. How CISOs Can Set Guardrails On AI Agents Without Killing Adoption

Nidhi Jain is CEO & Founder of CloudEagle.ai, an AI governance platform that secures AI agents, machine identities, and SaaS access.

In July 2026, the U.K.’s AI Security Institute disclosed that AI agents under evaluation had taken sustained, unsanctioned action against real people and organizations. In the most serious case, an agent researched the maintainers of a public open-source project on GitHub, created multiple fake identities and attempted to socially engineer a maintainer into approving a malicious pull request. The maintainer rejected the code. AISI detected unusual network traffic on July 28 and contained the incident within an hour of the alert.

Many enterprises deploying Salesforce Agentforce, Microsoft Copilot Studio, ServiceNow Now Assist, Google Vertex AI Agents and AWS Bedrock lack these safeguards.

Gartner predicts that 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. The Cloud Security Alliance found that 65% of enterprises have already experienced an AI agent-related security incident, and 82% have unknown AI agents running in their environment.

Blocking is not the answer. The question is what guardrails let adoption and security coexist.​

In almost every conversation I have with a CISO rolling out agents, the same assumption shows up: Governance is a Phase 2 problem. Deploy first; govern later. The CSA data shows what Phase 2 actually looks like.

AI agents break traditional access models in three ways:

• They inherit the deploying user’s permissions instead of their own scoped identity. A Salesforce Agentforce agent built by a sales ops lead inherits the sales ops lead’s full access. The agent runs with permissions it never needed.

• They act across systems through delegated OAuth. A ServiceNow Now Assist agent connected to Jira, Confluence and Slack holds OAuth tokens to all three. One compromise reaches four systems.

• They persist beyond the use case. CSA reported that only 21% of enterprises have formal decommissioning processes for AI agents. Most keep running long after the use case ends, with credentials still valid.​

Most CISOs I speak with are being asked to approve agents already in late-stage pilots. The checklist below is designed around one principle: Friction scales with risk.

Low-risk actions get no friction. High-risk actions get human review. The business keeps its speed; security keeps control over actions that matter:

1. Require a scoped-access review for every agent before deployment. The agent gets its own identity, scoped to the specific task. Microsoft Copilot Studio and Salesforce Agentforce both support agent-level identities, but most teams default to user inheritance.

2. Define human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-risk actions. Reading data: no checkpoint. Writing to a record of truth, moving money, sending an external communication or modifying production configurations: human approval before execution. This is a policy decision, not a technical one.

3. Mandate audit logging at the action level, not the prompt level. Prompt logs show what the user asked. Action logs show what the agent did across every system it touched. For AWS Bedrock Agents, Google Vertex AI and Anthropic Claude agents, action-level logging has to be configured at deployment, not retrofitted.

4. Set an expiration date for every agent. If the agent is still useful in six months, renew it with a fresh access review. If not, decommission. This single control closes the retirement debt CSA flagged.​

If agents are already live, discovery comes first:

1. Pull an inventory from every agent platform in use. Microsoft Copilot Studio, Salesforce Agentforce, ServiceNow Now Assist, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and any custom LangChain or CrewAI deployments. Admin consoles expose this; most security teams have not pulled the reports.

2. Cross-reference OAuth grants with agent identities. Grants to unfamiliar app IDs, especially those tied to AI model providers, are candidates for review.

3. Classify agents by action risk. An agent that reads Jira tickets is a different control problem than an agent that posts to customers or writes to the general ledger.

4. Revoke access for orphaned agents. When the builder leaves, the agent does not. If no human owner can be named, the agent is orphaned, and orphaned agents are retired.​

​There are three common objections when starting this work. The first is that guardrails will slow business adoption. They do not have to if they are designed around the risk of each action: Read-only agents can operate at full speed, while agents that write back to systems require approval. This preserves productivity across most use cases.

The second objection is that organizations cannot audit activity they cannot see. Yet the admin consoles for Microsoft, Salesforce, ServiceNow, AWS and Google already expose agent activity. In many cases, organizations simply have not enabled the relevant logs.

The third is that no one owns agent governance. Responsibility often falls between security, IT, legal and the business function that deployed the agent. Organizations making the most progress assign a cross-functional AI governance lead who reports to the CISO.​

The agent platforms have shipped faster than their security defaults can keep up.

Vendors should ship agents with least-privilege defaults, not broad inheritance. Action-level audit logging should be on by default. Decommissioning workflows should exist natively in every agent platform. Although frameworks such as the OWASP Agentic AI Top 10 and NIST AI RMF offer useful guidance, they stop short of making agent governance a core security requirement rather than an operational consideration.​​

The next AI agent incident will not look like a misconfiguration. It will look like an agent executing exactly what it was permitted to do, using credentials it inherited, with no human in the loop to catch the error.

Guardrails and adoption are not in opposition. The companies that figure out the balance now will be the ones setting the pace on AI agents in two years. The ones treating it as a trade-off will spend those two years explaining incidents instead of shipping agents.​

#3048. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3046. We Feel It Too, but Most Stocks Actually Held Up

Monday's selling stayed mostly in tech and energy, while eight of 11 sectors rose. Today's midterms are another reason to keep a long view.

The Nasdaq Composite fell about 1% on Monday. That followed Friday's drop and a rough October. If you own AI-linked tech stocks, it may have felt like more of the same. We invest our own savings and retirement money right alongside yours.

But across the S&P 500's large-, mid-, and small-cap indexes, more than twice as many stocks rose as fell. So far, the selling has hit one corner of the market.

In his October Quarterly Call, Motley Fool co-founder and CEO Tom Gardner pushed back on the idea that big, sudden moves show the most conviction. "I would argue that the best form of conviction is the step-by-step incremental moves where you have to rethink your thesis as you buy a stock or rethink your reasons for selling a stock in your portfolio," he said. That takes discipline when prices swing. Below, we share two habits that can help. But first, a reminder...

Monday's tech selling had familiar roots. Oracle (ORCL +6.00%) fell almost 9% after filing to raise $20 billion in stock and debt for its AI build-out. Marvell Technology (MRVL -0.10%) agreed to buy Lumentum (LITE -1.00%) in a $115 billion all-stock deal. Marvell shares dropped about 13%, and Lumentum fell nearly 19%. Both moves revived last week's doubts about whether all that AI spending will pay for itself.

The Nasdaq-100 fell 1.4%, and the technology sector lost nearly 3%. Energy fell about 4% as oil dropped more than 7% on signs of U.S.-Iran diplomacy.

Almost everywhere else, the day looked good. The Dow rose 0.4%, and eight of the 11 S&P 500 sectors gained. Only three fell: energy, technology, and healthcare, which slipped just 0.15%. Across the S&P 500, MidCap 400, SmallCap 600, and Nasdaq-100, 1,027 stocks rose, while 473 fell.

The regular S&P 500, which gives the biggest companies the most weight, fell 0.5%. An equal-weight version, which counts each company the same, rose 0.8%. So the typical company had a good day, and a handful of giants dragged the headline number down.

As we noted Friday, 10 companies make up 39% of the S&P 500's value. Their moves can swamp what the other 490 are doing.

Tech's pullback may not be over. But if you own a diversified portfolio, most of your stocks probably had a perfectly fine Monday. When you own businesses across many industries, gains in some can offset a rough day in others, as they did on Monday. When we launched our 50-stock Epic Portfolio in April, TMF Chief Investment Officer Andy Cross put it this way: "Fifty stocks provide a massive buffer against volatility."

Whatever your politics, you may feel tempted to trade on today's midterm results. History says it's rarely worth it.

In October, The Motley Fool studied every midterm election since 1874. The S&P 500 rose in the 12 months after 32 of 38 midterms. Its average total return in those years was 14%, versus 11% for any 12-month stretch.

Who won didn't matter much, either. Returns had little link to how many seats the president's party lost or which party ran Washington afterward. The few bad years had other causes, such as the Panic of 1907 and the Great Depression.

Averages aren't promises, of course. The month after a midterm has often been quiet. And 2026 brings its own worries: AI spending, high valuations, and a possible Fed rate hike.

None of this means stocks will rise because of the election. Over time, the businesses you own have mattered far more than who won. Leave portfolio decisions for a calmer day.

Friday's article covered buying in thirds, owning at least 50 stocks, sleep numbers, and cash. Here are two more ideas from our recent report, AI Concentration Calls for Cash and Calm.

Monday's selling was about financing. That makes this a good week to check whether your companies can pay their own way.

In our October Stock Advisor recommendation reveal, Team Rule Breakers' Toby Bordelon suggested four questions to ask any business. They matter most for smaller companies that rely on outside financing:

Then imagine the AI trend cools, and ask, "What else do you have beyond AI that you can keep going?" For some companies, Toby warned, "the idea of them dying actually is something you need to consider."

Heavy spending isn't always a red flag. A giant with little debt can keep it up far longer than a smaller company that borrows. If your holdings pass these questions, a falling share price is much less worrying.

When part of your portfolio is down, it's natural to buy more of the losers. TMF co-founder David Gardner calls that "throwing good money after bad." His alternative is the second habit of a Rule Breaker investor: "add up, don't double down" and put new savings into the businesses already proving you right.

"Most of our returns are probably gonna come from a few companies," Toby said. "And when we find those, let 'em [run]."

A falling stock can still be a good buy, but let the business make the case. Before adding to any position, ask whether the company is still delivering on the reasons you bought it.

The headlines have been red for several days now, but most businesses kept doing what they do. Before the week is out, try running your largest holdings through Toby's four questions. The answers will tell you far more about those companies than a day's stock price.

#3044. AI Is Making The App Optional

Haz Hubble is the Co-Founder and CEO at Pally (YC S25).

When I started building Pally, an AI assistant that keeps people on top of their messages, I assumed it needed its own app. We built one, with onboarding, settings and a home feed. Fewer than 20% of new users were still active in their second month.

We removed the app and moved the product into iMessage. Users now sign up by texting a number. With the same AI underneath, month-two retention rose to over 70%. That result made me question how much of consumer software exists only to support the app around it.

Every app asks people to do work before they get anything back. They have to find it, install it, create an account, learn where things are and remember that it exists. Some share of users gives up at each step.

The phone they’re installing it on is already crowded. The average user has more than 80 apps, and about 62% of them go unused in a given month. In the U.S., people spend around 80% of their app time in their three most-used apps. A new app is asking for a place that most people have stopped giving out.

The first is new hardware. OpenAI has said it will show its first consumer device, a screenless product designed with Jony Ive, in the second half of 2026. The last well-funded attempt, Humane’s AI Pin, failed. A common explanation is that it asked people to change their habits without giving them enough reason to.

The second is the super-app. WeChat hosts more than 4.3 million mini-programs, and roughly 764 million people used them each day in 2025. People in China order food and pay bills through services they never downloaded, because those services sit inside an app they already open all day. The model depends on one company controlling the platform, which is part of why nothing comparable exists in the U.S.

The third is putting AI inside the messaging apps people already use, such as iMessage, SMS, WhatsApp and email. Language models make this practical because a conversation can now do the job that buttons and menus used to do. The assistant can also message first, so users don’t have to remember to open anything. Of the three approaches, this is the only one that doesn’t ask people to form a new habit.

Satya Nadella made a version of this argument about business software in December 2024. He said, “The notion that business applications exist will probably collapse” as AI agents take on more work. He reasoned that most apps are databases with rules on top, and agents can apply those rules on a user’s behalf.

The same reasoning applies to consumer products. When an assistant can read your messages, check your calendar and act on a request written in plain English, many of an app’s screens become optional. Messaging is where this shows up first, because it’s where people already spend their attention.

Building inside another company’s messaging app means that company can shut you out. Meta did exactly that in January 2026, when WhatsApp stopped allowing general-purpose AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity on its business platform. After EU regulators intervened, Meta restored access in the European Economic Area in July. As of late July, the ban had not been lifted in the U.S.

Apple’s position is different. In June 2025, a federal judge refused to dismiss the Justice Department’s antitrust case against Apple, and the allegations the court let stand include restrictions on iMessage and on super-apps. Apple has reportedly made several settlement offers to the DOJ this year. While that case is open, blocking third-party assistants from iMessage would hand regulators a fresh example of the conduct they’re already suing over.

That doesn’t resolve the risk. Apple could still change its rules, and no messaging platform has made a lasting commitment to AI developers. Anyone building this way should plan for losing a channel.

1. Within five years, most consumer apps will work mainly as back-ends. Their data and logic will still matter, but people will reach them through an assistant instead of opening them.

2. A phone number will replace the App Store listing as the way many people first try a new product.

3. Screens will be generated when a task needs one, such as signing a contract or reading a chart, and will close when the task is done.

4. Consumer products will be judged by completed tasks. Time spent in an app will start to look like a cost to the user.

5. Regulators will treat AI access to messaging platforms the way they treated browser choice and app store rules, and at least one major platform will be required to open up to third-party assistants in the U.S.

If you’re building a consumer product today, make three changes.

• Track how long a new user takes to get value, counted in messages rather than screens. If the first exchange doesn’t help them, fix that before anything else.

• Build the version with no interface first. Add screens only where text doesn’t work, such as payments or reviewing long documents.

• Keep your data and logic on your own infrastructure, so you can move between iMessage, SMS, WhatsApp and email if a platform changes its rules.

For Pally, this means treating iMessage as our first channel, not our only one. We keep the product’s logic on our own infrastructure so it can run over SMS, WhatsApp or email if Apple’s rules change. We add a screen only when a user can’t finish a task in text, and every new feature has to work without asking anyone to open something new.

#3042. Rivian Raised Guidance to 67,000-70,000 Deliveries. Here's the Q4 Number the R2 Ramp Must Hit -- and What the Stock Does if It Doesn't.

The EV maker's newest vehicle could bring back the bulls.

Rivian (RIVN +1.14%) posted its third-quarter earnings on Oct. 29. Its revenue grew 38% year over year to $2.16 billion, beating analysts' estimates by $160 million. It narrowed its adjusted net loss to $0.48 per share from $0.65, beating the consensus estimate by $0.17.

Rivian's total deliveries rose 46% year over year to a record 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter, boosting its year-to-date deliveries to 41,804 vehicles. It also raised its full-year delivery guidance from 65,000-70,000 vehicles to 67,000-70,000 vehicles.

That means it will need to deliver roughly 25,000 to 28,000 vehicles in the fourth quarter. Let's see how Rivian plans to hit that target --- and what will happen to its stock if it misses.

When Rivian went public in late 2021, it only produced three electric vehicles: the R1T pickup, R1S SUV, and custom electric delivery vans (EDVs) for Amazon (AMZN +2.26%). It began producing EDVs for other customers after ending its exclusivity agreement with Amazon in 2023, and it launched its third consumer vehicle, the R2 SUV, in June 2026.

Rivian's deliveries surged in 2023, but declined over the following two years as it grappled with supply chain constraints, rising costs, and intense competition. To stabilize its business, Rivian unveiled the R2 -- an SUV that would cost $30,000-$40,000 less than the R1 and R1S -- to expand its total addressable market and widen its moat. Even though the R2 had a lower price tag, it could be sold at higher margins than the R1T and R1S because it used fewer electronic control units, had simpler wiring, larger castings, and an upgraded battery.

Rivian hasn't disclosed its exact number of R2 deliveries yet, but its founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said the R2 was its "best-selling vehicle by volume in the third quarter." Most analysts believe Rivian has delivered at least 10,000 R2s since its launch in June.

As of this writing, Rivian is only delivering its top-tier R2 Performance (Launch Package) vehicle, which starts at $57,990. It plans to launch the cheaper R2 Premium AWD for $53,990 in late 2026 or early 2027, followed by the R2 Standard RWD (Long Range) for $48,490 in early 2027, and the R2 Standard (Base) for $45,000 in late 2027.

That would make the R2 a direct competitor for Tesla's (TSLA -1.14%) Model Y, which costs between $44,990 (Long Range RWD) and $54,990 (Performance AWD). The persistent public backlash against Elon Musk over his political views could drive more new drivers and former Tesla owners to Rivian as it finally rolls out more affordable EVs.

Rivian is counting on the R2 to drive its annual deliveries to 67,000-70,000, but two challenges could prevent it from achieving that goal. First, persistent inflation and rising interest rates could throttle its sales of new EVs. Second, some of Rivian's potential customers could be waiting for its cheaper trims to hit the market next year.

At $13 per share, Rivian already trades 83% below its IPO price of $78. With an enterprise value of $20.5 billion, it trades at less than three times this year's sales. Tesla, with an enterprise value of $1.56 trillion, trades at 14.5 times this year's sales.

That low valuation should limit Rivian's downside potential, even if it fails to deliver more than 25,000 vehicles in the fourth quarter. But if it hits or beats that target, its stock could skyrocket as it's revalued as a high-growth EV stock again.

#3039. AI Pods Are Redefining The Unit Of Software Delivery

Alexey Spas is the founder and CEO of Instinctools, a software engineering company focused on AI-powered digital solutions.

For most of the software industry’s history, when a software backlog started growing faster than the team could handle it, a CTO or product leader knew what came next. It was either opening new roles or sending some work to an outside partner.

Whichever the option, the rule of thumb used to be the same: More software to build meant more people needed to build it, until AI put that long-held assumption into question.

A senior engineer working with coding agents can now produce far more raw output than before. That is why software delivery is beginning to reorganize around a different unit: a small senior team surrounded by AI-enabled workflows.

The label is still loose, but the operating idea is easy to picture: An AI pod is a compact, senior-led engineering team accountable for a defined software outcome. Specialized AI agents support the delivery flow from requirements drafting to code generation and testing, while humans keep their hands on the wheel when it comes to business context, quality, security and the final result.​​

And just like that, AI has completely reshuffled the deck for software engineering. An age-old dilemma is now taking on new contours: If companies need a different kind of delivery unit, where should it live? Some organizations will have good reasons to build it in-house. Others may prefer to bring in an external pod. For many, the most practical answer may sit somewhere in between.​

A big part of the appeal of an in-house AI pod is its lean structure, and it’s not hard to see why: Hiring one or two senior engineers supported by AI agents is a very different proposition from building a cross-functional team of five-plus people.

The strongest case for keeping the pod internal, though, may have less to do with headcount than with proximity of in-house engineers to the product, business context and the decisions. Moreover, the lessons learned while building AI-enabled delivery workflows remain inside the organization.

That advantage takes time to build. Giving experienced developers access to coding agents does not immediately produce an effective AI delivery system. Teams still have to determine what can safely be delegated, where human review belongs, which quality gates can be automated and how AI-generated work fits into the rest of the software lifecycle.

There is also the expertise question. A small pod can still draw on a broad range of skills. A modernization effort can suddenly require security input, an AI-heavy feature may call for data engineering or a customer-facing workflow may need experienced UX support. Building all of those competencies internally makes sense when the demand is sustained. It is harder to justify when the need appears for only a few weeks.​

There is no secret AI stack tool available only to software vendors. Anyone can access the same models, coding assistants and agentic frameworks. The advantage of an external pod usually comes from reducing the distance between access to AI and a delivery system that works.

If spinning up a few agents could solve the software delivery problem overnight, things would be simple. In practice, faster generation creates its own downstream load: More code has to be reviewed, tested, integrated and checked for security. The challenge is turning that AI-driven speed into production-ready software.

An outsourced team that has already cut its teeth on different projects can bring patterns refined across more than one production environment: agent configurations, evaluation methods, review workflows, reusable components and quality controls. I know—there’s a lot of skepticism when software development vendors talk about their “unique expertise.” But in this case, uniqueness does not mean exclusive knowledge that nobody else can acquire. It just implies a shorter route through mistakes someone else has already made and experience that has been tested often enough to become adaptable.

There is also a flip side to that breadth of experience. An external pod does not begin with the same institutional knowledge as an internal team, nor is it naturally as close to every product decision. The model makes the most sense when the value of faster ramp-up, cross-project experience or temporary capacity outweighs the benefits of having a team deeply embedded in the product.​

When a company needs AI-enabled delivery capability now but is not yet certain how much of it should become a fixed part of the organization, a hybrid model can be considered. Demand may surge around a product launch, modernization program or backlog push, and then ease again. An external pod can take the edge off this sudden spike without turning peak capacity into permanent headcount.

The same arrangement can also serve a longer-term purpose. A company that ultimately wants the capability in-house can use an outsourced pod as a working prototype for the team it may later build itself.

A “borrow, prove, then build” approach gives leaders a chance to observe which roles they repeatedly need, which workflows survive production, where human judgment remains essential and which metrics genuinely improve. The parts that prove strategic can then move inside the organization with much less guesswork.​

AI pods are making the old build-versus-buy decision more nuanced. For leaders, the choice comes down to a few practical questions: How enduring is the demand? How important is institutional knowledge? How quickly should the capability become operational?

The answers may change as the organization learns. That is probably the main point. AI is reshaping software delivery quickly enough that the operating model that fits today does not have to be the one a company commits to for good.​​

#3035. Alibaba Group Holding vs. Dick's Sporting Goods: Revenue Trends Between Online and Brick-and-Mortar Giants

While Alibaba maintains a much larger absolute revenue base, Dick's Sporting Goods has posted stronger year-over-year growth in recent quarters.

Alibaba Group Holding (BABA -1.04%) primarily generates revenue by operating extensive digital commerce marketplaces and providing cloud computing infrastructure.

It introduced new processors and detailed long-term artificial intelligence development plans at an annual technology conference, while it faced a securities fraud class action lawsuit regarding past disclosures.

Dick's Sporting Goods (DKS -3.82%) primarily operates omnichannel retail stores selling athletic apparel, specialty footwear, and outdoor sports equipment.

It announced plans to hire thousands of seasonal employees for the upcoming holiday period, and its executives faced a securities class action lawsuit over earlier statements about inventory health.

Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item, and it shows the top-line money generated before any business expenses are deducted.

Alibaba Group Holding vs. Dick's Sporting Goods Revenue over the last 8 quarters. Figures: Alibaba Group Holding shown in U.S. dollars, converted from Chinese yuan.

Normally, the first thing to note when examining a company's revenue trend is seasonality: some times of the year have stronger buying patterns than others. For most stocks, compare revenue year over year, by quarter. Retailers generally are known for having strong seasonality. This especially comes in the fourth quarter for U.S. retailers and in the fourth quarter and early weeks of the first quarter for Asia retailers.

Dick's Sporting Goods also should show some seasonality around summertime, when ball sports and camping are of high interest to consumers. Alibaba similarly has seasonality in the same periods, due to various holidays and events in the fourth quarter, like Singles' Day, and China's 618 shopping festival that occurs in June.

Understanding seasonality makes the trend of both retailers here less volatile than the chart shows. Both are showing year-over-year growth in comparable quarters--so Dick's first quarter 2026 shows revenue growth from the first quarter 2025. Similarly, Alibaba's fourth quarter shows a very slight rise on the graph. It is worth noting that the conversion of Alibaba's reporting currency of yuan to U.S. dollars could exacerbate or de-emphasize growth and seasonality for the company based on the trend of exchange rates (although China largely keeps its currency in lockstep with the U.S. dollar for various reasons).

In Alibaba's case, the company is making a significant effort to move further into AI services, which would mean less reliance on retail goods sales. In the future, it's possible the company could have far less seasonality--at least until seasonality is discovered in the AI business.

Revenue is perhaps the simplest metric investors have to judge a business by. As the chart shows, look for rising revenue, especially over similar periods of each year, and take comparable-quarter stagnation, or worse, declines, as a red flag.

Data source: Financial Modeling Prep. Alibaba Group Holding's figures are converted from Chinese yuan to U.S. dollars. Data as of Nov. 2, 2026.
